luke|23.claim: The repentant thief was saved without baptism, without good works and without the Church. So, it is argued, baptism and works are not needed: a moment of faith is enough, and anything more is human addition.
why: The thief died before the new covenant sacraments were given. Jesus commanded baptism after his resurrection (Matthew 28:19), and the Church received the Spirit at Pentecost. You cannot be bound by a command that has not yet been given.

The Church has never taught that God is bound to the sacraments. She teaches that we are bound to them. Someone who desires baptism but dies before receiving it can be saved by that desire joined to repentance and charity (CCC 1258–1260). The thief is a model of exactly that.

He was not saved by a bare mental assent. In his last hour he did everything he still could: he confessed his guilt ("we receive the due reward of our deeds"), defended Christ publicly, rebuked the other thief, and prayed. That is faith working through love (Galatians 5:6), which is what Catholics mean by saving faith.

An exception does not cancel the normal rule. A man rescued from a shipwreck without a boat does not prove that boats are unnecessary. The normal way Christ appointed is faith and baptism (Mark 16:16; John 3:5; Acts 2:38).

Some also use "this day you will be in paradise" against purgatory. But "paradise" here is the rest of the just who awaited Christ, the place he descended to after his death (1 Peter 3:19; CCC 633). The thief's suffering, accepted with contrition beside Christ, is itself a powerful purification.
luke|23.cath: The thief shows God's generosity to a sinner who repents at the very end. It is a reason never to despair, not a pattern for skipping what Christ commanded.

deep.ctx:
Luke alone records the conversation between Jesus and the two criminals crucified with him (23:39–43). One mocks him: “If thou be Christ, save thyself and us.” The other rebukes him: “Neither dost thou fear God, seeing thou art under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly: for we receive the due reward of our deeds. But this man hath done no evil.” Then he prays: “Lord, remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom.” Jesus answers: “Amen I say to thee, this day thou shalt be with me in paradise.”

The scene sits inside Luke’s great theme of mercy to sinners (the lost sheep, the prodigal son, Zacchaeus) and comes at the moment when Christ is offering his sacrifice. The thief’s salvation is the first fruit of the Cross.
deep.who:
The argument is used in two ways. (1) Against baptism: the thief was never baptized, yet he was saved, so baptism cannot be necessary for salvation; it is an outward sign of an inward faith that already saves. (2) Against works and the sacraments generally: he had no time to do good works, receive Communion, go to confession or join a church, yet Jesus promised him paradise, so salvation is by faith alone, received in a single moment of trust.

It is also used (3) against purgatory: he went to paradise “this day”, with no purification.

This reading is common in Baptist, evangelical and non-denominational preaching, and in the ‘sinner’s prayer’ tradition, where the thief is the model convert.
deep.lang:
“This day” (sēmeron) is emphatic in Greek and belongs with the promise (“today you will be with me”). A few Protestant groups that deny the soul’s survival after death (Seventh-day Adventists, Jehovah’s Witnesses) move the comma: “I say to you today, you will be with me”. Catholics and most Protestants rightly reject that, since Luke uses “today” for the arrival of salvation (2:11; 4:21; 19:9).

“Paradise” (paradeisos, a Persian loan-word for a walled garden) was used in Jewish writing of the time for the abode of the righteous dead, sometimes called “Abraham’s bosom” (Luke 16:22). Paul uses it for the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:4).
steps: The thief lived and died under the Old Covenant

Christian baptism was commanded by the risen Christ (Matthew 28:19) and first administered at Pentecost (Acts 2:38–41). When the thief died, the command had not yet been given, and the New Covenant was being sealed at that very hour. You cannot argue from someone who died before a law was promulgated to the conclusion that the law does not bind those who come after. The thief was no more bound to Christian baptism than Abraham was.
Catholic teaching already includes the thief

The Church does not teach that God is bound by the sacraments, only that we are. “God has bound salvation to the sacrament of Baptism, but he himself is not bound by his sacraments” (CCC 1257). Those who die before they can be baptized but with a sincere desire, repentance and charity are saved by the ‘baptism of desire’, and martyrs by the ‘baptism of blood’ (CCC 1258–1260; Trent, Session 6, ch. 4: justification comes through baptism “or the desire thereof”). The thief is a textbook case of both: he desires Christ’s kingdom and dies confessing him. So the passage confirms Catholic teaching rather than contradicting it.
He was not saved by a bare act of mental trust

Look at what the thief actually does in his last hour. He fears God. He confesses his sins openly and accepts his punishment as just (repentance and satisfaction). He defends Christ publicly when everyone else mocks (confession of faith before men, Matthew 10:32). He rebukes his companion (fraternal correction, an act of charity). He prays to Christ as King. That is not ‘faith alone’ in the Reformation sense; it is faith working through charity (Galatians 5:6), which is exactly what Trent says justifies. He did every good work it was possible for a crucified man to do.
An exception proves the rule; it does not abolish it

Every other conversion in the New Testament after Pentecost includes baptism: the 3,000 at Pentecost (Acts 2:41), the Samaritans (8:12), the Ethiopian (8:38), Saul (9:18; 22:16 “be baptized, and wash away thy sins”), Cornelius, even after receiving the Spirit (10:47–48), Lydia (16:15), the jailer at Philippi (16:33). The apostles never once cite the thief as a reason to skip baptism. A man pulled from a shipwreck without a lifeboat does not prove that ships may sail without lifeboats.
We do not know he was unbaptized

Scripture is silent. Some early writers speculated that he might have received John’s baptism earlier, or that he was baptized by the water from Christ’s side. Augustine at first used him as an example of baptism supplied by faith and conversion, and later noted that we cannot be certain he was not baptized. The honest point is that the argument from silence cannot carry the weight the objection puts on it. But the Catholic answer does not depend on this; see step 2.
“Paradise” does not refute purgatory

On Good Friday, Christ’s soul descended to the dead (1 Peter 3:19; CCC 632–635), to the righteous who awaited redemption. Heaven in the full sense, the vision of God, was opened by the Ascension (John 20:17: “I am not yet ascended to my Father”). So ‘paradise’ that day was the company of Christ among the just. Even if the thief entered glory at once, purgatory is not a necessary stage for everyone: martyrs and perfectly contrite souls need no further purification, and the thief’s suffering, accepted in union with Christ, is the most powerful penance imaginable (ST III q.52 a.4 ad 3; Suppl.).
fathers: Cyprian of Carthage, Letter 72 (73), 22 (c. 256)

Catechumens who are martyred before baptism are not deprived of the sacrament, since they are baptized with the most glorious baptism of blood (paraphrased). The principle the Church applies to the thief.
Augustine, On Baptism, against the Donatists IV.22.29 (c. 400)
Augustine uses the thief to show that where baptism cannot be had, faith and conversion of heart can supply what is wanting, provided the sacrament is not despised (paraphrased).
Augustine, Retractations II.18 (c. 427)
Reviewing his own works, he notes that the thief is not a certain example, since we do not know whether he had been baptized (paraphrased). A model of intellectual honesty.
Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.66 a.11; q.68 a.2

Three ‘baptisms’: of water, of blood, of desire (‘of the Spirit’). A man may be saved without the sacrament actually received, but not if he despises it; the desire of baptism comes from faith working by love.
Council of Trent, Session 6, ch. 4 (1547)
The passage from sin to grace cannot happen “without the laver of regeneration, or the desire thereof”.
obj: “If baptism of desire saves, then baptism is optional.”

No. Desire of baptism saves only someone who cannot receive it. A person who knows Christ commanded baptism and refuses it does not have the desire; he has the opposite. That is why Trent says ‘or the desire thereof’, and why Thomas adds: provided the sacrament is not despised (III q.68 a.2).
“You keep adding conditions. The thief just believed.”

The text records what he believed and did: fear of God, confession of guilt, defence of Christ, prayer. Which of those would an evangelical say is unnecessary? None. Everyone agrees saving faith repents and confesses Christ. The real question is whether that faith then obeys Christ’s commands when it is able, and every convert in Acts shows it does.
“Catholics say you need the Church, but the thief had no church.”

He was in the presence of the Head of the Church at the moment the Church was born from his side (John 19:34; CCC 766). Every saved person is united to Christ, and therefore to his Body, by grace, even when not by visible membership (CCC 846–848).
“Then why do you insist on baptism for babies who cannot believe?”

Because baptism is God’s act, not our achievement. Infants receive the gift as Israelite boys received circumcision, the sign of the covenant, on the eighth day (Colossians 2:11–12). ‘The promise is to you and to your children’ (Acts 2:39). Whole households were baptized (Acts 16:15, 33; 1 Corinthians 1:16).
deep.talk: “The thief is one of my favourite passages too. But notice three things. First, he died before Jesus commanded baptism, so he couldn’t disobey a command that didn’t exist yet. Second, Catholics have always taught that someone who wants baptism but can’t get it, and dies repenting, can be saved; the thief is the classic example. Third, look at what he actually did: he feared God, admitted his guilt, defended Jesus in public and prayed. That’s faith that loves and acts, and that’s what Catholics mean by saving faith. So the thief doesn’t teach us to skip what Jesus commanded. He teaches us never to give up on anyone, right up to the last breath.”
deep.avoid: Do not insist that the thief must have been baptized: Scripture does not say so, and Augustine himself withdrew that claim as uncertain. Do not say ‘paradise means purgatory’: it does not. And do not belittle deathbed conversions; the Church rejoices in them (Matthew 20:1–16).
read: CCC 1257–1261 (necessity of baptism), 632–637 (descent to the dead)
ST III q.66 a.11; q.68 a.2
Jimmy Akin (2010) The Salvation Controversy. El Cajon: Catholic Answers, ch. on baptism
Augustine, On Baptism IV.22.29; Retractations II.18

ephesians|2.t: "By grace you are saved through faith… not of works"
ephesians|2.claim: This verse is taken to prove that Catholics teach salvation by works, while the Bible teaches salvation by faith alone.
why: Catholics agree with every word of it. The Council of Trent taught that "none of those things which precede justification, whether faith or works, merit the grace itself of justification" (Session 6, ch. 8). Salvation begins as pure gift.

Read verse 10: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus in good works, which God hath prepared that we should walk in them." Works are not the price of grace; they are what grace produces. Paul joins the two; the slogan separates them.
The verse speaks of salvation coming "through faith" but never says "faith alone". The only place Scripture uses the phrase "faith alone" is James 2:24, which denies it.
What the Church rejects is not grace but the idea that a person, once justified, need not cooperate with grace, keep the commandments or persevere in love.
ephesians|2.cath: Saved by grace, through faith, for good works. The first move is God's; our works are his work in us, and he rewards his own gifts.
ephesians|2.src: Trent, Session 6, chs. 7–8, 16; CCC 1996–2011; ST I-II q.114 a.1–2

deep.ctx:
Ephesians 2:1–10 describes conversion in three stages. Before: “you were dead in your offences and sins” (2:1), “by nature children of wrath” (2:3). God’s act: “God, who is rich in mercy, for his exceeding charity wherewith he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together in Christ (by whose grace you are saved)” (2:4–5). After: “For by grace you are saved through faith: and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God. Not of works, that no man may glory. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus in good works, which God hath prepared that we should walk in them” (2:8–10).

The rest of the chapter (2:11–22) is about Jews and Gentiles being made one body, with the wall of the Law broken down (2:14–15). So ‘works’ here carries the shadow of the Law that divided Jew from Gentile.
deep.who:
Protestant preaching often treats Ephesians 2:8–9 as the clearest statement of the gospel: salvation is a free gift received by faith; anything we do contributes nothing, otherwise we could ‘boast’. Since Catholics speak of merit, sacraments, penance and good works as necessary for salvation, they are said to teach salvation by works and to deny grace.

The strongest form: ‘Paul excludes works from salvation without qualification (“not of works”), and gives the reason: so that no one may boast. Any system in which human cooperation makes the difference between the saved and the lost gives grounds for boasting. Catholicism is such a system.’
deep.lang:
“You are saved” (este sesōsmenoi) is a perfect passive periphrastic: you have been saved and remain in that state. Paul speaks of salvation in three tenses: we were saved (Romans 8:24, aorist), are being saved (1 Corinthians 1:18, present), and shall be saved (Romans 5:9–10, future). No single verse captures the whole.

“And that not of yourselves” (kai touto ouk ex hymōn): ‘that’ (touto) is neuter, while ‘grace’ and ‘faith’ are feminine, so it most naturally refers to the whole event of being saved by grace through faith. Even faith is a gift, which Catholics fully affirm (Council of Orange, 529, canon 5; Trent, Session 6, ch. 8).

“Workmanship” (poiēma, whence ‘poem’) and “created… in good works” (ktisthentes… epi ergois agathois): good works are the purpose of the new creation, ‘prepared beforehand’ (proētoimasen) by God.
steps: Catholics affirm every word of 2:8–9

Trent, the council that answered the Reformers, says: we are “said to be justified freely, because none of those things which precede justification, whether faith or works, merit the grace itself of justification” (Session 6, ch. 8). The Council of Orange (529) taught that even the beginning of faith is a gift of grace (canon 5). The Catechism: “The merits of our good works are gifts of the divine goodness” (CCC 2009). No Catholic believes we can earn the first grace or initial justification.
Read verse 10

Paul does not stop at verse 9. We are “created in Christ Jesus in good works”. Works are not the root of salvation but its fruit, and they are not optional decorations; they are what the new creation is for. Catholic teaching is the whole paragraph: grace (v.8), not earned (v.9), producing works God himself prepared (v.10).
The works Paul excludes are works done to earn grace

‘Not of works, that no man may glory’ excludes works considered as our own achievement, done apart from grace, giving a claim on God. Works done in Christ by grace are “his workmanship”; boasting in them is boasting in God (1 Corinthians 1:31; 15:10: “not I, but the grace of God with me”). So Catholic merit, which is grace crowning grace, gives no ground for boasting. Augustine: when God crowns our merits, he crowns nothing but his own gifts (Letter 194, 5.19).
The verse does not say ‘faith alone’

Paul says “through faith”. Catholics agree that faith is the beginning, foundation and root of justification (Trent, Session 6, ch. 8). But Paul never adds ‘alone’; the only verse with that phrase denies it (James 2:24). And Paul’s ‘faith’ is the faith that ‘worketh by charity’ (Galatians 5:6), without which ‘I am nothing’ (1 Corinthians 13:2).
The same Paul makes works necessary for final salvation

God “will render to every man according to his works: to them indeed who, according to patience in good work, seek glory and honour and incorruption, eternal life” (Romans 2:6–7). “If you live according to the flesh, you shall die” (Romans 8:13). “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling” (Philippians 2:12). Paul is not contradicting himself; he is distinguishing the gift that starts the Christian life from the cooperation that the gift makes possible.
Who is the real target?

In Ephesians 2:11–22 Paul turns to the ‘works’ that divided Jew and Gentile: circumcision and the ‘law of commandments contained in decrees’ (2:15). Jewish Christians could be tempted to ‘boast’ in their covenant status. The verse is first about that: no ethnic or ritual privilege saves; grace does, for Jew and Gentile alike.
fathers: Council of Orange (529), canons 5–7
Both the increase and the beginning of faith, and the very desire to believe, are from grace, not from nature. A Catholic council, a thousand years before Luther.
Augustine, Letter 194, 5.19 (c. 418)
When God crowns our merits, he crowns nothing other than his own gifts.
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Ephesians, ch. 2, lect. 3
On ‘not of works’: works are excluded as a cause meriting grace, but grace is given so that we may do good works; works follow grace, they do not precede it (paraphrased).
Council of Trent, Session 6, chs. 8 and 16 (1547)
Justified ‘freely’ because nothing before justification merits it; eternal life is both grace mercifully promised and a reward faithfully given for good works done in grace.
Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999)

Lutherans and Catholics confess together: “By grace alone, in faith in Christ’s saving work and not because of any merit on our part, we are accepted by God” (§15). Disagreements remain, but not about Ephesians 2:8–9.
obj: “If works are necessary in any sense, salvation isn’t a gift.”

An inheritance is a gift, yet an heir can forfeit it by renouncing the family. A gift that transforms the receiver and is meant to be used is still a gift. Paul calls eternal life both ‘the grace of God’ (Romans 6:23) and the reward of ‘patience in good work’ (Romans 2:7). If Paul can hold both, so can we.
“Merit means boasting.”

Not if the merit is itself grace. ‘What hast thou that thou hast not received? And if thou hast received, why dost thou glory?’ (1 Corinthians 4:7). Catholic merit is God rewarding what he himself works in us (CCC 2006–2011). Scripture uses the language of reward constantly (Matthew 5:12; 16:27; 25:34–40; 2 Timothy 4:8).
“Catholics have to do things to stay saved, so they are earning it.”

A married couple must remain faithful to stay married; nobody says they ‘earn’ their marriage. Remaining in grace means not rejecting it by grave sin (1 Corinthians 6:9–10; Galatians 5:19–21). Even perseverance is a gift (Trent, Session 6, ch. 13).
deep.talk: “I agree with Ephesians 2:8–9 completely, and so does the Catholic Church: the Council of Trent says nothing before justification, not even faith, earns grace. But keep reading: verse 10 says we are created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared for us. Grace isn’t only a pardon; it’s a new creation that produces good works. We don’t work to get saved. We work because we have been saved, and God, who gives the grace, also rewards what his grace does in us.”
deep.avoid: Do not say ‘we are saved by faith and works’ as if they were two independent contributions; that is exactly the caricature Protestants fear. Say: by grace, through faith, working through love. And do not deny that Catholics in practice sometimes act as if they could earn heaven; admit it, and point to what the Church actually teaches.
read: Council of Trent, Session 6 (1547), Decree on Justification, chs. 5–8, 16
Lutheran World Federation and Catholic Church (1999) Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Ephesians, ch. 2

romans|3.t: "Justified by faith, without the works of the law"
romans|3.claim: This is often read as "justified by faith alone, apart from any good works", and Luther added the word "alone" to his German translation.
why: The "works of the law" in Romans are the works of the Mosaic Law, especially circumcision. Paul's very next sentence explains: "Is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles?" (3:29). The point is that a Gentile does not have to become a Jew to be saved.

Paul never writes "faith alone". Luther added "allein" in 1522 and defended the addition as conveying the sense. The only verse with the words "faith alone" is James 2:24: "by works a man is justified, and not by faith only."
Paul himself says God "will render to every man according to his works" (Romans 2:6) and that what counts is "faith that worketh by charity" (Galatians 5:6).
So Paul and James do not contradict each other. Paul excludes the old Law as a way of earning God's favour; James excludes a dead faith that does nothing.
romans|3.cath: We are justified by faith that is alive with love, not by keeping the ritual law of Moses.
romans|3.src: Trent, Session 6, chs. 7–10; CCC 1987–1995; Luther, Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen (1530)

deep.ctx: Romans 1–3 argues that both Gentiles (1:18–32) and Jews (2:1–3:20) stand guilty before God, so that “by the works of the law no flesh shall be justified before him” (3:20). Then Paul announces that “the justice of God without the law is made manifest… by faith of Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all them that believe in him” (3:21–22). Verse 28 sums up: “For we account a man to be justified by faith, without the works of the law.” The very next verses explain why it matters: “Is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also. For it is one God, that justifieth circumcision by faith, and uncircumcision through faith” (3:29–30). Chapter 4 then uses Abraham, justified before he was circumcised (4:9–12).
deep.who:
This is the verse at the heart of the Reformation. Luther translated it in 1522 as “allein durch den Glauben” (‘by faith alone’), adding the word ‘alone’, and defended the addition in his Open Letter on Translating (1530): German idiom needs ‘alone’ to bring out Paul’s sense. The Reformation formula sola fide follows: justification is received by faith alone, apart from any works, including works of charity done in grace.

The strongest form: ‘Paul excludes “works of the law”, and “law” in Romans includes the moral law (3:20: “by the law is the knowledge of sin”; 7:7 “thou shalt not covet”). If even keeping the moral commandments does not justify, then nothing but faith does, and adding “alone” only makes explicit what Paul means.’
deep.lang:
Greek: logizometha gar dikaiousthai pistei anthrōpon chōris ergōn nomou. ‘For we reckon a man to be justified by faith apart from works of law.’ There is no word for ‘alone’ (monos) in any Greek manuscript.

“Works of the law” (erga nomou) is a technical phrase. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, a text known as 4QMMT (c. 150 BC) lists ‘some of the works of the law’, mostly purity and calendar rules that marked off the faithful community. Paul’s argument in 3:29–30 and chapter 4 (circumcision) shows he especially means the Torah as the covenant badge of Israel.

The only place in the New Testament where pistis and monon (‘only’) occur together is James 2:24: “Do you see that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only (ouk ek pisteōs monon)?”
steps: The word ‘alone’ is not in the text

Every Greek manuscript lacks it. Luther knew this and defended it as a translation choice, writing in 1530 that the papists stare at the four letters s-o-l-a like cows at a new gate (paraphrased from his Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen). The question is whether the addition is faithful to Paul’s meaning. The only text that pairs ‘faith’ and ‘only’ says the opposite (James 2:24).
Paul’s own explanation is about Jew and Gentile

Verse 29 begins with ‘Or’ (ē): ‘Or is he the God of the Jews only?’ The point of 3:28 is that justification does not come through becoming a Jew under the Mosaic covenant, so it is open to Gentiles on equal terms. Chapter 4 proves it from Abraham: righteousness was reckoned to him ‘not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision’ (4:10). This is the ‘works of the law’ Paul has in view: circumcision, Sabbath, food laws, the whole Torah as a covenant charter.
Even if the moral law is included, ‘works of the law’ are works done without grace

Catholics accept that keeping the moral law by our own strength cannot justify; Paul says the Law gave knowledge of sin but not power over it (7:7–25). But Paul never says works done in Christ, by the Spirit, are irrelevant. In the same letter: “Not the hearers of the law are just before God: but the doers of the law shall be justified” (2:13), and “if by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you shall live” (8:13). The Spirit fulfils the law in us (8:4); love is the fulfilling of the law (13:10).
Paul and James answer different errors

Paul opposes the idea that the Torah (and human effort without grace) makes us right with God. James opposes a ‘faith’ that is mere assent and produces nothing: “the devils also believe and tremble” (James 2:19). Both use Abraham. Paul looks at Genesis 15:6 (faith before circumcision); James at Genesis 22 (faith perfected in obedience). Catholic teaching holds both: faith is the start and root, and living faith works through love (Galatians 5:6).
Faith in Paul is never mere trust without obedience

Paul’s mission is to bring about “the obedience of faith” (hypakoē pisteōs) among the nations (Romans 1:5; 16:26). In Romans 10:16 ‘they did not all obey the gospel’ is parallel to ‘who hath believed our report?’ Faith in Paul includes surrender of the whole person. The Catholic definition is the same: faith is the submission of intellect and will to God revealing (Dei Verbum 5; CCC 143).
What Trent condemned

Trent did not condemn the phrase ‘justified by faith’. It condemned the claim that the sinner is justified by faith alone, in the sense that nothing else is required to cooperate in obtaining justification (canon 9), or that justifying faith is nothing but confidence that one’s sins are forgiven (canon 12). It affirms that faith is ‘the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and root of all justification’ (ch. 8).
fathers: Augustine, On Faith and Works 14.21 (c. 413)

Augustine says that even in the apostles’ day some misunderstood Paul as teaching that faith without works suffices, and that this is why James, Peter, John and Jude wrote so strongly against it (paraphrased).
Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter 26.45 (412)
Commenting on 2:13: the doers of the law shall be justified, not as if they were doers first and justified afterwards, but justified so that they might become doers (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Romans, ch. 3, lect. 4

The ‘works of the law’ excluded are both ceremonial and moral works considered as done by human effort before grace; works done after justification flow from it. Thomas can say ‘by faith alone’ elsewhere (Commentary on 1 Timothy, ch. 1, lect. 3), meaning faith as opposed to the ceremonies of the Law, never faith without charity.
Council of Trent, Session 6, canons 9, 12, 24 (1547)
Condemns ‘faith alone’ as excluding all cooperation; affirms that justification, once received, is increased by good works.
Luther, Preface to James (1522)
Called James ‘an epistle of straw’ compared with Paul’s letters, because it ‘has nothing of the nature of the gospel about it’. Showing that the tension with James was felt from the start.
obj: “Some Church Fathers used ‘faith alone’ too.”

True. Origen, Ambrosiaster, Chrysostom and Thomas occasionally use ‘by faith alone’ (sola fide). But they mean faith without the works of the Mosaic Law, or the faith by which a convert first comes to God, not a faith that excludes charity and obedience. The words are the same; the doctrine is different.
“James means ‘shown to be righteous before men’, not justified before God.”

James’ question is ‘can faith save him?’ (2:14), which is salvation before God. And Abraham was ‘justified by works, offering up Isaac’ (2:21), an act no human saw except Isaac. James’ verdict, ‘faith without works is dead’ (2:26), is about whether faith is alive, not how it looks.
“Works of the law includes the moral law, so all works are excluded.”

Grant it for the sake of argument. Paul still excludes works as our own achievement before grace, not the Spirit’s fruit in the justified. He says ‘faith that worketh by charity’ is what avails (Galatians 5:6), and that without charity even faith that moves mountains is ‘nothing’ (1 Corinthians 13:2). A faith that is nothing cannot justify.
deep.talk: “The word ‘alone’ isn’t in Romans 3:28; Luther added it in 1522 and admitted he added it. The only Bible verse that puts ‘faith’ and ‘only’ together is James 2:24, and it says ‘not by faith only’. Look at Paul’s next sentence: ‘Is God the God of the Jews only?’ His point is that you don’t have to become a Jew and keep the Law of Moses to be saved. Catholics agree completely. We’re justified by faith, a living faith that works through love, as Paul says in Galatians 5:6.”
deep.avoid: Do not say Paul and James contradict each other or that Paul is ‘balanced out’ by James; both are inspired and agree. Do not claim Catholics reject ‘justification by faith’; we reject faith alone in the sense Trent defined. And do not dismiss the Reformers’ pastoral concern; much late medieval preaching did obscure grace.
read: Council of Trent, Session 6, chs. 7–10, canons 9–12, 24
Augustine, On Faith and Works; On the Spirit and the Letter
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Romans, ch. 3, lect. 4
Luther (1530) Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen [Open Letter on Translating]
N.T. Wright (2009) Justification. London: SPCK (a Protestant scholar on ‘works of the law’)

romans|3.claim: If all have sinned, Mary must have sinned too, so the Immaculate Conception is unbiblical.
why: Paul is showing that Jews and Gentiles alike need Christ. He is not listing exceptions. Infants who die before committing any sin, and Christ himself, who was truly human, are obvious exceptions to "all have sinned" as personal sin.

The Church does not say Mary did not need a Saviour. She calls God "my Saviour" (Luke 1:47). She was saved in a more perfect way: preserved from sin from her conception by the merits of Christ, like someone pulled back before falling into a pit rather than lifted out after.
The angel greets her as kecharitomene, "full of grace" (Luke 1:28): one who has been, and remains, filled with God's favour.
romans|3.cath: Mary was redeemed by Christ, by being kept from all sin from the first moment of her existence.

deep.ctx: Romans 3:9–26: Paul concludes his indictment of Jews and Gentiles: ‘we have charged both Jews, and Greeks, that they are all under sin. As it is written: There is not any man just. There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God… For all have sinned, and do need the glory of God. Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption, that is in Christ Jesus’ (3:9–11, 23–24). The quotations come from the Psalms (13:1–3; 5:10; 139:4; 9:28; 35:2 in the Douay) and Isaiah 59:7–8.
deep.who: If all have sinned, Mary has sinned. Therefore the Immaculate Conception (that Mary was preserved from original sin) and Mary’s sinlessness contradict Scripture. Mary also calls God ‘my Saviour’ (Luke 1:47), so she needed saving from sin.
deep.lang:
“All have sinned” (pantes hēmarton): ‘all’ in the context of Jews and Gentiles as groups (3:9, 22: ‘there is no distinction’). The Psalm quoted in 3:10–12 (Psalm 13) is about ‘the fool’ and the wicked, and itself speaks of ‘the just generation’ (13:5 Douay).

“Do need” (hysterountai): fall short of, lack.
steps: Paul’s point is universal need of grace, Jew and Gentile alike
Romans 1–3 proves that Jews have no advantage over Gentiles in the matter of sin: ‘there is no distinction’ (3:22). ‘All’ is about groups, not a census of every individual.
‘All’ has obvious exceptions

Jesus never sinned (Hebrews 4:15). Infants and those who never reach the use of reason commit no personal sins. Paul himself says Jacob and Esau, before birth, ‘had not done any good or evil’ (Romans 9:11). So ‘all have sinned’ cannot mean every human being without exception has personally sinned.
The Psalms quoted distinguish the wicked and the just

Psalm 13 (14) describes the fool who says ‘there is no God’, and continues: ‘God is in the just generation’ (13:5 Douay). Luke calls Zachary and Elizabeth ‘both just before God, walking in all the commandments’ (Luke 1:6). Paul uses the Psalms rhetorically to show universal sinfulness, not to deny any righteous person ever existed.
Mary was redeemed: preserved rather than cleansed

Pius IX defined (Ineffabilis Deus, 1854) that Mary was preserved from original sin ‘by a singular grace and privilege of almighty God, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Saviour of the human race’. She needed a Saviour and had one; she was redeemed in a more perfect way, by prevention. Analogy (from Duns Scotus’ argument): a man may be saved from a pit by being pulled out after falling in, or by being held back before he falls. Both are rescued; the second more perfectly.
Scriptural foundations

Luke 1:28: the angel greets her as kecharitōmenē, ‘one who has been graced’ (perfect participle), used as a name. Genesis 3:15 promises enmity between the woman and the serpent. The Fathers called her ‘all-holy’ (panagia) and the new Eve.
An honest note about Thomas

Thomas Aquinas did not accept that Mary was conceived without original sin; he held that she was sanctified in the womb after conception, though she never committed personal sin (ST III q.27 a.2, a.4). Bernard of Clairvaux also opposed the feast. The decisive argument came from Duns Scotus (d. 1308): preservative redemption. The Church defined it in 1854. Thomas’ concern, that Mary too must be redeemed by Christ, is fully preserved in the definition.
fathers: Augustine, On Nature and Grace 36.42 (415)
Except the holy Virgin Mary, about whom, out of honour to the Lord, I wish to raise no question when sin is discussed (paraphrased).
Ephrem the Syrian, Carmina Nisibena 27 (c. 370)
‘You alone and your Mother are more beautiful than any others; for there is no blemish in you, nor any stain upon your Mother’ (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.27 a.4
Mary committed no actual sin, mortal or venial.
Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus (1854)
Defines the Immaculate Conception, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Saviour.
obj: “Luke 1:47: Mary calls God ‘my Saviour’.”
Yes: she was saved, by preservation. The definition itself says ‘in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Saviour’. See the note on Luke 1:47.
“Mary offered a sin offering after childbirth (Luke 2:24).”
The purification offering (Leviticus 12:6–8) was for ritual impurity after childbirth, not for moral sin. Jesus too was presented and circumcised and baptized, though sinless.
deep.talk: “Paul is saying Jews and Gentiles are all in the same boat; nobody gets an advantage. But ‘all’ can’t mean every single person: Jesus never sinned, and babies haven’t committed sins. Catholics believe Mary needed a Saviour, and she was saved in a special way: preserved from sin instead of cleaned up afterwards, through Christ’s merits. It’s like being stopped before falling into a pit, rather than pulled out once you’re in.”
deep.avoid: Do not pretend the Immaculate Conception was always held by everyone or by Thomas; be honest about the history and show why the definition answers the earlier concerns.
read: Tim Staples (2014) Behold Your Mother, chs. 3–5

galatians|2.t: "Not justified by the works of the law"
galatians|2.claim: Taken as proof that any good work done by a Christian plays no part in salvation.
why: The context is Peter withdrawing from table fellowship with Gentile Christians to please those who insisted on circumcision (2:11–14). The "works of the law" are the Jewish ceremonial law, not love of neighbour.

In the same letter Paul says that those who do the works of the flesh "shall not obtain the kingdom of God" (5:21), and that "what things a man shall sow, those also shall he reap" (6:7). Behaviour matters for salvation.
Catholics fully accept that no one is justified by the Mosaic Law. Justification comes through faith in Christ, received in baptism, and lived out in charity.
galatians|2.cath: Christ, not circumcision and the old ceremonies, makes us right with God.
galatians|2.src: CCC 1992; Trent, Session 6, ch. 7; Thomas, Commentary on Galatians, ch. 2, lect. 4

deep.ctx: Galatians is Paul’s fiercest letter. Some Jewish Christians (‘the circumcision’) were telling Gentile converts in Galatia that they had to be circumcised and keep the Mosaic Law to be full members of God’s people. In 2:11–14 Paul recounts confronting Peter at Antioch, who had stopped eating with Gentile Christians for fear of these men. Then: “knowing that man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ; we also believe in Christ Jesus, that we may be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: because by the works of the law no flesh shall be justified” (2:16). The letter’s practical conclusion: “in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision: but faith that worketh by charity” (5:6).
deep.who: Galatians is read as Paul’s manifesto against all religion of works: any attempt to add something to faith in Christ (circumcision then; sacraments, penance, merit, saints, Mass now) is ‘another gospel’ (1:6–9). Catholicism, it is argued, is the Galatian heresy reborn: Christ plus human additions.
deep.lang:
“Works of the law” (erga nomou) appears three times in this verse. ‘Faith of Jesus Christ’ (pistis Iēsou Christou) can be read as faith in Christ or as Christ’s own faithfulness; scholars are divided, and both readings place the saving initiative with Christ.

In 5:6 the decisive phrase is pistis di’ agapēs energoumenē: ‘faith working (energized) through love’. Energoumenē is the root of ‘energy’: love is the activity of living faith.
steps: The issue in Galatia was circumcision and the Torah

The whole letter turns on it: Titus was not compelled to be circumcised (2:3); ‘if you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing’ (5:2); the false teachers ‘would have you to be circumcised’ (6:12–13). Peter’s fault at Antioch was withdrawing from table fellowship with Gentiles (2:12). Paul is fighting the idea that Gentiles must become Jews, not the idea that Christians must love their neighbour.
Paul makes conduct decisive in the same letter

“The works of the flesh are manifest, which are fornication, uncleanness… envies, murders, drunkenness… of the which I foretell you, as I have foretold to you, that they who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God” (5:19–21). “What things a man shall sow, those also shall he reap. For he that soweth in his flesh, of the flesh also shall reap corruption. But he that soweth in the spirit, of the spirit shall reap life everlasting” (6:7–8). “In doing good, let us not fail. For in due time we shall reap, not failing” (6:9). That is not ‘faith alone’.
The Catholic sacraments are not ‘works of the law’

Baptism is Christ’s own command (Matthew 28:19), and Paul in this very letter says: ‘as many of you as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ’ (3:27). Paul treats baptism as the means by which we are clothed with Christ, not as a rival to faith. The sacraments are Christ acting, not human achievements.
Faith working through charity

Galatians 5:6 is the key to the letter, and it is the Catholic formula. Trent: through justification, faith, hope and charity are infused, ‘for faith, unless hope and charity be added thereto, neither unites man perfectly with Christ, nor makes him a living member of his body’ (Session 6, ch. 7). Thomas calls this ‘formed faith’ (fides formata), faith given its form by charity (ST II-II q.4 a.3).
‘Another gospel’ cuts both ways

Paul anathematizes a gospel ‘besides that which we have preached’ (1:8), which the Galatians had ‘received’ (1:9, parelabete, the word for receiving tradition). The question is which community has kept the gospel as first received. The Catholic Church can show continuous teaching on baptism, the Eucharist and the necessity of charity from the first century; sola fide as formulated in 1520s Wittenberg cannot.
fathers: Jerome, Commentary on Galatians (386)
Reads ‘works of the law’ as the Jewish ceremonies: circumcision, Sabbath, new moons, food laws (paraphrased).
John Chrysostom, Homilies on Galatians (c. 395)
The Galatians were not denying Christ but adding circumcision as necessary, which overturned grace (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Galatians, ch. 5, lect. 2
On 5:6: the faith that justifies is faith formed by charity; unformed faith, without charity, is dead (paraphrased).
Council of Trent, Session 6, ch. 7
Quotes Galatians 5:6: faith that works by charity, with hope and charity infused, makes us living members of Christ.
obj: “Paul says if righteousness came by the law Christ died in vain (2:21). Catholics make Christ’s death insufficient.”

Catholics say Christ’s death is the sole meritorious cause of our justification (Trent, Session 6, ch. 7). What we add is not to Christ’s merits but our acceptance of them, which is itself grace. Paul’s own words: ‘I live, now not I, but Christ liveth in me’ (2:20). Christ living in us produces works; that is the point.
“Galatians 3:10: ‘as many as are of the works of the law are under a curse’. Any reliance on works brings a curse.”

Paul’s proof (3:10) quotes Deuteronomy 27:26: cursed is everyone who does not keep everything in the Law. The curse falls on those who rely on the Mosaic covenant as their charter of righteousness. Christ ‘redeemed us from the curse of the law’ (3:13) so that ‘the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles’ (3:14). The contrast is Torah versus Christ, not obedience versus faith.
deep.talk: “Galatians is about circumcision. False teachers were telling Gentile Christians they had to become Jews to be saved, and Paul says no: the Law of Moses doesn’t justify anyone. Catholics agree. But the same letter says people who live in fornication, drunkenness and hatred won’t inherit the kingdom (5:21), and that what counts is ‘faith working through love’ (5:6). That’s the Catholic position in Paul’s own words.”
deep.avoid: Do not say Paul is ‘only’ talking about Jewish identity markers as if he had no wider principle; he also teaches that no one can earn grace by human effort, which Catholics affirm. Do not equate Catholic devotions with the Mosaic Law; make the distinction clearly.
read: Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Galatians, chs. 2, 3, 5
Scott Hahn (2002) A Father Who Keeps His Promises. Cincinnati: Servant, chs. 8–9

romans|4.claim: The idea is that God only declares a sinner righteous, like a judge acquitting a guilty man, while the person stays inwardly unchanged ("imputed" righteousness).
why: When God declares something, it happens: "God said: Be light made. And light was made" (Genesis 1:3). God's verdict is not a legal fiction but a creative word.

Paul says that by Christ's obedience "many shall be made just" (Romans 5:19), that God's love "is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Ghost" (5:5), and that anyone in Christ is "a new creature" (2 Corinthians 5:17). Justification changes us.
Trent puts it this way: we are not only reputed but truly called and are just, receiving justice within us (Session 6, ch. 7).
romans|4.cath: God does not merely cover sin; he removes it and makes the sinner holy by grace poured into the soul.
romans|4.src: Trent, Session 6, ch. 7 and canon 11; CCC 1989–1992; ST I-II q.113 a.1–2

deep.ctx: Romans 4 uses Abraham to prove that righteousness comes by faith. “Abraham believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice” (4:3, quoting Genesis 15:6). Verses 4–5: “Now to him that worketh, the reward is not reckoned according to grace, but according to debt. But to him that worketh not, yet believeth in him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is reputed to justice, according to the purpose of the grace of God.” Then Paul quotes David (Psalm 31:1–2, ‘Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven’) and shows that Abraham was reckoned righteous before his circumcision (4:9–12).
deep.who:
This verse is the centre of the Reformed doctrine of ‘imputed righteousness’: justification is a forensic (legal) declaration. God, as judge, counts Christ’s righteousness to the believer’s account. The believer is not made inwardly righteous by justification; he is declared righteous while remaining a sinner. Luther’s phrase: simul iustus et peccator, at once righteous and a sinner. Sanctification (actual inward change) follows as a separate process but contributes nothing to our standing before God.

The strongest form: ‘The verb logizomai is an accounting term, “to credit to an account”. God justifies “the ungodly”, so justification cannot be a description of what we already are; it is a verdict credited to us.’
deep.lang:
Logizomai (‘to reckon, account, credit’) appears 11 times in Romans 4. The Greek translation of Genesis 15:6 uses it, and so does Psalm 105:31 (106:31 in Hebrew numbering), of Phinehas: his zealous act ‘was reputed to him unto justice’. The same formula is used of a deed, not only of faith.

“Justifieth” (dikaiounta) is present tense: God is the one who makes righteous. In Hebrew, ‘justify’ (hitsdiq) can mean to declare righteous in court; but when God speaks, his word accomplishes what it says (Isaiah 55:11).
steps: God’s declaration is creative, not fictional

When a human judge declares a guilty man innocent, the declaration is false (Proverbs 17:15: ‘he that justifieth the wicked… is abominable before God’). God cannot declare something true that is not. When God declares, it comes to be: ‘God said: Be light made. And light was made’ (Genesis 1:3). So God’s verdict ‘righteous’ makes the sinner righteous. The Catholic Church agrees justification is God’s declaration; it denies that the declaration is a legal fiction.
Paul describes justification as transformation

Within the same letter: ‘the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts, by the Holy Ghost, who is given to us’ (5:5); ‘by the obedience of one, many shall be made just’ (5:19, katastathēsontai, ‘constituted’); ‘we are buried together with him by baptism into death… that we also may walk in newness of life’ (6:4); ‘he that is dead is justified from sin’ (6:7). Elsewhere: ‘you are washed, you are sanctified, you are justified’ (1 Corinthians 6:11); ‘if any be in Christ a new creature’ (2 Corinthians 5:17).
‘To him that worketh not’ means the one working for wages

Verse 4 defines the ‘worker’: one to whom the reward is reckoned ‘according to debt’, as wages owed. Paul excludes the idea that we put God in our debt. Catholics agree: no one can merit the first grace (Trent, Session 6, ch. 8). He does not say that the justified person does nothing; he goes on to say the justified must walk in newness of life (6:4) and be ‘servants of justice’ (6:18).
Abraham was ‘justified’ more than once

Abraham had faith and obeyed God long before Genesis 15: ‘By faith Abraham… obeyed to go out into a place which he was to receive for an inheritance’ (Hebrews 11:8, referring to Genesis 12). Genesis 15:6 is a later moment, and James 2:21–23 sees Genesis 22, the offering of Isaac, as the fulfilment of 15:6. So Scripture presents Abraham’s righteousness as growing through faith and obedience over his life: exactly the Catholic doctrine of increase in justification (Trent, Session 6, ch. 10).
The same ‘reckoning’ formula is used of an act

Psalm 105:30–31: Phinehas ‘stood up and pacified’ God, ‘and it was reputed to him unto justice, to generation and generation for evermore’. If ‘reckoned as righteousness’ meant crediting an alien righteousness instead of a real one, it could not describe a deed. It means that God recognizes and rewards true righteousness, which he himself has worked.
Forgiveness removes sin; it does not merely cover it

Paul quotes Psalm 31: ‘whose sins are covered’. Protestants read ‘covered’ as hidden but still present. But Scripture uses many images: sins are ‘blotted out’ (Isaiah 43:25; Acts 3:19), ‘washed’ (Psalm 50:4, 9: ‘thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow’), removed ‘as far as the east is from the west’ (Psalm 102:12). Covering is one image among several, and the others show that the stain is truly taken away.
fathers: Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter 26.45 (412)
‘Justified’ means ‘made just’: ‘what else is “being justified” than being made just by him who justifies the ungodly, so that from ungodly he becomes just?’ (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, ST I-II q.113 a.1 and q.110 a.2
Justification is a movement from the state of injustice to the state of justice; grace is a real quality in the soul, not only God’s favour.
Council of Trent, Session 6, ch. 7 and canon 11 (1547)

We are ‘not only reputed, but are truly called, and are, just, receiving justice within us’. Condemns the claim that we are justified ‘by the sole imputation of the justice of Christ… to the exclusion of the grace and charity which is poured forth in their hearts by the Holy Ghost’.
Joint Declaration on Justification (1999), §§22–24
Catholics and Lutherans agree that God both forgives sin and frees from its power; they differ on how to describe the remaining concupiscence.
obj: “If justification makes us inwardly righteous, why do Christians still sin?”

Because concupiscence, the inclination to sin, remains after baptism for the struggle (Trent, Session 5, canon 5; CCC 1264, 1426). Concupiscence is not itself sin unless consented to. Venial sins do not destroy grace. Justification is real but not yet complete in glory; that is why it can grow (2 Peter 3:18) and why we pray ‘forgive us our trespasses’.
“Imputation protects assurance: if my standing depends on inner change, I can never be sure.”

The firm ground of hope is God’s faithfulness, not my self-inspection (Romans 8:31–39; Hebrews 6:18–19). Catholics have a confident hope, not an anxious calculation. But Scripture itself warns that the justified can fall (Romans 11:22; 1 Corinthians 10:12), which pure imputation cannot easily explain.
“Christ’s righteousness is credited to us (2 Corinthians 5:21).”

‘That we might be made (genōmetha, become) the justice of God in him.’ Paul says ‘become’, not ‘be credited with’. Catholics affirm that Christ’s merits are the meritorious cause of our justification; what we receive is a real sharing in God’s righteousness (2 Peter 1:4, ‘partakers of the divine nature’).
deep.talk: “When God says something, it happens. ‘Let there be light’ and there was light. So when God declares a sinner righteous, he doesn’t pretend; he makes it true. That’s why Paul, a few verses later, says God’s love is poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit (Romans 5:5) and that through Christ many are made righteous (5:19). Catholics believe justification is God’s verdict, and it’s a verdict that changes us, not a paper transaction.”
deep.avoid: Do not say Catholics reject the legal or forensic dimension; Trent accepts that justification includes the forgiveness of sins. The disagreement is whether it is only that. Do not caricature imputation as ‘snow-covered dung’ and attribute the phrase to Luther; it is not found in his writings.
read: Council of Trent, Session 6, chs. 7, 10, canons 10–11
Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter
John Henry Newman (1838) Lectures on Justification
Michael Bird (2007) The Saving Righteousness of God. Milton Keynes: Paternoster (an evangelical scholar who questions strict imputation)

romans|10.t: Confess with your mouth and you will be saved
romans|10.claim: Used for the "sinner's prayer": say the words once, sincerely, and you are saved for good.
why: Paul is describing the faith that saves, not offering a one-time formula. The same Paul says we are saved by baptism, "buried together with him by baptism into death" (Romans 6:3–4).
Jesus warns: "Not every one that saith to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven: but he that doth the will of my Father" (Matthew 7:21).
In the early Church this confession, "Jesus is Lord", was made at baptism. Confession of faith, baptism and a changed life belong together (Acts 2:38).
romans|10.cath: Confessing Christ is necessary, and it is the beginning of a life of faith lived in the Church, not the end of the matter.

deep.ctx: Romans 9–11 deals with Israel’s unbelief. In 10:5–13 Paul contrasts the righteousness of the Law with the righteousness of faith, quoting Deuteronomy 30:14: ‘The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart.’ Then: “For if thou confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in thy heart that God hath raised him up from the dead, thou shalt be saved. For, with the heart, we believe unto justice; but, with the mouth, confession is made unto salvation” (10:9–10). He quotes Joel 2:32: ‘Whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved’ (10:13), and then asks how people can call without preachers who are sent (10:14–15).
deep.who: Evangelical altar calls and the ‘sinner’s prayer’ rest heavily on this verse: if you sincerely say ‘Jesus is Lord’ and believe in the resurrection, you are saved, at that moment, permanently. Baptism, Church membership and sacraments are good but not part of salvation itself.
deep.lang:
“Confess” (homologeō) means to agree publicly, to declare allegiance. ‘Jesus is Lord’ (Kyrios Iēsous) was the earliest baptismal creed (1 Corinthians 12:3; Philippians 2:11). In a Roman context, where ‘Caesar is Lord’ was the civic confession, it was a dangerous public act of allegiance, often sealed with martyrdom.

“Shall be saved” (sōthēsē) is future tense.
steps: Paul describes saving faith; he does not offer a formula

Nowhere in the New Testament is a convert told to pray a prayer and then be assured of salvation. The ‘sinner’s prayer’ as an evangelistic technique dates from 18th- and 19th-century revivalism (popularized by preachers such as Charles Finney and, in the 20th century, Billy Graham’s crusades). Paul’s point is that salvation is near and simple: faith in the heart, confession with the lips. Catholics fully agree.
Confession of ‘Jesus is Lord’ was made at baptism

In the early Church the creed was professed at baptism (Acts 8:37 in some manuscripts: ‘I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God’; the Didache and Hippolytus’ Apostolic Tradition describe baptismal professions). Paul’s readers would hear 10:9 as describing what they did when they were baptized, a few chapters after he has taught that we are ‘buried together with him by baptism into death’ (6:4).
Calling on the name of the Lord, in Acts, includes baptism

Paul is told: ‘Rise up, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, invoking his name’ (Acts 22:16). Peter at Pentecost quotes the same Joel prophecy (Acts 2:21) and then answers ‘what shall we do?’ with ‘Do penance, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ, for the remission of your sins’ (2:38). Calling on the name and being baptized go together.
Confession of Christ is lifelong

Jesus: ‘Every one therefore that shall confess me before men, I will also confess him before my Father’ (Matthew 10:32), and ‘he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved’ (10:22). A confession once made and later denied by one’s life does not save: ‘They profess that they know God: but in their works they deny him’ (Titus 1:16). ‘Not every one that saith to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 7:21).
Paul immediately points to the Church’s mission

10:14–15: ‘How shall they believe him, of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear, without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they be sent?’ Faith comes through the preaching of those sent by Christ (10:17). The verse leads straight into the apostolic Church, not away from it.
fathers: Hippolytus (attributed), Apostolic Tradition 21 (c. 215)
Describes baptism in Rome: the candidate is asked ‘Do you believe in Christ Jesus, the Son of God…?’, answers ‘I believe’, and is immersed after each profession.
Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lectures 5.12 (c. 350)
The creed is taught to catechumens to be confessed with the mouth and kept in the heart (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Romans, ch. 10, lect. 2
Interior faith is enough for justification in the heart, but outward confession is necessary for salvation when occasion demands it, as with the martyrs (paraphrased).
obj: “The verse doesn’t mention baptism, so it isn’t necessary.”

Romans 10:9 doesn’t mention repentance either, yet everyone agrees repentance is necessary. Scripture must be read whole. Mark 16:16, John 3:5, Acts 2:38, Romans 6:3–4 and 1 Peter 3:21 all speak of baptism.
“I prayed the sinner’s prayer sincerely, so I know I’m saved.”

Rejoice that you came to Christ: that was grace. Catholics would say the next step Christ himself asks is baptism into his Church, if you have not received valid baptism, and a life of faithful discipleship (Matthew 28:19–20). Most Protestant baptisms are valid and recognized by the Catholic Church (CCC 1271).
deep.talk: “Romans 10:9 is beautiful and true: faith in the heart and confessing Jesus as Lord is how salvation begins. In the early Church, that confession was made out loud at baptism; that’s why Acts 22:16 says ‘be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name’. And Jesus said not everyone who says ‘Lord, Lord’ will enter the kingdom, but whoever does the Father’s will. So the confession is a beginning, and it has to be lived out.”
deep.avoid: Do not mock people who came to faith through a sinner’s prayer; God uses it. Do not say evangelicals ‘aren’t saved’; the Church recognizes valid baptism and real faith among them (CCC 818, 838).
read: Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Romans, ch. 10

1-john|5.t: "That you may know that you have eternal life"
1-john|5.claim: Read as proof of "once saved, always saved": a believer can be absolutely certain of final salvation.
why: John writes so that believers may have confidence, and Catholics share that hope. But John himself attaches a condition: "He that keepeth his commandments, abideth in him" (1 John 3:24), and he distinguishes sin that leads to death from sin that does not (5:16–17).

Scripture warns believers that they can fall away: "work out your salvation with fear and trembling" (Philippians 2:12); "he that thinketh himself to stand, let him take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:12); Hebrews 6:4–6.
Paul himself says he disciplines his body "lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway" (1 Corinthians 9:27).
The Church teaches firm hope, not presumption. Without a special revelation no one can know with the certainty of faith that he will persevere to the end (Trent, Session 6, chs. 9 and 13).
1-john|5.cath: We can be confident in God's faithfulness, and we must stay faithful ourselves. Hope, not a guarantee that ignores how we live.

deep.ctx: 1 John is written to reassure a community shaken by a schism: some had ‘gone out from us’ (2:19), denying that Jesus Christ came in the flesh (4:2–3). John gives ‘tests’ by which believers can know they are in the truth: keeping the commandments (2:3–5), loving the brethren (3:14), confessing Christ come in the flesh (4:2), the Spirit’s witness (4:13). Then 5:13: “These things I write to you, that you may know that you have eternal life, you who believe in the name of the Son of God.” A few verses later: “He that knoweth his brother to sin a sin which is not to death, let him ask, and life shall be given to him… There is a sin unto death: for that I say not that any man ask” (5:16).
deep.who: This verse is the main text for ‘assurance of salvation’: believers can know with certainty, now, that they are going to heaven. In Calvinist form this is tied to ‘perseverance of the saints’ (the truly elect cannot fall away); in Baptist and evangelical form, ‘once saved, always saved’ (eternal security). Catholics, who say no one can be absolutely certain of final salvation without special revelation, are accused of robbing believers of the joy John wants them to have.
deep.lang:
“That you may know” (hina eidēte): eidō, ‘know’ in the sense of being aware, assured. John uses ‘know’ (ginōskō and eidō) over 30 times in the letter, almost always with a condition: ‘by this we know that we have known him, if we keep his commandments’ (2:3); ‘in this we know that we are in him’ (2:5).

“You have eternal life” (zōēn echete aiōnion), present tense: eternal life is a present possession, the life of grace (John 17:3).
steps: Catholics affirm a real, joyful confidence

The Church teaches the virtue of hope: a ‘firm’ and ‘certain’ trust in God’s promises (CCC 1817–1821; Hebrews 6:19, ‘an anchor of the soul, sure and firm’). Trent says no one should doubt God’s mercy, Christ’s merits or the power of the sacraments (Session 6, ch. 9). What Trent rejects is the claim that a believer must be certain, with the certainty of faith, that he himself is predestined and will persevere, as if this were part of saving faith (canons 15–16).
John’s assurance is conditional on a living faith

In the same letter: ‘He that saith he knoweth him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar’ (2:4). ‘Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in himself’ (3:15). ‘If we walk in the light… the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin’ (1:7). You can know you have eternal life now, if you believe, love and keep the commandments. That is exactly Catholic teaching: a person in the state of grace has eternal life and can know it with moral certainty.
Having eternal life now is not the same as being unable to lose it

Eternal life is the life of God in the soul. It can be killed by grave sin. John himself says there is ‘a sin unto death’ (5:16), committed by a ‘brother’, that is, a Christian. Jesus: ‘If any one abide not in me, he shall be cast forth as a branch, and shall wither’ (John 15:6). Paul: ‘Wherefore he that thinketh himself to stand, let him take heed lest he fall’ (1 Corinthians 10:12).
Paul did not claim absolute certainty about himself

‘I am not conscious to myself of any thing, yet am I not hereby justified; but he that judgeth me, is the Lord’ (1 Corinthians 4:4). ‘I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection: lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should become reprobate’ (9:27, adokimos). ‘Not as though I had already attained… but I follow after’ (Philippians 3:12). Near the end of his life, with the race finished, he says ‘there is laid up for me a crown of justice’ (2 Timothy 4:7–8).
Mortal and venial sin come from this very chapter

1 John 5:16–17 distinguishes ‘sin unto death’ and ‘sin not unto death’: ‘All iniquity is sin. And there is a sin unto death.’ This is a scriptural root of the Catholic distinction between mortal and venial sin (CCC 1854). A believer can know he is in grace (no unrepented mortal sin) and has eternal life, while humbly entrusting final perseverance to God.
fathers: Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace 13.40 (426–427)
No one can be certain that he is among the predestined while in this life, lest pride creep in; ‘let him that thinketh himself to stand take heed lest he fall’ (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, ST I-II q.112 a.5

No one can know with certainty that he has grace, except by special revelation; but one can know it conjecturally by signs: delight in God, contempt of worldly things, not being conscious of mortal sin.
Council of Trent, Session 6, chs. 9, 12, 13; canons 15–16
Against vain confidence; no one can know with the certainty of faith that he is predestined, except by special revelation; perseverance is a ‘great gift’ to be hoped for and prayed for.
We cannot be certain by our feelings, but reflection on God’s blessings gives assurance that grace is at work; we can and should hope for final perseverance.
obj: “If I can’t be 100% sure, I’ll live in fear.”

Catholics live in hope, which casts out servile fear (1 John 4:18). A child who knows his father loves him is not terrified, even though he knows he could run away. The Catholic’s confidence rests on Christ, the sacraments (especially confession) and God’s faithfulness, not on calculation.
“Someone who falls away was never truly saved (1 John 2:19).”

2:19 describes the specific schismatics who left, ‘that they may be manifest, that they are not all of us’. It is not a general rule that every apostate was never a believer. Hebrews 6:4–6 and 2 Peter 2:20–22 describe people who were truly enlightened, ‘made partakers of the Holy Ghost’, ‘escaped the pollutions of the world’, and then fell. And the ‘never truly saved’ answer destroys assurance far more: no one can know he is not a false believer until he dies.
“John says ‘know’, not ‘hope’.”
Yes: you can know you have eternal life now, if you are believing and obeying. Catholic confession gives exactly that knowledge. What John does not say is that you can know you will never fall.
deep.talk: “I love that verse: John wants Christians to be confident. Catholics can be confident too: if you trust Christ, are keeping his commandments and loving your neighbour, you have eternal life right now. But read the whole letter: John also says whoever says he knows God but doesn’t keep his commandments is a liar, and that there’s a ‘sin unto death’ a Christian can commit. So the confidence is real, but it’s the confidence of a child walking with his Father, not a ticket you can’t lose.”
deep.avoid: Do not tell anyone Catholics ‘can never know’ if they are in grace; Thomas and the Catechism say we can know by signs and should have confident hope. Do not imply Protestants all teach the same thing; Methodists and many Pentecostals reject ‘once saved, always saved’ too.
read: Council of Trent, Session 6, chs. 9–13, canons 15–16, 23
Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace; On the Gift of Perseverance

philippians|2.t: Work out your salvation with fear and trembling
philippians|2.claim: A Catholic proof-text, sometimes dismissed by Protestants as meaning only "show outwardly the salvation you already have for certain".
why: Paul addresses believers and asks them to work at their salvation, with fear. The next verse gives the balance: "For it is God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish" (2:13).
Both are true at once: God acts first and throughout, and we really cooperate. This is the Catholic teaching on grace and freedom.
philippians|2.cath: God works in us, and we work with him. Salvation is a gift we can still refuse.

deep.ctx: Philippians 2:5–11 is the great hymn of Christ’s self-emptying and exaltation. Paul immediately applies it: “Wherefore, my dearly beloved, (as you have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but much more now in my absence,) with fear and trembling work out your salvation. For it is God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will” (2:12–13). Then: ‘Do ye all things without murmurings… that you may be blameless’ (2:14–15), ‘holding forth the word of life to my glory in the day of Christ, because I have not run in vain’ (2:16).
deep.who: This is a verse Catholics usually quote, and Protestants answer it. The typical Protestant reading: ‘work out’ means ‘express outwardly’ or ‘bring to completion in daily life’ a salvation already fully possessed; it is about sanctification, not justification, and verse 13 shows God does it all. Some also say ‘salvation’ here means the health of the community, not individual eternal salvation.
deep.lang:
“Work out” (katergazesthe) means to accomplish, bring about, carry through to completion (the same verb in Romans 7:18, ‘to accomplish that which is good’). It is present imperative, plural: keep on working it out, all of you.

“Fear and trembling” (phobou kai tromou) is used for reverent awe in God’s presence (Psalm 2:11; 1 Corinthians 2:3; Ephesians 6:5).

“God who worketh in you” (ho energōn): the same root as ‘energy’. God is energizing your willing and working.
steps: Both verbs are real: we work because God works

Verse 12 commands our action; verse 13 grounds it in God’s action. Paul does not say ‘do nothing, because God does everything’, nor ‘God does part and you do part’. He says God works in us both the willing and the doing, so we can and must work. This is precisely the Catholic doctrine of grace and cooperation: grace does not compete with our freedom, it creates and frees it (CCC 2001–2002; Trent, Session 6, ch. 5).
‘Salvation’ in Paul includes final salvation

Paul speaks of salvation as future and not yet completed: ‘now our salvation is nearer than when we believed’ (Romans 13:11); ‘he that shall persevere to the end, he shall be saved’ (Matthew 24:13). In Philippians, Paul hopes ‘if by any means I may attain to the resurrection which is from the dead’ (3:11) and says he has ‘not already attained’ (3:12). The ‘day of Christ’ (2:16) is the final judgment.
‘Fear and trembling’ would make no sense if nothing were at stake

If salvation were already secured beyond any possibility of loss, why fear and tremble? The awe is the right attitude of a creature who knows that God is at work in him and that he can resist that work. ‘Be not highminded, but fear’ (Romans 11:20).
Perseverance is God’s gift and our task

Augustine and Trent both teach that final perseverance is a gift that cannot be merited, which God gives to those he will, and which we should pray for constantly (Trent, Session 6, ch. 13). This verse unites both sides: work with fear and trembling, because it is God who works in you.
fathers: Augustine, Sermon 169, 11.13 (c. 416)
‘He who made you without you will not justify you without you. He made you without your knowing it; he justifies you with your willing it’ (paraphrased translation).
Augustine, On Grace and Free Will 16.32 (426–427)
It is certain that we will when we will, but he makes us will; it is certain that we act when we act, but he makes us act (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Philippians, ch. 2, lect. 3
We are to work out salvation with fear, both because of our own weakness and because of the danger; yet not with despair, since God works in us (paraphrased).
Council of Trent, Session 6, ch. 13
Quotes this verse: let those who think they stand take heed lest they fall, and with fear and trembling work out their salvation.
obj: “It means working out what is already worked in, like working out a math problem already solved.”

‘Work out’ (katergazomai) does mean bring to completion, and Catholics agree that what God begins he means to complete (Philippians 1:6). But completion is not automatic; the command is addressed to their freedom, with ‘fear and trembling’, ‘that you may be blameless’ (2:15), ‘that I have not run in vain’ (2:16). Paul could ‘run in vain’ if they did not persevere.
“This is about sanctification, not justification.”

The Reformation distinction between justification (a once-for-all verdict) and sanctification (lifelong change) is not how Paul uses his vocabulary. He can speak of being ‘sanctified’ as past (1 Corinthians 6:11) and justification as future (Romans 2:13; Galatians 5:5, ‘we wait for the hope of justice’). Salvation includes both.
deep.talk: “Paul says, ‘work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you both to will and to do.’ Notice both halves. God does all of it, and we really do it, because he’s working through our freedom, not around it. Catholics don’t think we earn salvation. We think grace makes us able to cooperate, and that we have to keep cooperating until the end, with reverent fear, but without despair.”
deep.avoid: Do not use this verse alone to prove salvation by works; verse 13 is part of the sentence. Quote them together.
read: Augustine, On Grace and Free Will
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Philippians, ch. 2

hebrews|6.t: Those who fall away after being enlightened
hebrews|6.claim: Some Protestant traditions hold that a truly saved person can never lose salvation, so they explain this text as describing people who were never really believers.
why: The description is of genuine Christians: "once illuminated", having "tasted the heavenly gift", "made partakers of the Holy Ghost". The Fathers often read "illuminated" as meaning baptised.

The warning only makes sense if real believers can fall. Its point is that apostasy is extremely serious, not that repentance is impossible for God: the Church has always reconciled repentant sinners (2 Corinthians 2:7–8).
hebrews|6.cath: A Christian can fall from grace by grave sin, and can be restored by repentance and the sacrament of penance.

deep.ctx: Hebrews is written to Jewish Christians tempted to drift back from Christ to the old Temple system under pressure (10:32–39). In 5:11–6:3 the author rebukes them for spiritual immaturity. Then the warning: “For it is impossible for those who were once illuminated, have tasted also the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, have moreover tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come, and are fallen away: to be renewed again to penance, crucifying again to themselves the Son of God, and making him a mockery” (6:4–6). Verses 7–8: land that drinks the rain and bears thorns ‘is reprobate, and very near unto a curse’. Verse 9: ‘But… we trust better things of you.’
deep.who: This is a passage Catholics (and Arminian Protestants) use against eternal security. Calvinists and Baptists answer in three main ways: (1) the people described were never truly regenerated; they only ‘tasted’; (2) the passage is hypothetical (‘if they fell away, which cannot happen’); (3) the loss is of rewards, not salvation. Separately, the verse was historically used by rigorists (Montanists, Novatianists) to claim that Christians who apostatize cannot be forgiven.
deep.lang:
“Once illuminated” (hapax phōtisthentas): ‘illumination’ (phōtismos) was an early Christian name for baptism (Justin Martyr, First Apology 61, c. 155).

“Partakers of the Holy Ghost” (metochous pneumatos hagiou): the same word metochos is used in 3:14, ‘we are made partakers (metochoi) of Christ, yet so if we hold the beginning of his substance firm unto the end’, a real participation.

“Tasted” (geusamenous): the same verb is used of Christ ‘tasting death for all’ (2:9). Tasting in Hebrews means real experience, not a sample.

“Fallen away” (parapesontas) is an aorist participle in the same series as the others: it is not grammatically ‘if they fall away’; it simply describes them.
steps: The description is of real Christians

Every phrase describes genuine Christian experience: baptismal illumination, receiving the heavenly gift (the Eucharist or grace), sharing in the Holy Spirit, experiencing the word and miracles. The same author uses ‘partakers’ for real union with Christ (3:14) and ‘tasted’ for Christ’s real death (2:9). If these are unregenerate people, words have no meaning. Hebrews’ whole purpose is to warn real believers against apostasy (2:1–3; 3:12–14; 10:26–31; 12:15–17).
So a true believer can fall away

That is the plain sense, and the consistent teaching of the Catholic Church (Trent, Session 6, canon 23 condemns the claim that a justified person cannot lose grace). The whole of Hebrews 3 builds on Israel in the desert: they were truly delivered from Egypt and still ‘their bodies were overthrown in the desert’ (1 Corinthians 10:5).
‘Impossible to renew to penance’ does not mean God cannot forgive

Read in context, the author says it is impossible for them to be renewed while they keep on crucifying Christ (anastaurountas, present participle: ‘while they are crucifying’). As long as someone persists in repudiating Christ, the only sacrifice that saves, there is nothing else to turn to (10:26: ‘there is now left no sacrifice for sins’). The Church condemned the Novatianist reading that apostates can never be reconciled; Peter himself denied Christ three times and was restored (John 21:15–17).
The Fathers read ‘renewal’ as re-baptism

Many Fathers and Thomas read ‘impossible to renew’ as: it is impossible to be baptized a second time. Baptism is given once (Ephesians 4:5); the sinner after baptism is restored by penance, the ‘second plank after shipwreck’ (Tertullian; Jerome; Trent, Session 14, ch. 2).
The ‘hypothetical’ reading empties the warning

A warning about something that cannot happen is no warning. And verse 9, ‘we trust better things of you’, assumes the readers could go either way; the author is hopeful, not certain. 10:38–39: ‘if he withdraw himself, he shall not please my soul. But we are not the children of withdrawing unto perdition.’
fathers: Justin Martyr, First Apology 61 (c. 155)
‘This washing is called illumination, because they who learn these things are illuminated in their understandings.’
John Chrysostom, Homilies on Hebrews 9 (c. 400)
Explains ‘impossible to renew’ as: there is no second baptism; but repentance is still possible (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Hebrews, ch. 6, lect. 1
Impossible to be renewed by baptism again, since baptism configures to Christ’s death, which happened once; but not impossible to be restored by penance (paraphrased).
Council of Trent, Session 6, ch. 14 and canon 23; Session 14, ch. 2
The justified can lose grace by mortal sin and recover it by the sacrament of penance.
obj: “They only tasted; they never really ate.”
Hebrews 2:9: Jesus ‘tasted death for all’. Did he only sample death? The word means to experience fully.
“John 10:28 says no one can snatch Christ’s sheep.”

No outside power can. But the sheep can stop following (10:27, ‘my sheep… follow me’, present tense). Hebrews warns about our own unbelief: ‘lest perhaps there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, to depart from the living God’ (3:12).
“If Christians can fall, salvation depends on us.”

It depends on God, who gives both the grace and the perseverance; but God does not save us against our will. A gift can be rejected. That is why Hebrews tells us to ‘hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering’ (10:23).
deep.talk: “Look at how Hebrews describes these people: they’ve been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit, tasted God’s word and the powers of the age to come. That’s a Christian. And then they fall away. The writer isn’t speaking of fake believers; he’s warning real ones. Catholics read it that way: a Christian can walk away from Christ. The good news is that as long as we’re alive, we can come back, like Peter did after denying him.”
deep.avoid: Do not use this verse to suggest apostates can never return; that was the Novatianist heresy. Do not suggest Calvinists ‘don’t care’ about holiness; they argue perseverance shows itself in holiness.
read: Council of Trent, Session 6, chs. 12–15, canon 23; Session 14, chs. 1–2
