Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Hebrews, ch. 6
Scot McKnight (1992) ‘The Warning Passages of Hebrews’, Trinity Journal 13, 21–59 (an evangelical scholar who reads them as real warnings)

2-timothy|3.claim: Taken as proof of sola scriptura: the Bible alone is the sufficient rule of faith, so tradition and the teaching authority of the Church are unnecessary.
why: The verse says Scripture is inspired and "profitable". It does not say it is the only authority. A thing can be profitable without being the only thing needed.
The "scripture" Timothy knew "from thy infancy" (3:15) was the Old Testament. If the verse proved sufficiency, it would prove the Old Testament was sufficient without the New.

Paul tells the same Church to "hold the traditions, which you have learned, whether by word or by our epistle" (2 Thessalonians 2:14), and calls the Church, not the Bible, "the pillar and ground of the truth" (1 Timothy 3:15).
No verse lists which books belong in the Bible. That was recognised by the Church in councils such as Rome (382), Hippo (393) and Carthage (397). Sola scriptura cannot be proved from Scripture alone.
2-timothy|3.cath: Scripture is God's inspired word, handed on and interpreted within the living Tradition of the Church, which wrote, collected and guards it.

deep.ctx: 2 Timothy is Paul’s last letter, written from prison in Rome to his disciple Timothy, whom he had placed over the church at Ephesus. Chapter 3 warns of ‘dangerous times’ and false teachers (3:1–9). Then: ‘But continue thou in those things which thou hast learned, and which have been committed to thee: knowing of whom thou hast learned them; and because from thy infancy thou hast known the holy scriptures, which can instruct thee to salvation, by the faith which is in Christ Jesus. All scripture, inspired of God, is profitable to teach, to reprove, to correct, to instruct in justice, that the man of God may be perfect, furnished to every good work’ (3:14–17). Chapter 4 then commands Timothy to ‘preach the word’ (4:2). Earlier Paul had told him: ‘the things which thou hast heard of me by many witnesses, the same commend to faithful men, who shall be fit to teach others also’ (2:2).
deep.who:
This is the central proof-text for sola scriptura, the Reformation principle that Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith: all that is necessary for salvation is contained in Scripture, either explicitly or by necessary inference (Westminster Confession, 1646, I.6). The argument: Scripture is God-breathed; it makes the man of God ‘complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work’; if Scripture equips completely, nothing else (Tradition, Magisterium) is needed as a rule of faith.

The strongest form does not deny that tradition and church authority exist; it says they are fallible and subordinate, while only Scripture is ‘God-breathed’.
deep.lang:
“Inspired of God” (theopneustos): literally ‘God-breathed’. Catholics fully affirm it (Dei Verbum 11).

“Profitable” (ōphelimos): useful, beneficial. It does not mean ‘sufficient’ (hikanos).

“Perfect” (artios) and “furnished” (exērtismenos): fit, complete, equipped. The same kind of language is used elsewhere of other means: ‘let patience have its perfect work; that you may be perfect (teleioi) and entire (holoklēroi), failing in nothing’ (James 1:4).

“The man of God” is a title for a minister of God (1 Timothy 6:11; used of prophets in the Old Testament): Paul is speaking of Timothy’s equipment as a pastor.
steps: Catholics affirm that all Scripture is God-breathed

The Church teaches that the books of Scripture have God as their author and teach ‘solidly, faithfully and without error that truth which God wanted put into sacred writings for the sake of salvation’ (Dei Verbum 11). The disagreement is not about inspiration but about whether Scripture is the only rule of faith.
‘Profitable’ is not ‘sufficient’

Paul says Scripture is useful for teaching, reproof, correction and training. Something can be necessary and useful without being the only thing needed. Water is profitable for life, and you still need food. The verse never says ‘only Scripture’.
The verse proves too much, if it proves sola scriptura

The Scriptures Timothy knew ‘from infancy’ (3:15) were the Old Testament. Much of the New Testament had not yet been written, and no list of New Testament books existed. If 3:16 means ‘Scripture alone is sufficient’, then the Old Testament alone was sufficient, and the New Testament unnecessary. No Protestant accepts that conclusion.
‘Perfect, furnished’ does not exclude other means

James 1:4 says patience makes us ‘perfect and entire, failing in nothing’. No one concludes that patience alone suffices for the Christian life. Ephesians 4:11–13 says Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers ‘for the perfecting of the saints… unto a perfect man’. If ‘equipped’ language makes Scripture sole, it makes pastors sole too.
The same letter commands oral tradition

‘The things which thou hast heard of me by many witnesses, the same commend to faithful men, who shall be fit to teach others also’ (2:2): four generations of oral transmission (Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others). 3:14: ‘continue in those things which thou hast learned… knowing of whom thou hast learned them’. And 2 Thessalonians 2:14: ‘hold the traditions, which you have learned, whether by word, or by our epistle’.
Scripture does not tell us which books are Scripture

No inspired list of the 27 New Testament books exists. Some books were disputed for centuries (Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude, Revelation). The canon was recognized by the Church: the earliest list matching our 27 books is Athanasius’ Festal Letter 39 (367); councils at Rome (382), Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) set out the canon. Sola scriptura depends on a list that Scripture itself does not provide.
Scripture itself points to a living authority

‘The church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth’ (1 Timothy 3:15). ‘If he will not hear the church, let him be to thee as the heathen’ (Matthew 18:17). In Acts 15 a disputed question is settled by the apostles and elders in council: ‘it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us’ (15:28). Scripture never says the Church’s teaching authority will cease when the last apostle dies.
fathers: Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.4.1 (c. 180)

Even if the apostles had left no writings, we should follow the order of tradition they handed to those to whom they entrusted the churches; many barbarian peoples believe in Christ without paper or ink, keeping the ancient tradition (paraphrased).
Basil the Great, On the Holy Spirit 27.66 (c. 375)

Of the beliefs and practices preserved in the Church, some come from written teaching, others from apostolic tradition handed down ‘in a mystery’; both have the same force (paraphrased). Examples he gives: the sign of the Cross, facing east in prayer, the words of the epiclesis.
Vincent of Lérins, Commonitorium 2.5 (434)

The canon of Scripture is complete and sufficient, yet because people interpret it in different ways, it must be read according to the Church’s tradition: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all (paraphrased).
Athanasius, Festal Letter 39 (367)
The first surviving list of exactly the 27 books of the New Testament.
Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum 9–10 (1965)
Scripture and Tradition flow from the same divine wellspring; the Magisterium is not above the Word of God but serves it.
obj: “Tradition can be corrupted; Scripture can’t.”

Scripture cannot be corrupted, but interpretations of it can, and have been, which is why there are thousands of Protestant denominations disagreeing about baptism, the Eucharist, predestination and church order, all claiming Scripture alone. The question is not whether Scripture is infallible but who has authority to interpret it when Christians disagree (2 Peter 3:16: ‘things hard to be understood, which the unlearned and unstable wrest… to their own destruction’).
“Paul’s oral traditions were later written down in the New Testament.”

That is an assumption, not something Scripture says. Paul never says that his oral teaching would all be written, or that the written record would replace the living teaching office he set up in each city (Titus 1:5). And the Church’s acceptance of infant baptism, Sunday worship, the canon itself and the Trinitarian formulation of the creeds rely on tradition interpreting Scripture.
“The Bereans tested Paul by Scripture (Acts 17:11).”
See the note on Acts 17:11: they checked whether the Old Testament supported an oral apostolic message, then accepted that message, which was more than the Old Testament contained.
“Jesus rebuked tradition (Mark 7).”
He rebuked human traditions that contradicted God’s law. See the note on Mark 7:8.
deep.talk: “I believe every word of 2 Timothy 3:16: all Scripture is God-breathed. But it says Scripture is ‘profitable’, not that it’s the only authority. And the Scripture Timothy knew from childhood was the Old Testament; if this verse meant ‘Scripture alone is enough’, he’d have no need of the New Testament. In the same letter Paul tells Timothy to pass on what he heard from Paul orally to faithful men who will teach others (2:2), and in 2 Thessalonians he says to hold the traditions ‘whether by word or by letter’. So the Bible itself points to Scripture and apostolic Tradition together, with the Church as ‘the pillar and foundation of the truth’.”
deep.avoid: Do not say Catholics believe Tradition is a second set of doctrines unrelated to Scripture; Dei Verbum calls them one deposit. Do not suggest the Church ‘created’ the Bible; she recognized and received the inspired books. And do not overclaim the Council of Rome (382): its list survives in a later document whose dating is debated.
read: Yves Congar (1966) Tradition and Traditions. London: Burns & Oates
Keith Mathison (2001) The Shape of Sola Scriptura. Moscow, ID: Canon Press (a careful Protestant defence, for comparison)

mark|7.claim: Jesus condemned tradition, so Catholic tradition must be condemned too.
why: Jesus condemns human traditions that cancel God's commandment. His example is "Corban", a custom that let people avoid supporting their parents (7:10–13). He is not condemning tradition as such.

The New Testament praises apostolic tradition: "I praise you, brethren… that you keep my ordinances [traditions] as I delivered them to you" (1 Corinthians 11:2); "hold the traditions" (2 Thessalonians 2:14).
Even the Gospels were tradition preached by word before they were written down (Luke 1:1–2).
mark|7.cath: Human customs that override God's law are rejected. The apostolic Tradition handed on from Christ is part of God's word.

deep.ctx: Mark 7:1–13. Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem see Jesus’ disciples eating with unwashed hands, against ‘the tradition of the ancients’ (7:3). Mark explains for Gentile readers the Pharisaic washings of hands, cups and pots (7:3–4). Jesus answers with Isaiah 29:13 (‘This people honoureth me with their lips…’) and then: ‘For leaving the commandment of God, you hold the tradition of men, the washing of pots and of cups… Well do you make void the commandment of God, that you may keep your own tradition’ (7:8–9). His example: the custom of ‘Corban’, by which a son could declare his goods dedicated to God and so avoid supporting his parents, breaking the fourth commandment (7:10–13).
deep.who: Jesus condemns ‘the tradition of men’. Catholic tradition (Mary’s assumption, purgatory, indulgences, the papacy, devotions) is said to be exactly this: human additions that make void God’s word. True Christians follow Scripture alone and reject human traditions.
deep.lang:
“Tradition” (paradosis) means ‘that which is handed over’. The New Testament uses it negatively for human customs that contradict God (Mark 7:8–9, 13; Colossians 2:8) and positively for apostolic teaching: ‘keep my ordinances (paradoseis) as I have delivered them to you’ (1 Corinthians 11:2); ‘hold the traditions (paradoseis)’ (2 Thessalonians 2:14); ‘withdraw yourselves from every brother walking disorderly, and not according to the tradition (paradosin) which they have received of us’ (2 Thessalonians 3:6).

“Of men” (tōn anthrōpōn) is the key qualifier.
steps: Jesus condemns traditions that nullify God’s commandment

His charge is precise: ‘you make void the commandment of God, that you may keep your own tradition’ (7:9). The Corban custom cancelled the duty to honour parents. Any tradition that contradicts God’s word stands condemned. Catholics agree.
The New Testament praises apostolic tradition

The same word, paradosis, is used with approval for what the apostles handed on (1 Corinthians 11:2; 2 Thessalonians 2:14; 3:6). Paul ‘delivered’ (paredōka) the Eucharist (1 Corinthians 11:23) and the creed of the resurrection (15:3). The distinction is between traditions of men and the tradition of God given through Christ and the apostles.
Jesus himself honoured Jewish tradition where it was faithful

‘The scribes and the Pharisees have sitten on the chair of Moses. All things therefore whatsoever they shall say to you, observe and do’ (Matthew 23:2–3). The ‘chair of Moses’ is not in the Old Testament; it is a tradition of teaching authority. Jesus attended synagogue on the Sabbath (Luke 4:16), a practice developed after the Exile, and the feast of Dedication (John 10:22), which comes from the Maccabees, not the Torah.
The New Testament draws on oral tradition

Jude 9 mentions Michael disputing with the devil over Moses’ body; 2 Timothy 3:8 names Jannes and Jambres, Pharaoh’s magicians; 1 Corinthians 10:4 speaks of the rock that ‘followed’ Israel; Matthew 2:23 cites a prophecy (‘he shall be called a Nazarene’) found in no prophetic book. None of these is in the Old Testament.
Test each Catholic doctrine, don’t assume

The fair question is whether a given Catholic teaching contradicts Scripture as Corban did. Purgatory, praying for the dead, honouring Mary, the papacy: Catholics argue each is rooted in Scripture and early tradition and contradicts none of it (see the other notes). Labelling them ‘traditions of men’ assumes what needs to be proved.
fathers: Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.3.1–3 (c. 180)
The tradition of the apostles is manifest in every church, through the succession of bishops; he lists the bishops of Rome from Peter and Paul to Eleutherius (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, Catena Aurea on Mark 7
Collects patristic comments that the Lord condemns traditions which, invented by men, are preferred to God’s commandments (paraphrased).
obj: “All extra-biblical tradition is ‘of men’.”

Then the Christian canon, the doctrine of the Trinity in its developed form, Sunday worship and infant baptism would also be ‘traditions of men’, since Scripture does not explicitly define them. Most Protestants accept these because the early Church handed them on.
“Paul’s traditions were later fully written down.”
Possibly some were; but Scripture never says all were, and 2 Thessalonians 2:14 names both channels side by side.
deep.talk: “Jesus condemned traditions that cancel God’s commandments, like Corban, which let people dodge supporting their parents. Catholics agree; any custom like that is wrong. But the same word ‘tradition’ is used positively by Paul: ‘hold the traditions you were taught, whether by word or by letter’ (2 Thessalonians 2:15 in most Bibles). So the question isn’t whether tradition exists, but whose: human customs against God’s word, or what the apostles handed on.”
deep.avoid: Do not deny that some popular Catholic customs have become superstitious at times; the Church herself has reformed them (Trent, Session 25). Distinguish dogma from piety.

matthew|15.claim: Used against Catholic practices such as fasting rules, feast days or priestly celibacy as "commandments of men".
why: Jesus applies Isaiah to those who use human rules to escape God's law. The Church's disciplines are not taught as divine law where they are not, and they help people keep God's law.
Christ gave his apostles authority to bind and loose (Matthew 18:18), and they made disciplinary rules themselves (Acts 15:28–29).
matthew|15.cath: The Church distinguishes unchangeable doctrine from disciplines she sets with Christ's authority for the good of souls.

deep.ctx: Matthew 15:1–20 is Matthew’s version of the dispute in Mark 7. Pharisees ask why the disciples ‘transgress the tradition of the ancients’ by not washing their hands. Jesus replies: ‘Why do you also transgress the commandment of God for your tradition?’ (15:3), gives the Corban example (15:4–6), and quotes Isaiah 29:13: ‘This people honoureth me with their lips: but their heart is far from me. And in vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men’ (15:8–9). He then teaches that what defiles a man comes from the heart (15:10–20).
deep.who: Used like Mark 7:8: Catholic doctrines are ‘commandments of men’, so Catholic worship is ‘in vain’. Often applied to rules such as Friday abstinence, clerical celibacy, holy days of obligation and the Rosary.
deep.lang: Jesus quotes the Greek Old Testament of Isaiah 29:13: didaskontes didaskalias entalmata anthrōpōn, ‘teaching as doctrines the precepts of men’. The fault is presenting human precepts as if they were God’s, while the heart is far from God.
steps: The target is hypocrisy and the cancelling of God’s law

Isaiah’s charge is lip-service with a distant heart. Jesus applies it to leaders who use their customs to escape God’s commandment. Catholics accept the warning for themselves: external religion without a converted heart is vain (CCC 2111; Isaiah 1:11–17).
Jesus gave his apostles authority to bind and loose

‘Whatsoever you shall bind upon earth, shall be bound also in heaven’ (Matthew 18:18; 16:19). In rabbinic language ‘binding and loosing’ meant declaring what is forbidden or permitted. Christ gave this authority to the apostles, and they used it: the Council of Jerusalem bound Gentile Christians to abstain from blood and things strangled (Acts 15:28–29), a rule not found in any Gospel.
Church disciplines are not passed off as divine doctrine

The Church distinguishes clearly between divine law (unchangeable) and ecclesiastical law (changeable disciplines such as Friday penance, fasting rules, celibacy in the Latin Church). She does not claim that Friday abstinence is a commandment from Sinai; she binds it, as the apostles did in Acts 15, for the good of souls (CCC 2041–2043). That is the opposite of what Isaiah condemns.
Every Christian community has ‘precepts’

Protestant churches set the time of Sunday worship, communion practice, membership rules and pastors’ qualifications. These are not in Scripture in detail either. Authority to order the community for worship is biblical (1 Corinthians 14:40; Hebrews 13:17).
fathers: Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, on 15:9 (398)
The Lord condemns those who prefer the traditions of the Pharisees to the commandments of God, as in the matter of honouring parents (paraphrased).
Augustine, Letter 54 to Januarius 1.1 (c. 400)

Some customs are observed throughout the world by apostolic tradition or by councils; others vary by place. Where a custom is neither against faith nor morals, follow the custom of the church where you are (paraphrased).
obj: “Celibacy and fasting rules are exactly commandments of men.”

They are commandments of the Church, which has authority from Christ to bind (Matthew 18:18), and they contradict no commandment of God. Paul himself praises celibacy (1 Corinthians 7:7–8, 32–35), and Jesus said his disciples would fast (Matthew 9:15).
deep.talk: “Jesus is quoting Isaiah against people who honoured God with their lips while using their customs to avoid God’s actual commandments. That warning is for all of us. But Jesus also gave his apostles authority to bind and loose, and they used it: in Acts 15 they made rules for Gentile Christians that aren’t in the Gospels. When the Church sets a fasting rule, she isn’t claiming it came from Sinai; she’s using that same authority for our good.”
deep.avoid: Do not present disciplines (like Friday abstinence) as dogmas. That actually would be the error the verse condemns.

revelation|22.t: "If any man shall add to these things"
revelation|22.claim: Used to say Catholics "added books" to the Bible (Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, the Maccabees).
why: The warning is about "the words of the prophecy of this book", that is, Revelation itself. Deuteronomy 4:2 has a similar warning, and later books were still added to Scripture after it.

The deuterocanonical books were not added by Catholics. They were in the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament that the apostles mostly quoted, and in the canon lists of the councils of Rome (382), Hippo (393) and Carthage (397). The Reformers removed them in the 1500s.
The New Testament echoes them: Hebrews 11:35 refers to the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 7, and Wisdom 2:12–20 is closely paralleled in Matthew 27:41–43.
revelation|22.cath: The Church received a canon of 73 books from the early centuries and has kept it.

deep.ctx: These are the last words of the last book of the Bible. ‘For I testify to every one that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book: If any man shall add to these things, God shall add unto him the plagues written in this book. And if any man shall take away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part out of the book of life, and out of the holy city’ (22:18–19).
deep.who: This warning is applied to the whole Bible: nothing may be added to God’s word. Catholic dogmas not found in Scripture (the Assumption, the Immaculate Conception, papal infallibility, purgatory) are said to ‘add to’ Scripture and fall under this curse.
deep.lang: “This book” (tou bibliou toutou) and ‘the words of the prophecy of this book’ refer to the book of Revelation itself, the scroll John was told to write (1:11, 19). When Revelation was written, the books of the New Testament had not been gathered into one volume; there was no ‘Bible’ in our sense for ‘this book’ to mean.
steps: The warning protects the text of Revelation

Ancient authors and copyists sometimes added warnings to protect a document from tampering. John warns copyists and readers not to alter this prophecy. The Church agrees entirely and has never added words to Revelation.
Moses said the same thing, and many books followed

‘You shall not add to the word that I speak to you, neither shall you take away from it’ (Deuteronomy 4:2; 12:32). If that meant ‘no more inspired writing’, the Prophets, Psalms and the whole New Testament would be forbidden additions. It meant: do not alter what God has given.
Proverbs 30:6 is the same principle
‘Add not any thing to his words, lest thou be reproved, and found a liar.’ Yet Proverbs was followed by many inspired books. The principle forbids falsifying God’s word, not receiving more of it.
Doctrinal definitions do not add to revelation

When the Church defines a dogma, she does not claim new revelation: public revelation ended with the apostles (Dei Verbum 4; CCC 66). She declares what was always part of the deposit of faith, received in Scripture and Tradition, as the Council of Nicaea did when it defined that the Son is ‘consubstantial’ with the Father, a word not in Scripture. Protestants accept Nicaea’s ‘addition’ of homoousios for the same reason.
‘Taking away’ cuts both ways

The verse also warns against taking away. The Reformers removed seven books that had been read in the Church’s Bible for over a thousand years (Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1–2 Maccabees), and Luther initially wanted to relegate James, Jude, Hebrews and Revelation to an appendix. Catholics should not use this to score points, but it shows that the verse is about the integrity of Revelation’s own text.
fathers: Irenaeus, Against Heresies V.30.1 (c. 180)

Warns of those who alter the number of the beast in Revelation, and cites the curse on those who add or subtract from the prophecy (paraphrased): an early example of reading it as protecting Revelation’s text.
‘The Christian economy… will never pass away; and no new public revelation is to be expected’; yet the Church grows in understanding of what was revealed.
obj: “God providentially placed this warning at the end of the Bible to close the canon.”

The order of books in our Bibles comes from later Christian tradition (the Church’s), not from the authors. Revelation may not even have been the last New Testament book written. To make the warning about the whole canon you must rely on the Church’s ordering of the books.
“Catholic dogmas are additions.”
Each must be shown to contradict or exceed the apostolic deposit. A definition that explains what was received (as Nicaea explained the Son’s divinity) is not an addition.
deep.talk: “John is talking about ‘the words of the prophecy of this book’: the book of Revelation. Moses said the same in Deuteronomy, ‘don’t add to or subtract from what I command you’, and God still gave the prophets and the New Testament afterwards. It’s a warning not to tamper with the text, not a statement about the whole Bible, which didn’t exist as one book yet.”
deep.avoid: Do not imply the Church can create new revelation; she cannot (CCC 66).

john|6.claim: Read as Jesus explaining that the "eat my flesh" discourse was only symbolic: he meant spiritual believing, not real eating.
why: Jesus does not say "my flesh profits nothing". His flesh is given "for the life of the world" (6:52). "The flesh" here means the merely natural, unaided way of understanding, as in "flesh and blood hath not revealed it to thee" (Matthew 16:17).
"The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life" means they are words of the Holy Spirit, to be received by faith, not that they are figures of speech.

Watch what happens next: "many of his disciples went back and walked no more with him" (6:67). If he had meant a symbol, he would have called them back and explained, as he did elsewhere when people misunderstood (Matthew 16:6–12). He let them go and asked the Twelve if they would leave too.
Peter answers, "Lord, to whom shall we go? Thou hast the words of eternal life" (6:69). He accepts without understanding.
john|6.cath: Only faith, given by the Spirit, can accept that the bread Christ gives is his real flesh. That is why "the flesh", unaided human reason, profits nothing here.
john|6.src: CCC 1336, 1374–1381; Trent, Session 13; Augustine, Tractates on John 27

deep.ctx: John 6 opens with the feeding of the five thousand at Passover time (6:4). The next day Jesus teaches in the synagogue at Capernaum: ‘I am the bread of life’ (6:35, 48). Then he goes further: ‘the bread that I will give, is my flesh, for the life of the world’ (6:52). The Jews dispute: ‘How can this man give us his flesh to eat?’ Jesus does not soften it: ‘Amen, amen I say unto you: Except you eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you. He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath everlasting life… For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed’ (6:54–56). Many disciples say: ‘This saying is hard, and who can hear it?’ (6:61). Jesus answers: ‘Doth this scandalize you? If then you shall see the Son of man ascend up where he was before? It is the spirit that quickeneth: the flesh profiteth nothing. The words that I have spoken to you, are spirit and life. But there are some of you that believe not’ (6:62–65). ‘After this many of his disciples went back; and walked no more with him’ (6:67). Peter: ‘Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life’ (6:69).
deep.who: Verse 64 (63 in most Bibles) is the main text for a symbolic or ‘spiritual’ reading of John 6. Zwingli made it central in his debate with Luther at Marburg (1529): Jesus himself explains that eating his flesh would profit nothing; his words are ‘spirit’, meaning they are to be understood spiritually, as believing in him. Eating = believing (6:35: ‘he that cometh to me shall not hunger: and he that believeth in me shall never thirst’). The discourse is about faith, not a sacrament.
deep.lang:
Verse numbers: Douay 6:52 = KJV 6:51; 6:54–59 = 6:53–58; 6:64 = 6:63; 6:67 = 6:66; 6:69 = 6:68.

From 6:55 (KJV 6:54) Jesus switches from the ordinary verb for eating (phagein/esthiō) to trōgō, ‘to chew, munch’, four times (KJV 6:54, 56, 57, 58). It is a vivid physical verb; elsewhere in John only at 13:18 (‘he that eateth (trōgōn) bread with me’).

“Meat indeed… drink indeed” (alēthēs brōsis… alēthēs posis): ‘true food… true drink’.

“The flesh” in 6:64 is hē sarx, without ‘my’. In John ‘flesh’ alone means human nature left to itself, natural understanding: ‘That which is born of the flesh, is flesh’ (3:6); ‘You judge according to the flesh’ (8:15).

In Hebrew and Aramaic idiom, ‘to eat someone’s flesh’ figuratively meant to slander or attack them: ‘whilst the wicked draw near against me, to eat my flesh’ (Psalm 26:2, 27:2 in most Bibles); Micah 3:3.
steps: Jesus does not say ‘my flesh profiteth nothing’

He says ‘the flesh’. His own flesh, he has just said, is ‘given for the life of the world’ (6:52). If his flesh profits nothing, the Incarnation and the Cross profit nothing. No Christian believes that. ‘The flesh’ here is the natural, unaided way of understanding (as in 3:6; 8:15), the way the crowd was hearing him: as if he meant cannibalism, cutting off pieces of a corpse.
‘Spirit and life’ means his words are true and life-giving

‘The words that I have spoken to you, are spirit and life.’ Spirit in John is not the opposite of ‘real’ or ‘physical’; God is spirit (4:24) and supremely real. Jesus says his words must be received by the Spirit, by faith, not by fleshly reasoning. That is why he adds: ‘there are some of you that believe not’ (6:65). The problem is not that they took him too literally; it is that they did not believe.
Jesus intensifies, he does not soften

When the crowd objects ‘How can this man give us his flesh to eat?’ (6:53), Jesus repeats the point more strongly six times, uses the physical verb trōgō, and says his flesh is ‘true food’. If he meant only ‘believe in me’, he could have said so and kept his disciples. Elsewhere, when people misunderstood a metaphor, Jesus corrected them (Matthew 16:6–12, ‘the leaven of the Pharisees’; John 3:3–5; 11:11–14).
He lets disciples leave rather than explain it away

‘After this many of his disciples went back; and walked no more with him’ (6:67): the only time in the Gospels that disciples leave Jesus over a doctrine. He turns to the Twelve: ‘Will you also go away?’ He accepts losing them rather than say ‘I only meant it symbolically’. Peter does not understand either, but trusts: ‘thou hast the words of eternal life’.
A metaphorical reading would mean ‘slander me’

In the biblical idiom, eating someone’s flesh and drinking his blood figuratively meant to assault or revile him (Psalm 26:2; Micah 3:3; also Revelation 17:6, 16). If Jesus were speaking metaphorically, he would be saying ‘unless you revile me, you shall not have life’. The figure does not work.
The discourse has two parts

Catholics agree that the first part (6:35–51) is about believing in Jesus, the bread from heaven. But from 6:52 the gift shifts to the future (‘the bread that I will give’), the content to ‘my flesh… for the life of the world’, and the act from coming and believing to eating and drinking. The setting is Passover (6:4), when the lamb was eaten. The Last Supper fulfils it: ‘This is my body… This is my blood’.
The earliest Christians read it literally

See the Fathers below: Ignatius (c. 107), Justin (c. 155), Irenaeus (c. 180), Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 350). The symbolic reading of the Eucharist as only a sign appears in a developed form in the 9th century (Ratramnus, disputed) and 11th century (Berengar, who recanted), and became widespread only with Zwingli in the 1520s. Luther himself rejected Zwingli’s reading and insisted ‘This is my body’ means what it says (Marburg, 1529).
fathers: Ignatius of Antioch, Letter to the Smyrnaeans 7.1 (c. 107)
Of the Docetist heretics: ‘They abstain from the Eucharist and from prayer, because they confess not the Eucharist to be the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins.’
Justin Martyr, First Apology 66 (c. 155)
‘Not as common bread and common drink do we receive these… the food which is blessed by the prayer of his word… is the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh.’
Irenaeus, Against Heresies V.2.2–3 (c. 180)
The bread which receives the word of God becomes the Eucharist, the body of Christ, and our bodies nourished by it are prepared for resurrection (paraphrased).
Cyril of Jerusalem, Mystagogical Catecheses 4.6 (c. 350)
‘Do not regard them as bare bread and wine; for they are, according to the Lord’s declaration, the body and blood of Christ. Though sense suggests this to you, let faith establish you’ (paraphrased).
Augustine, Tractates on John 27.5 (c. 414)

On 6:64: they understood the flesh carnally, as if it were to be cut up like meat in the market; ‘the flesh profiteth nothing’ means flesh understood that way (paraphrased). Augustine also stresses spiritual eating by faith.
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on John, ch. 6, lect. 8
‘The flesh’ means carnal understanding; Christ’s flesh, united to the Word and the Spirit, profits much (paraphrased).
obj: “Jesus also said ‘I am the door’ and ‘I am the vine’. He speaks in metaphors.”

True, and no one walked away from him over ‘I am the door’. The metaphors are obvious and point to a single feature. In John 6 his hearers understood him literally, he repeated himself more strongly, and he let them go. That is not how Jesus handles a metaphor.
“Eating is believing; 6:35 equates them.”

6:35 uses hunger and thirst as images of faith, and Catholics accept that part of the chapter is about faith. But in 6:52–59 Jesus speaks of his flesh given for the life of the world, of drinking his blood (which has no ‘faith’ parallel), and of future giving. And faith is required to receive the Eucharist; the two are not alternatives.
“Drinking blood was forbidden by the Law (Leviticus 17:10–14).”

Precisely why the crowd was scandalized, and why Jesus’ insistence is so striking. The Law forbade blood because ‘the life of the flesh is in the blood’ (Leviticus 17:11). Jesus gives his life to us in his blood. The Eucharist is not cannibalism: we receive the living, risen Christ under sacramental signs, not dead flesh.
“Augustine was a symbolist.”

Augustine uses the language of sign and sacrament and stresses faith, but he also writes that Christ ‘held himself in his own hands’ at the Supper (Exposition on Psalm 33, Sermon 1.10), that no one eats that flesh without first adoring it (Exposition on Psalm 98.9), and that the bread on the altar, sanctified by the word, is the body of Christ (Sermon 227). Sign and reality go together for him.
deep.talk: “Jesus didn’t say ‘my flesh profits nothing’; he said ‘the flesh’, meaning purely human understanding, the way the crowd heard him, as if they’d be cutting him up like meat. His own flesh, he’d just said, is given for the life of the world. And look what happens: many disciples walk away, and Jesus lets them go rather than say ‘I only meant it as a symbol’. The early Christians, like Ignatius of Antioch around 107 AD, said heretics stayed away from the Eucharist ‘because they don’t confess it to be the flesh of our Saviour’.”
deep.avoid: Do not imply Catholics think the Eucharist is ‘flesh’ in a crude physical sense (pieces of muscle); Christ is present sacramentally, by way of substance (ST III q.76). Do not say every Protestant is a symbolist; Lutherans affirm the real presence.
read: Brant Pitre (2011) Jesus and the Jewish Roots of the Eucharist. New York: Doubleday
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on John, ch. 6, lects. 6–8

luke|22.t: "Do this for a commemoration of me"
luke|22.claim: Taken to mean the Lord's Supper is only a memorial: we remember a past event, and the bread stays bread.
why: The Greek word is anamnesis. In the Passover, which Jesus is celebrating, a "memorial" (Exodus 12:14) is not just thinking about the past; it makes the saving event present to those who celebrate it.

Jesus does not say "this represents my body" but "this is my body, which is given for you". Paul says the cup is "the communion of the blood of Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:16) and that receiving unworthily makes a person "guilty of the body and of the blood of the Lord" (11:27). You cannot be guilty of the body of a symbol.
Every Christian writer of the first thousand years who discusses it takes the presence as real, for example Ignatius of Antioch (c. 107): "the Eucharist is the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ".
luke|22.cath: The Eucharist is a memorial in the biblical sense: it makes Christ's one sacrifice and his very Body and Blood present.
luke|22.src: CCC 1362–1366, 1374; Trent, Session 13 and 22; Ignatius, Letter to the Smyrnaeans 7

deep.ctx: The Last Supper in Luke 22:14–20 takes place at Passover (22:7–8, 15: ‘With desire I have desired to eat this pasch with you, before I suffer’). ‘And taking bread, he gave thanks, and brake; and gave to them, saying: This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me. In like manner the chalice also, after he had supped, saying: This is the chalice, the new testament in my blood, which shall be shed for you’ (22:19–20). Paul gives an almost identical account, which he says he ‘received of the Lord’ and ‘delivered’ to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 11:23–25), written around AD 54.
deep.who: The command ‘Do this in remembrance of me’ is read as instituting a memorial meal: Christians remember Christ’s death by sharing bread and wine, which symbolize his body and blood. ‘Remembrance’ means mental recollection, not a sacrifice or a real presence. ‘This is my body’ is a figure of speech, like ‘I am the vine’: ‘this represents my body’.
deep.lang:
“This is my body” (touto estin to sōma mou). The verb ‘is’ (estin) is the ordinary verb of identity. ‘This’ (touto, neuter) does not match ‘bread’ (artos, masculine): it points to ‘this thing I am giving you’, not ‘this bread’.

“Given” (didomenon) and “shed” (ekchynnomenon) are present participles: ‘being given’, ‘being poured out’. These are sacrificial verbs (cf. Leviticus 4:7, the blood poured out at the altar).

“Commemoration” (anamnēsis). In the Greek Old Testament, anamnēsis is used for sacrificial memorials before God: the showbread offering ‘for a memorial’ (Leviticus 24:7) and sacrifices that ‘may be to you for a remembrance before your God’ (Numbers 10:10). The Passover itself was a ‘memorial’ by which each generation shared in the Exodus (Exodus 12:14; 13:8).

“Do” (poieite) can also have a sacrificial sense, ‘offer’, in the Greek Old Testament (e.g. Exodus 29:38–39, ‘this is what you shall offer (poiēseis) upon the altar’). This is a possible connotation, not a proof.

“The new testament in my blood” echoes Exodus 24:8 (‘This is the blood of the covenant’) and Jeremiah 31:31 (the new covenant).
steps: The words are plain and repeated four times

Matthew, Mark, Luke and Paul all record ‘This is my body… this is my blood’ (Matthew 26:26–28; Mark 14:22–24; 1 Corinthians 11:24–25). None of them adds an explanation that it is only a figure. In the context of John 6, which the evangelist placed at Passover, the disciples had already heard that they must eat his flesh.
Unlike ‘I am the vine’, there is no metaphorical frame

‘I am the vine’ is part of an extended parable (John 15:1–8) whose meaning is obvious. At the Supper, Jesus takes a particular object in his hands and identifies it. Paul then treats the identity as real: ‘The chalice of benediction, which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? And the bread, which we break, is it not the partaking of the body of the Lord?’ (1 Corinthians 10:16); one who receives unworthily is ‘guilty of the body and of the blood of the Lord’ (11:27). You cannot be guilty of the body of someone through misusing a symbol of him.
‘Remembrance’ is biblical memorial, which makes present

For Israel, remembering the Passover was not daydreaming about history: ‘This day shall be for a memorial to you’ (Exodus 12:14); ‘This is what the Lord did to me when I came forth out of Egypt’ (13:8), said by every generation. The memorial made the saving event present. The Mass is the memorial of Christ’s sacrifice in the same sense: it makes the one sacrifice present (CCC 1362–1366).
Sacrificial language throughout

Body ‘given’, blood ‘shed for you’, ‘new testament in my blood’ (covenants were sealed in sacrificial blood, Exodus 24:5–8), at a Passover where the lamb was sacrificed and eaten. Christ offers himself at the Supper, under the signs of bread and wine, and commands the apostles to ‘do this’. That is the institution of both the Eucharist and the apostolic priesthood (Trent, Session 22, ch. 1 and canon 2).
The universal witness of the early Church

Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Cyprian, Cyril, Ambrose, Augustine, Chrysostom: all treat the Eucharist as Christ’s body and blood and as a sacrifice. No early Christian writer argues that ‘this is my body’ means ‘this symbolizes my body’ in the Zwinglian sense.
fathers: Didache 14 (late 1st century)
Christians gather on the Lord’s day, break bread and give thanks, having confessed their sins, ‘that your sacrifice may be pure’, citing Malachi 1:11.
Justin Martyr, First Apology 66 (c. 155)

The apostles handed on in the memoirs called Gospels that Jesus took bread and said ‘This do in remembrance of me, this is my body’; this food is the flesh and blood of the incarnate Jesus (paraphrased).
Cyprian, Letter 63, 14 (c. 253)
The priest who imitates what Christ did truly fulfils Christ’s office and offers a true and full sacrifice in the Church to God the Father (paraphrased).
Ambrose, On the Mysteries 9.52–54 (c. 390)
If the word of Elijah could bring down fire, will not the word of Christ change the nature of the elements? Before consecration it is called bread; after, the body of Christ (paraphrased).
Council of Trent, Session 22, canon 2 (1562)
By ‘Do this for a commemoration of me’ Christ instituted the apostles priests and ordained that they and other priests should offer his body and blood.
obj: “Jesus was physically present holding the bread. It can’t have been his body.”

God can do what we cannot imagine. The same Jesus walked on water and passed through locked doors (John 20:19). Christ is present in the Eucharist not by occupying space as his natural body does, but sacramentally, by way of substance (ST III q.76 a.5). Catholics hold that at the Supper he gave himself under the signs while visibly present.
“Aramaic has no verb ‘is’, so Jesus might have said ‘this, my body’ meaning ‘represents’.”
Aramaic can omit the copula, but a juxtaposition ‘this, my body’ is a statement of identity just as strong. And the inspired Greek text has estin. The Church reads what the evangelists wrote.
“If it were real, Paul would not call it ‘bread’ afterwards (1 Corinthians 11:26).”
See the note on 11:26. Scripture names things by their appearance: angels appearing as men are called ‘men’ (Genesis 18:2; Acts 1:10). After Cana the steward tastes ‘the water made wine’ (John 2:9).
deep.talk: “Jesus didn’t say ‘this represents my body’; four separate New Testament accounts say ‘This is my body’. Paul says that whoever eats unworthily is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, which only makes sense if it really is his body. And ‘remembrance’ in the Bible is the word used for the Passover memorial, which made the Exodus present to every generation. That’s what the Mass is: Christ’s one sacrifice made present, and Christ himself given to us.”
deep.avoid: Do not rely on the Aramaic argument either way; we have the Greek. Do not imply that the Mass repeats or adds to Calvary (see Hebrews 10:10).
read: Council of Trent, Session 13 and Session 22
John Paul II (2003) Ecclesia de Eucharistia, chs. 1–2
Joachim Jeremias (1966) The Eucharistic Words of Jesus. London: SCM (a Lutheran scholar on anamnēsis)

hebrews|10.claim: Christ's sacrifice was offered once for all, so the Mass, which Catholics call a sacrifice, must either repeat the Cross or deny that it was sufficient.
why: The Church agrees completely that the Cross was once for all and is all-sufficient. The Mass does not repeat it or add to it.

The Mass is the same sacrifice made present. The victim is the same, Christ; the one who offers is the same, Christ, now through the ministry of priests; only the manner is different: bloody on Calvary, unbloody on the altar (Trent, Session 22, ch. 2).

Hebrews itself shows Christ's offering continuing in heaven: he "always liveth to make intercession for us" (7:25), and Revelation shows him as "a Lamb standing as it were slain" (5:6). The Mass joins the Church on earth to that heavenly offering.

Malachi foretold that "in every place there is sacrifice, and there is offered to my name a clean oblation" among the nations (Malachi 1:11). The early Church applied this to the Eucharist (Didache 14).
hebrews|10.cath: One sacrifice, once for all, made present on every altar so that its fruits reach every generation.
hebrews|10.src: Trent, Session 22, chs. 1–2; CCC 1364–1367; ST III q.83 a.1

deep.ctx: Hebrews 9–10 contrasts the old sacrifices, repeated year after year, with Christ’s. ‘In the which will, we are sanctified by the oblation of the body of Jesus Christ once. And every priest indeed standeth daily ministering, and often offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins: but this man offering one sacrifice for sins, for ever sitteth on the right hand of God… For by one oblation he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified’ (10:10–14). ‘Now where there is a remission of these, there is no more an oblation for sin’ (10:18). Yet the same letter says: ‘every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices: wherefore it is necessary that he also should have some thing to offer’ (8:3); and ‘we have an altar, whereof they have no power to eat who serve the tabernacle’ (13:10).
deep.who: This is the central Protestant objection to the sacrifice of the Mass. Christ was offered ‘once for all’ (ephapax). The Mass, which Catholics call a sacrifice offered daily for the sins of the living and the dead, appears to repeat Calvary, to add to it, or to imply it was not enough. Luther called it ‘the most wicked abuse of all’ (Babylonian Captivity, 1520); the Anglican Thirty-Nine Articles (1571), article 31, called the sacrifices of Masses ‘blasphemous fables and dangerous deceits’.
deep.lang:
“Once” (ephapax, 10:10; also 7:27; 9:12): once for all, never to be repeated.

“Offering” (prosphora, 10:10, 14, 18): offering, oblation.

In 8:3 ‘that he also should have some thing to offer’ (ho prosenenkē) is in the context of Christ’s present heavenly ministry (8:1–2). Hebrews also uses the present tense of Christ’s ongoing priestly work: ‘he is able also to save for ever them that come to God by him; always living to make intercession for us’ (7:25); ‘to appear now in the presence of God for us’ (9:24).
steps: Catholics affirm ‘once for all’

The Council of Trent itself teaches that Christ offered himself ‘once’ on the altar of the Cross (Session 22, ch. 1), and condemns anyone who says the Mass detracts from the sacrifice of the Cross (canon 4). Christ will never die again (Romans 6:9). The Catholic Church does not claim the Mass is a second sacrifice or that Calvary was insufficient.
The Mass is the same sacrifice, made present, not a new one

Trent: ‘the victim is one and the same, the same now offering by the ministry of priests, who then offered himself on the cross, the manner alone of offering being different’ (Session 22, ch. 2). CCC 1367: ‘The sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice.’ The Mass re-presents (makes present) the one sacrifice and applies its fruits; it does not add to it.
Hebrews itself shows that Christ’s offering is ongoing in heaven

Christ ‘continueth for ever’ as priest (7:24); ‘it is necessary that he also should have something to offer’ (8:3); he ‘appears now in the presence of God for us’ (9:24); he ‘always lives to make intercession’ (7:25). John sees in heaven ‘a Lamb standing as it were slain’ (Revelation 5:6). The once-for-all death is eternally present before the Father. The Mass joins the Church on earth to this heavenly offering (Hebrews 12:22–24: ‘you are come to mount Sion… and to Jesus the mediator of the new testament, and to the sprinkling of blood’).
The contrast in Hebrews is with repeated Levitical sacrifices

The old priests offered ‘often’ ‘the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins’ (10:11): many different animals, each a new sacrifice, none effective. The Mass is not many victims but the one Victim, Christ, who is the effective sacrifice. Multiplying Masses does not multiply sacrifices any more than multiplying preachings multiplies the gospel.
Malachi foretold a pure offering among the nations

‘From the rising of the sun even to the going down, my name is great among the Gentiles, and in every place there is sacrifice, and there is offered to my name a clean oblation’ (Malachi 1:11). This cannot be the Cross, offered once in one place. The earliest Christians applied it to the Eucharist (Didache 14; Justin, Dialogue 41; Irenaeus IV.17.5).
‘We have an altar’

Hebrews 13:10: Christians have an altar from which those who serve the old tabernacle ‘have no power to eat’. An altar from which one eats implies a sacrifice that is eaten, as in the Passover and peace offerings (1 Corinthians 10:18: ‘they that eat of the sacrifices, are they not partakers of the altar?’).
fathers: Didache 14 (late 1st century)
Calls the Sunday Eucharist ‘your sacrifice’ and quotes Malachi 1:11.
John Chrysostom, Homilies on Hebrews 17.6 (c. 400)

‘Do we not offer every day? We offer indeed, but making a remembrance of his death; and this is one, not many… We offer always the same, not one sheep now and tomorrow another, but always the same thing; so the sacrifice is one’ (paraphrased).
Augustine, City of God X.20 (c. 420)
Christ is both priest and oblation, and he wished the daily sacrifice of the Church to be the sacrament of this (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.83 a.1
The Mass is called a sacrifice because it represents Christ’s Passion and makes us partakers of its fruit; quoting Chrysostom: we do not offer another victim, but the same.
Council of Trent, Session 22, chs. 1–2, canons 1–4 (1562)
The Mass is a true and proper sacrifice, the same as the Cross in victim and priest, different only in manner, and it takes nothing away from the Cross.
obj: “10:18: where there is forgiveness there is no more offering for sin.”

No more new offering: no further sacrifice beyond Christ’s is needed or possible. The Mass is not a further offering; it is the one offering of Christ, present sacramentally. See the note on Hebrews 10:18.
“If Christ’s sacrifice is finished, why apply it?”

Because each person must receive what Christ won. Preaching applies it, faith receives it, baptism applies it. Protestants agree that Christ’s finished work must be applied to individuals; Catholics say the Mass is one of the ways Christ himself applies it.
“Catholics say Christ is ‘immolated’ in the Mass. That means killed again.”

Trent says ‘immolated in an unbloody manner’, i.e. sacramentally, by the separate consecration of bread and wine that signifies his death, while he remains living and glorious (ST III q.76 a.2; Academy module T13m, Lesson 4). He does not suffer or die again.
deep.talk: “Catholics completely agree that Christ was offered once for all and will never die again; the Council of Trent says so. The Mass isn’t another sacrifice; it’s the same one, made present. Hebrews says Christ is still a priest in heaven, ‘appearing before God for us’, and John sees him there as ‘a Lamb standing as though slain’. At Mass, the Church on earth is joined to that one offering. Malachi even foretold a pure offering to God ‘in every place’ among the nations, and the very first Christians, in the Didache, applied that to the Eucharist.”
deep.avoid: Do not use language that suggests Christ dies again or suffers at Mass. Do not deny that late medieval abuses (Masses as business) existed; Trent reformed them.
read: Charles Journet (1958) The Mass: The Presence of the Sacrifice of the Cross

hebrews|10.t: "There is no more an oblation for sin"
hebrews|10.claim: Since Christ's sacrifice has obtained forgiveness, there can be no further offering for sin. The Mass, offered "for sins", is therefore excluded.
why: The verse rules out any further, different sacrifice. The Mass is not a different sacrifice but the one sacrifice of Christ, made present (Trent, Session 22, ch. 2).
Hebrews itself says Christ continues his priestly offering in heaven (8:3; 9:24) and that Christians "have an altar" (13:10).
The Mass does not obtain a new forgiveness beyond Calvary; it applies the forgiveness won on Calvary.
The context contrasts the Levitical sacrifices, repeated because they never forgave sin, with Christ's, which did.
hebrews|10.cath: No new offering beyond Christ's; the Mass is that offering, present for us.

deep.ctx: Hebrews 10:15–18 quotes Jeremiah’s new-covenant prophecy (‘their sins and iniquities I will remember no more’, Jeremiah 31:34) and concludes: ‘Now where there is a remission of these, there is no more an oblation for sin’ (10:18). The next verses invite Christians to draw near ‘into the holies by the blood of Christ’ (10:19) and warn against deliberate sin after receiving the truth: ‘there is now left no sacrifice for sins’ (10:26).
deep.who: Combined with 10:10–14, this verse is used to say that any further ‘offering for sin’, especially a Mass described as ‘propitiatory’ for the living and the dead (Trent, Session 22, canon 3), contradicts Scripture.
deep.lang: “Oblation” (prosphora): offering. “No more” (ouketi): no longer, i.e. no further offering of a different kind is needed, as the Levitical ones were.
steps: ‘No more offering’ means no other offering

The author has just said the old sacrifices were repeated because they did not remove sin (10:1–4, 11). Once forgiveness is accomplished by Christ, there is no place for any other sacrifice for sin. Catholics agree: there is no sacrifice other than Christ’s.
10:26 confirms the meaning

‘If we sin wilfully after having the knowledge of the truth, there is now left no sacrifice for sins.’ Whoever rejects Christ’s sacrifice has no other to turn to. The point is the uniqueness of Christ’s sacrifice, not the absence of any sacramental making-present of it.
The Mass is the one offering

Trent: the Mass is offered to ‘represent’ the bloody sacrifice of the Cross, keep its memory to the end of the world and ‘apply its saving virtue to the remission of those sins which we daily commit’ (Session 22, ch. 1). It obtains nothing that Calvary did not already merit. It is the channel, not a new source.
Propitiatory because it is Calvary present

The Mass is called propitiatory (Trent, canon 3) because the same propitiation that Christ offered (1 John 2:2) is present and offered. It turns away God’s just anger not by a new merit but by presenting the one perfect Victim.
fathers: John Chrysostom, Homilies on Hebrews 17.6
We offer the same sacrifice, not another; or rather we make a remembrance of the sacrifice (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Hebrews, ch. 10, lect. 1–2
The Church’s offering is not distinct from Christ’s, but a commemoration of it (paraphrased).
obj: “Then why must Masses be offered again and again?”
Not because Calvary is incomplete, but because each generation, each day, each soul needs its fruits applied, as the gospel is preached again and again although Christ’s word was spoken once.
deep.talk: “Hebrews means there’s no other sacrifice besides Christ’s; the Old Testament sacrifices are over. Catholics agree. The Mass isn’t another sacrifice; it’s Christ’s one sacrifice made present, so that its forgiveness reaches us today. It doesn’t add anything to Calvary; it delivers Calvary.”
deep.avoid: Avoid saying the Mass ‘earns’ new forgiveness; say it applies Christ’s.

1-corinthians|11.t: Guilty of the body and blood of the Lord
1-corinthians|11.claim: A Catholic proof-text. Some answer that the guilt is only for disrespecting a memorial meal.
why: Paul says the unworthy communicant is "guilty of the body and of the blood of the Lord" and eats "judgment to himself, not discerning the body" (11:29). Some, he says, had become sick and died (11:30).
That language belongs to an offence against a person, not against a picture. It fits the real presence.
1-corinthians|11.cath: Because Christ is truly present, we examine our conscience before receiving and go to confession first after grave sin.

deep.ctx: 1 Corinthians 11:17–34 rebukes abuses at the Corinthian Lord’s Supper: divisions, some going hungry while others get drunk (11:21). Paul hands on the words of institution (11:23–25), then: ‘Therefore whosoever shall eat this bread, or drink the chalice of the Lord unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and of the blood of the Lord. But let a man prove himself: and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of the chalice. For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment to himself, not discerning the body of the Lord. Therefore are there many infirm and weak among you, and many sleep’ (11:27–30).
deep.who: Symbolist Protestants read ‘not discerning the body’ as failing to recognize the Church, the body of Christ (the community), as the Corinthians did by humiliating the poor. Unworthy eating is an ethical failure, a sin against the community and against the memory of Christ’s death, not a sin against a real presence in the bread.
deep.lang:
“Guilty of” (enochos): liable, answerable for. The same word is used in Matthew 5:21–22 (‘liable to the judgment’) and James 2:10 (‘guilty of all’). To be ‘guilty of the body and blood’ is a phrase for responsibility for someone’s death (compare Hebrews 10:29, ‘trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath esteemed the blood of the testament unclean’).

“Discerning” (diakrinōn): distinguishing, judging rightly.

“Body of the Lord” (to sōma tou kyriou, some manuscripts simply to sōma).
steps: Guilt for the body and blood implies their presence

One can be ‘guilty of the blood’ of a person only by harming that person. If the bread were only a symbol, unworthy eating would be disrespect toward a symbol, not guilt of the body and blood themselves. Paul treats sacrilege against the Eucharist as a sin against Christ himself.
The punishment is real and severe

‘Many infirm and weak among you, and many sleep (have died).’ Paul attributes illness and death to receiving unworthily. This is the language of sacrilege, comparable to Uzzah touching the ark (2 Samuel 6:6–7).
‘The body’ is linked to ‘this bread’ and ‘the chalice’

The paragraph moves from the words ‘This is my body’ (11:24) to eating ‘this bread’ unworthily (11:27) to ‘not discerning the body’ (11:29). The natural antecedent is the eucharistic body just mentioned. Paul does elsewhere speak of the Church as the body (10:17; 12:27), and Catholic teaching holds both: the one bread makes us one body (10:17). Abusing the poor at the Lord’s Supper is also a failure to discern Christ’s body. But the primary sense in 11:27–29 is the sacrament.
Paul says the same in chapter 10

‘The chalice of benediction, which we bless, is it not the communion (koinōnia) of the blood of Christ? And the bread, which we break, is it not the partaking of the body of the Lord?’ (10:16). He compares the Eucharist with Jewish and pagan sacrificial meals (10:18–21) and warns against provoking the Lord to jealousy.
Hence the Church’s discipline

Because the Eucharist is Christ, one who is conscious of grave sin must go to confession before receiving Communion (CCC 1385; CIC 916). This practice comes straight from 11:28, ‘let a man prove himself’.
fathers: Didache 14 (late 1st century)
Confess your transgressions before breaking bread, ‘that your sacrifice may be pure’; let no one at variance with his neighbour come until reconciled.
Origen, Homilies on Exodus 13.3 (c. 240)
You who are used to the divine mysteries know how carefully you guard the body of the Lord lest any crumb fall, and rightly think yourselves guilty if anything falls through negligence (paraphrased).
John Chrysostom, Homilies on 1 Corinthians 24 and 28 (c. 392)
To approach unworthily is like the guilt of those who crucified him (paraphrased).
obj: “Paul still calls it ‘bread’ (11:26–28).”
Scripture names it by appearance and as ‘the bread from heaven’ (John 6). See the note on 11:26.
“‘The body’ is the church community.”

Catholics accept that the social dimension matters; Paul is condemning humiliation of the poor. But ‘guilty of the body and of the blood of the Lord’ cannot mean ‘guilty of the community and of the blood’. The blood is not the community.
deep.talk: “Paul says whoever receives unworthily is ‘guilty of the body and blood of the Lord’, and that some Corinthians had become sick and even died because of it. You can’t be guilty of someone’s body and blood by disrespecting a symbol. That only makes sense if it really is Christ. That’s why Catholics go to confession first if they’re conscious of serious sin.”
deep.avoid: Do not use this verse to shame people who cannot receive Communion; it is about honesty before God, and confession restores us.
read: Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on 1 Corinthians, ch. 11, lects. 6–7

1-corinthians|11.t: "As often as you shall eat this bread"
1-corinthians|11.claim: Paul still calls it "bread" after consecration and says it "shews the death of the Lord": a symbolic proclamation, not a real presence or a sacrifice.
why: In the next verse Paul says unworthy eating makes one "guilty of the body and of the blood of the Lord" (11:27).
Christ called himself "the living bread" (John 6:51–52); "bread" is a name for the Eucharist, not a denial of the change.
Appearances remain after consecration, and Scripture names things by appearance (Genesis 18:2; John 2:9).
To "shew the death of the Lord" (katangellete, "proclaim") fits the Mass perfectly: the sacrament makes present and proclaims the sacrifice of Calvary until he comes.
1-corinthians|11.cath: The Eucharist is called bread because it looks like bread and because it is the true bread from heaven; and it proclaims his death because it makes his sacrifice present.

deep.ctx: After handing on the words of institution (11:23–25), Paul says: ‘For as often as you shall eat this bread, and drink the chalice, you shall shew the death of the Lord, until he come’ (11:26). Then: ‘Therefore whosoever shall eat this bread, or drink the chalice of the Lord unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and of the blood of the Lord’ (11:27).
deep.who: The proclamation reading: the Lord’s Supper is a dramatic proclamation of Christ’s death, an enacted sermon; Paul’s calling it ‘bread’ shows the element remains bread. Some Reformed theologians speak of a spiritual presence received by faith while the bread remains bread.
deep.lang:
“Shew” (katangellete) means ‘announce, proclaim’. It is used of preaching (1 Corinthians 9:14). Present tense: every celebration proclaims.

“This bread” (ton arton touton): ‘this’ refers back to the bread over which Christ said ‘This is my body’ (11:24).
steps: ‘Bread’ is a scriptural name for the Eucharist

Jesus: ‘I am the living bread which came down from heaven… the bread that I will give, is my flesh’ (John 6:51–52). The Eucharist is called ‘bread’ because it is the true bread of life and because it keeps the appearances of bread. The Church still calls it ‘the Bread of Life’ in the liturgy.
Paul immediately says ‘guilty of the body and blood’
Read 11:26 with 11:27–29 (see that note). The same ‘bread’ eaten unworthily brings guilt of the Lord’s body and blood.
Proclaiming his death is what the Mass does

The Mass is the memorial that makes present Christ’s death. It proclaims it not as a sermon only but as an action: the separate consecration of body and blood sacramentally shows forth his death (ST III q.76 a.2 ad 1; Academy T13m, Lesson 4). The Church at every Mass acclaims: ‘We proclaim your Death, O Lord… until you come again’.
‘Until he come’ does not mean he is absent
Christ is present in the Eucharist sacramentally, not in the manner of his visible coming in glory. The real presence and the expectation of his return belong together (CCC 1344, 1402–1405).
fathers: Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.75 a.2 ad 1
The Apostle calls it bread after consecration because it has the appearance of bread, and because it is the bread from heaven (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on 1 Corinthians, ch. 11, lect. 6
We proclaim the Lord’s death by eating, because the sacrament represents his Passion (paraphrased).
obj: “The plainest reading is that bread stays bread.”
The plainest reading of ‘This is my body’ two verses earlier is that it is his body. Both must be read together, and the early Church read them as Catholics do.
deep.talk: “Paul calls it bread because it still looks like bread, and because Jesus is ‘the living bread from heaven’. But in the very next verse he says that whoever eats it unworthily is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. And ‘proclaiming his death’ is exactly what the Mass does: it makes his sacrifice present until he comes back.”
deep.avoid: Do not deny that the Eucharist is a proclamation; it is, and more.
read: ST III q.75 a.2; q.76 a.2

1-peter|2.claim: All believers are priests, so there is no need for a separate ordained priesthood.
why: Peter is quoting Exodus 19:6, where God called all Israel "a priestly kingdom". Israel still had an ordained priesthood of Aaron. A priestly people and a ministerial priesthood existed together.

Catholics teach the same: all the baptised share in Christ's priesthood by offering their lives, prayer and work to God. Some are ordained to act in the person of Christ the Head, especially at the Eucharist (Luke 22:19; Romans 15:16, where Paul calls his ministry a priestly service).
1-peter|2.cath: The common priesthood of all the faithful and the ministerial priesthood differ in kind, and each serves the other.

deep.ctx: 1 Peter 2:4–10 describes Christians as ‘living stones built up, a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ’ (2:5). Then: ‘But you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation, a purchased people: that you may declare his virtues, who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light’ (2:9). Peter is quoting God’s words to Israel at Sinai: ‘you shall be to me a priestly kingdom, and a holy nation’ (Exodus 19:6).
deep.who: This verse is the basis of Luther’s ‘priesthood of all believers’ (To the Christian Nobility, 1520): all baptized Christians are equally priests; there is no special sacramental priesthood; ministers are only functionaries chosen by the congregation to preach and administer the sacraments for the sake of order. A Catholic priesthood that alone can consecrate the Eucharist and absolve sins denies the priesthood of believers.
deep.lang:
“Kingly priesthood” (basileion hierateuma): the collective noun hierateuma, ‘priestly body’, from Exodus 19:6 in the Greek Old Testament.

“Spiritual sacrifices” (pneumatikas thysias, 2:5): the offering of the whole life (Romans 12:1; Hebrews 13:15–16).

The New Testament uses hiereus (priest) of Christ and of Old Testament priests; Christian ministers are called presbyteroi (‘elders’, whence the English word ‘priest’) and episkopoi (overseers, bishops). But Paul describes his own ministry with priestly language: ‘ministering (hierourgounta, performing priestly service) the gospel of God, that the oblation of the Gentiles may be made acceptable’ (Romans 15:16).
steps: Catholics affirm the common priesthood of all the baptized

Vatican II: ‘The baptized, by regeneration and the anointing of the Holy Spirit, are consecrated as a spiritual house and a holy priesthood’ (Lumen Gentium 10, quoting 1 Peter 2). The faithful offer spiritual sacrifices, join in offering the Eucharist, and witness to Christ (CCC 1141, 1268, 1546). This is not a Protestant discovery; it is Catholic doctrine.
Israel was a priestly nation and still had a ministerial priesthood

Peter quotes Exodus 19:6. At Sinai the whole of Israel was called ‘a priestly kingdom’, and yet in the very next chapters God appoints Aaron and his sons as priests (Exodus 28–29). The two were never in competition: the nation was priestly, and within it was a ministerial priesthood serving the nation.
Korah’s rebellion used the same argument

Korah, Dathan and Abiram rose against Moses and Aaron saying: ‘all the multitude consisteth of holy ones, and the Lord is among them: Why lift you up yourselves above the people of the Lord?’ (Numbers 16:3). God vindicated Aaron’s priesthood dramatically (16:31–35; 17:1–10). Jude 11 warns Christians against ‘the contradiction of Core (Korah)’.
The New Testament has ordained ministers with specific powers

The apostles were told ‘do this’ (Luke 22:19) and ‘whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them’ (John 20:23), not the whole crowd. They appointed presbyters by the laying on of hands (Acts 14:22; 1 Timothy 4:14; 5:22; 2 Timothy 1:6; Titus 1:5). Presbyters anoint the sick and pray over them so that sins are forgiven (James 5:14–15). Not every Christian did these things.
Isaiah foretold priests taken from the Gentiles

‘And I will take of them to be priests, and Levites, saith the Lord’ (Isaiah 66:21), in a prophecy of the nations coming to worship. Paul sees his ministry as priestly service offering the Gentiles to God (Romans 15:16).
Two participations in Christ’s one priesthood

The common priesthood and the ministerial priesthood ‘differ essentially and not only in degree’, yet both share in the one priesthood of Christ (LG 10; CCC 1547). The ministerial priest acts in persona Christi capitis, in the person of Christ the head, to build up the common priesthood of all.
fathers: Clement of Rome, Letter to the Corinthians 40–44 (c. 96)

Compares the Christian ministry to the ordered priesthood of the Old Testament; the apostles appointed bishops and deacons and provided for succession; it is a sin to remove those who have blamelessly offered the gifts (paraphrased).
Ignatius of Antioch, Letter to the Smyrnaeans 8 (c. 107)
Let that be considered a valid Eucharist which is celebrated by the bishop, or by one whom he has appointed (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.63 a.3–6
Baptism and confirmation give a participation in Christ’s priesthood to all; holy orders gives a power to consecrate and to act in Christ’s person.
Second Vatican Council, Lumen Gentium 10 (1964)
The common priesthood and the ministerial priesthood differ in essence, not only in degree, but are ordered to one another.
obj: “The New Testament never calls Christian ministers hiereis (priests).”

True of the word, and significant: the early Christians avoided confusion with the Temple priests while it still stood. But the realities are there: an altar (Hebrews 13:10), a sacrifice (Malachi 1:11; Didache 14), ordained presbyters who forgive sins and anoint. By the late 2nd century, writers such as Tertullian and Hippolytus already use priestly language for bishops (‘high priest’, Apostolic Tradition 3).
“If all are priests, why can only an ordained priest consecrate?”

Because Christ gave the command ‘Do this’ to the apostles, and they handed on the ministry by the laying on of hands. The whole people offers the sacrifice with the priest (‘my sacrifice and yours’), but the priest acts in Christ’s person to make it present.
deep.talk: “Peter is quoting what God said to Israel at Sinai: ‘you shall be a kingdom of priests’. Yet in the very same book God set apart Aaron and his sons as priests within that priestly nation. Catholics believe both: all the baptized share Christ’s priesthood, and some are ordained to serve the rest, the way the apostles were told ‘do this in memory of me’ and ‘whose sins you forgive are forgiven’. Korah actually used your argument against Aaron in Numbers 16, and it didn’t go well for him.”
deep.avoid: Do not say lay people are not priests at all; that contradicts Vatican II. Use the Korah example gently; it can sound like a threat.

matthew|16.t: "Upon this rock I will build my church"
matthew|16.claim: The "rock" is said to be Peter's confession of faith, or Christ himself, not Peter.
why: Jesus spoke Aramaic. Simon is renamed Kepha, "Rock" (John 1:42). "You are Kepha, and on this kepha I will build my church" is a direct play on his new name. The Greek difference between petros and petra is the masculine form needed for a man's name.
The next verse gives Peter "the keys of the kingdom of heaven", echoing Isaiah 22:22, where the keys mark the office of the king's chief steward, an office with successors.
Many Protestant scholars now agree the rock is Peter himself, for example Oscar Cullmann (Peter: Disciple, Apostle, Martyr, 1953). The debate is really about whether the office continues.
matthew|16.cath: Christ is the foundation of the Church (1 Corinthians 3:11) and chose to make Peter the visible rock and steward, an office continued in his successors.
matthew|16.src: CCC 552–553, 881–882; Vatican I, Pastor Aeternus (1870), ch. 1

deep.ctx: At Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks: ‘Whom do men say that the Son of man is?’ After various answers, ‘Simon Peter answered and said: Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God. And Jesus answering, said to him: Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-Jona: because flesh and blood hath not revealed it to thee, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to thee: That thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give to thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatsoever thou shalt bind upon earth, it shall be bound also in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth, it shall be loosed also in heaven’ (16:13–19). A few verses later Jesus rebukes Peter: ‘Go behind me, Satan’ (16:23).
deep.who: Protestant readings take the ‘rock’ to be (1) Peter’s confession of faith, (2) Christ himself (1 Corinthians 3:11; 10:4), or (3) Peter, but only personally as the first preacher, with no successors. The popular grammatical argument: Peter is Petros (masculine, ‘a small stone’), while the rock is petra (feminine, ‘bedrock’), so Jesus distinguishes the small stone Peter from the great rock of faith or of Christ. Even granting Peter is the rock, nothing in the text speaks of a succession of bishops in Rome.
deep.lang:
Jesus spoke Aramaic. John 1:42 gives Peter’s Aramaic name: ‘thou shalt be called Cephas, which is interpreted Peter.’ Kēpha (Cephas) means ‘rock’, and Paul calls him ‘Cephas’ eight times. In Aramaic the sentence would be ‘you are Kēpha, and on this kēpha I will build’, the same word twice.

In Greek, petra is the ordinary word for rock; to make it a man’s name it had to become masculine, Petros. In earlier classical poetry petros could mean a stone, but in the Koine Greek of the first century the two words were used largely interchangeably. Several Protestant scholars accept that the rock is Peter: Oscar Cullmann (Peter: Disciple, Apostle, Martyr, 1952) and D. A. Carson (Expositor’s Bible Commentary on Matthew, 1984) among them.

“This rock” (tautē tē petra): ‘this’ points back to the nearest referent, Peter just named.

“Keys” (kleidas): the image comes from Isaiah 22:20–22, where God gives Eliakim ‘the key of the house of David… he shall open, and none shall shut’. Eliakim was the ‘one over the house’, the royal steward, an office with predecessors and successors.
steps: The wordplay requires Peter to be the rock

Jesus gives Simon a new name, ‘Rock’, in the same breath as ‘on this rock I will build’. In Aramaic it is the same word. A play on words that means ‘you are Rock, but I will build on something else’ would be a strange way to bless him. Jesus is answering Peter’s confession with a matching declaration: ‘You said who I am; now I tell you who you are.’
Three gifts to one man

Everything in 16:17–19 is addressed to Peter in the singular (‘to thee’, soi): the blessing, the name, the keys, the power to bind and loose. Elsewhere all the apostles receive binding and loosing (18:18), but the keys are given to Peter alone.
The keys are an office with succession

Isaiah 22: Shebna is removed as royal steward and Eliakim given ‘the key of the house of David’, wearing the steward’s robe and authority. The steward governed the house in the king’s name, and the office passed to successors. Jesus, the Son of David, appoints a steward for his kingdom. An office of this kind does not end with its first holder.
Peter acts as the leader in the New Testament

He is always named first in lists of the apostles (Matthew 10:2: ‘the first, Simon who is called Peter’). Jesus prays for him that his faith fail not and tells him to confirm his brethren (Luke 22:31–32). The risen Lord tells him three times, ‘Feed my sheep’ (John 21:15–17). He leads the choice of Matthias (Acts 1:15–26), preaches at Pentecost (2:14), opens the Church to the Gentiles (10), and speaks decisively at the Council of Jerusalem (15:7–11).
Christ as foundation, Peter as rock: both are true

Scripture uses building images flexibly. Christ is the one foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11) and the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20); the apostles are the foundation too (Ephesians 2:20; Revelation 21:14, ‘the twelve foundations… the twelve names of the twelve apostles’). Peter is the rock by sharing in Christ’s own stability, as a vicar shares the authority of the one he represents (CCC 881).
The Church needed Peter’s office to continue

Jesus promised that the gates of hell would not prevail against his Church, which lasts until the end of the world (Matthew 28:20). If the rock and keys were needed to found and govern the Church in its first generation, they are needed in every generation. The early Church saw the bishop of Rome as holding Peter’s chair: Clement of Rome intervenes in Corinth (c. 96); Irenaeus lists the Roman succession (c. 180); Cyprian calls Rome ‘the chair of Peter’ (Letter 59.14, c. 252).
fathers: Tertullian, On Modesty 21 (c. 220)
Writing as a Montanist critic of the bishop of Rome, he still says the Lord built the Church on Peter and gave him the keys (paraphrased).
Cyprian, On the Unity of the Catholic Church 4 (c. 251)

The Lord builds his Church on one man, Peter; though he gives equal power to all the apostles, he establishes one chair, so that the origin of unity might be shown (paraphrased; the text survives in two versions).
Augustine, Retractations I.21 (c. 427)

He had earlier said the rock was Peter, later often that it was Christ whom Peter confessed; he leaves the reader to choose which is more probable (paraphrased). Augustine nonetheless affirmed the Roman see’s primacy (Letter 43.7; Against the Letter of Mani 4.5).
Leo the Great, Sermon 4 (c. 445)
Peter’s solid faith, praised by the Lord, endures in his see; Peter still governs the Church through his successors (paraphrased).
First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus ch. 1–2 (1870)
Defines that Peter received a primacy of jurisdiction from Christ, and that by Christ’s institution Peter has perpetual successors, the Roman Pontiffs.
obj: “Petros is a small stone, petra a big rock.”
