Then Adam’s life of grace was not grace, and the angels who fell never had God’s favour. ‘Eternal’ describes the kind of life (God’s), not a guarantee against our refusing it.
deep.talk: “Jesus says the one who keeps hearing and believing has eternal life right now. That’s grace, and it’s wonderful. But a few verses later he says people will rise to life or to judgment depending on whether they’ve done good or evil. And in John 15 he says branches in him that stop bearing fruit are cut off. So eternal life is a present gift we have to abide in, not a ticket we can’t lose.”
deep.avoid: Do not deny present possession of eternal life; Catholics who are in grace have it.
read: Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on John, ch. 5

john|10.t: "No man shall pluck them out of my hand"
john|10.claim: This is the classic text for "once saved, always saved": a true believer is held by Christ and the Father and can never be lost.
why: The promise is about outside powers: no one can snatch Christ's sheep from him. It does not say a sheep cannot walk away.
The sheep are those who "hear my voice… and follow me" (10:27), present tense: they keep on following.
Elsewhere Scripture warns real disciples that they can fall: "he that thinketh himself to stand, let him take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:12); John 15:6; Hebrews 6:4–6.
Catholics take great comfort in this verse: no devil, persecution or power can take us from Christ. Only our own free and grave sin can separate us.
john|10.cath: Christ's hold on his sheep is stronger than any enemy; the only danger is our own refusal to follow.

deep.ctx: John 10 is the Good Shepherd discourse. Jesus is the door of the sheep (10:7) and the good shepherd who lays down his life (10:11). At the feast of Dedication, the Jews ask him to say plainly if he is the Christ (10:24). He answers: ‘you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep. My sheep hear my voice: and I know them, and they follow me. And I give them life everlasting; and they shall not perish for ever, and no man shall pluck them out of my hand. That which my Father hath given me, is greater than all: and no one can snatch them out of the hand of my Father. I and the Father are one’ (10:26–30).
deep.who: Calvinist and Baptist theology uses this verse as the strongest proof of the ‘perseverance of the saints’: the elect, held in the hands of both Son and Father, cannot be lost. If a professed believer falls away, he was never truly one of the sheep.
deep.lang:
“They shall not perish for ever” (ou mē apolōntai eis ton aiōna): emphatic double negative, ‘they will certainly not perish’. “Pluck/snatch” (harpasei, harpazein) means to seize by force, as a wolf does (10:12, the same verb: ‘the wolf catcheth (harpazei) and scattereth the sheep’).

“Hear… follow” (akouousin… akolouthousin) are present tense: they keep hearing and following.
steps: The threat in view is outside force

The verb harpazō is the wolf’s verb (10:12). Jesus promises that no thief, wolf or hireling, no human or demonic power, can tear his sheep from him. Catholics wholeheartedly affirm this: Satan cannot take a soul from Christ by force.
The promise is to those who keep following

10:27 defines the sheep: they hear and follow (present tense). The promise of 10:28 is for those who do this. Jesus does not say a sheep cannot stop following. Elsewhere he speaks of disciples who ‘went back; and walked no more with him’ (6:67) and of Judas, whom the Father had given him and who was lost (17:12).
Scripture warns believers that they can fall away

Paul: ‘thou standest by faith… otherwise thou also shalt be cut off’ (Romans 11:20–22); ‘you are fallen from grace’ (Galatians 5:4). Peter: ‘if, flying from the pollutions of the world… they be again entangled in them and overcome: their latter state is become unto them worse than the former’ (2 Peter 2:20). Jesus: branches in him cast into the fire (John 15:6). If falling away were impossible, these warnings would be pointless.
The Catholic reading keeps both comfort and warning

Final perseverance is a gift of God (Trent, Session 6, ch. 13), and God is faithful. We should have firm hope that he who began a good work will complete it (Philippians 1:6). But we can resist grace, and so we pray daily, ‘lead us not into temptation’. Those who persevere to the end were held by Christ; that is the elect. But no one can know with the certainty of faith that he is among them (canon 16).
The ‘never truly saved’ answer undermines assurance

If every apostate was never a real believer, then no one can know he is a real believer until he dies faithful: someone who seems to have every mark of grace may be a false convert. So eternal security does not actually provide the certainty it promises.
fathers: Augustine, Tractates on John 48.6 (c. 416)
The wolf cannot snatch, the thief cannot steal, the robber cannot kill those whom Christ knows as his own, the predestined; but this is known to God (paraphrased).
Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace 13.40
Of those who are called and justified, some do not persevere; we do not know who will, so we must not be proud (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on John, ch. 10, lect. 5
No one can snatch the sheep by violence; but a sheep can depart of its own will through sin (paraphrased).
obj: “If no one can snatch them, that includes the sheep themselves.”

The sheep don’t ‘snatch’ themselves; snatching is forcible seizure by another. The question of the sheep’s own will is answered in 10:27: they follow. Judas, ‘given’ to Christ (17:12), was lost by his own choice.
“Those who fall away show they were never sheep (1 John 2:19).”
See the note on 1 John 5:13. That verse describes particular schismatics. And it cannot explain Hebrews 6:4–6 or 2 Peter 2:20–22, which describe true conversion followed by falling.
deep.talk: “John 10:28 is one of my favourite verses too. No one can rip a Christian out of Christ’s hand: not the devil, not persecution, nothing. But look at verse 27: his sheep are those who keep listening and keep following. The danger isn’t a wolf snatching us; it’s us walking away, like Judas did. So we trust Christ completely, and we keep following him.”
deep.avoid: Do not tell Calvinists they don’t care about holiness, or that they think they can sin freely; they teach that true believers will persevere in holiness.
read: Council of Trent, Session 6, chs. 12–13, canons 15–16, 22–23
Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace; On the Gift of Perseverance
I. Howard Marshall (1969) Kept by the Power of God. London: Epworth (a Protestant scholar against unconditional security)

romans|8.t: "Nothing shall be able to separate us from the love of God"
romans|8.claim: Paul's list (death, life, angels, powers, things present or to come, any creature) is read as a guarantee that a believer can never be separated from God, so salvation cannot be lost.
why: Every item on the list is an outside power or circumstance. Sin, our own free choice to turn from God, is not on the list.
God's love for us never ends; the question is whether we remain in it. Jesus: "Abide in my love… If you keep my commandments, you shall abide in my love" (John 15:9–10).
Three chapters later, Paul warns believers: "otherwise thou also shalt be cut off" (Romans 11:22).
Catholics read the verse as the great charter of Christian hope: nothing outside us can defeat God's love.
romans|8.cath: No power in creation can tear us from God's love. Only our own grave sin can turn us away from it, and even then God's mercy calls us back.

deep.ctx: Romans 8 is the climax of Paul’s teaching on life in the Spirit. ‘If God be for us, who is against us?’ (8:31). ‘Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation? or distress? or famine? or nakedness? or danger? or persecution? or the sword?’ (8:35). ‘For I am sure that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor might, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord’ (8:38–39). But earlier in the chapter: ‘if you live according to the flesh, you shall die’ (8:13); ‘heirs… yet so, if we suffer with him’ (8:17).
deep.who: This passage is used as the final word for eternal security: ‘nor any other creature’ includes you; therefore not even your own sin can separate you from God.
deep.lang: “I am sure” (pepeismai, perfect): I am fully persuaded. “Any other creature” (tis ktisis hetera): ‘any other created thing’.
steps: The list is of external powers

Tribulation, persecution, sword (8:35), death and life, angels and principalities, present and future, height and depth: all are forces that act on the Christian from outside. Paul is answering the fear that suffering or spiritual powers could cut us off from God. They cannot.
‘Any other creature’ means anything else in creation of that kind

Paul’s point is that no power in the created order can overcome God’s love. Reading ‘any creature’ to include our own free refusal makes Paul contradict 8:13 (‘if you live according to the flesh, you shall die’) and 11:22 (‘otherwise thou also shalt be cut off’).
God’s love does not stop; we can stop receiving it

God loves even sinners in hell, in the sense that he wills their existence; but they have refused communion with him. Jesus distinguishes God’s love toward us and our abiding in it: ‘abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you shall abide in my love’ (John 15:9–10). Jude 21: ‘Keep yourselves in the love of God.’ You cannot be told to keep yourself in something you cannot leave.
The condition stated in 8:17
‘Heirs indeed of God, and joint heirs with Christ: yet so, if we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified with him.’ The ‘if’ is part of the same chapter.
fathers: John Chrysostom, Homilies on Romans 15 (c. 390)
Paul is speaking of his own love for Christ that no tribulation could overcome, and of God’s love that is stronger than every power (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Romans, ch. 8, lect. 7
Nothing external can separate the saints from charity, though the free will can turn away through sin; Paul speaks of the predestined, who in fact will not be separated (paraphrased).
obj: “You are a creature, so you can’t separate yourself either.”
Then Paul contradicts himself three chapters later (11:22) and five verses earlier (8:13). Jude 21 tells Christians to keep themselves in God’s love, which presupposes they could fail to.
deep.talk: “Romans 8 is the most hopeful chapter in the Bible: nothing in all creation can tear us from God’s love. But notice everything on the list is something outside us: death, angels, persecution, the future. What isn’t on the list is our own sin. That’s why Paul also says in the same chapter, ‘if you live according to the flesh, you will die’, and Jude says ‘keep yourselves in the love of God’.”
deep.avoid: Do not reduce this verse to a warning; it is first a song of confidence. Lead with the comfort.
read: Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Romans, ch. 8, lect. 7

romans|8.claim: Christians are free from condemnation, so they cannot be punished after death. Purgatory, as a place of punishment, contradicts this.
why: Purgatory is not condemnation. Souls in purgatory are saved; condemnation means hell.

The verse in the Douay (and KJV) adds "who walk not according to the flesh": the promise belongs to those who live in the Spirit. Many modern Bibles end the verse earlier, but 8:4 has the same clause.
Romans 8 itself says "if you live according to the flesh, you shall die" (8:13).
Purgatory is the purifying love of God completing the healing of the saved, not a sentence of guilt.
romans|8.cath: No condemnation for those in Christ; purification for those not yet perfect.

deep.ctx: Romans 7 describes the struggle of a person under the Law, ending in ‘Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God, by Jesus Christ our Lord’ (7:24–25). Romans 8:1–4: ‘There is now therefore no condemnation to them that are in Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh. For the law of the spirit of life, in Christ Jesus, hath delivered me from the law of sin and of death… that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit.’
deep.who: Used against purgatory and against the Catholic distinction between eternal and temporal punishment: if no condemnation remains, no punishment remains either.
deep.lang:
“Condemnation” (katakrima): a sentence of condemnation, the verdict of guilt leading to penalty, particularly death (5:16, 18).

Textual note: the clause ‘who walk not according to the flesh’ in 8:1 is in the Vulgate and the Byzantine manuscripts (hence Douay and KJV); the earliest manuscripts lack it there, and modern translations omit it. It is certainly original in 8:4.
steps: Purgatory is for those not under condemnation
The Church teaches that all in purgatory ‘are assured of their eternal salvation’ (CCC 1030). They are in Christ, free from condemnation. Purgatory is not a lesser hell or a sentence of guilt.
Discipline is not condemnation

Hebrews 12:6–11: ‘whom the Lord loveth, he chastiseth… for the present all chastisement seemeth to bring not joy, but sorrow: but afterwards it will yield… the most peaceable fruit of justice’. God disciplines his children because they are his, not because they are condemned. Purgatory is the final form of this purifying love (Spe Salvi 47).
The promise is to those who walk in the Spirit
Romans 8 makes the condition explicit (8:4, 13). It is not a guarantee that someone who lives according to the flesh escapes condemnation.
1 Corinthians 3 describes a saved person suffering loss
‘If any man’s work burn, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as by fire’ (1 Corinthians 3:15). Saved, not condemned, yet suffering loss and passing through fire.
fathers: Augustine, Exposition on Psalm 37.3 (c. 400)
Some will be saved through fire; and though saved, that fire will be more grievous than anything a man can suffer in this life (paraphrased).
Benedict XVI, Spe Salvi 47 (2007)
The encounter with Christ is the decisive act of judgment; his gaze burns and transforms us, a blessed pain in which his love penetrates us like a flame (paraphrased).
obj: “If Christ took all punishment, none remains.”

Christ took the eternal punishment of sin. Scripture shows forgiven people still undergoing temporal consequences and discipline (2 Samuel 12:13–14; Hebrews 12). Purgatory belongs to that category: healing, not condemnation.
deep.talk: “Purgatory isn’t condemnation at all. Everyone in purgatory is saved and on their way to heaven. It’s God finishing the job of making us holy, like the discipline Hebrews 12 talks about: painful, but because he loves us as his children. Paul describes it in 1 Corinthians 3: someone saved, ‘yet as through fire’.”
deep.avoid: Do not describe purgatory in terms that sound like punishment by an angry judge; stress love and purification.

isaiah|64.t: "All our justices as the rag of a menstruous woman"
isaiah|64.claim: Often quoted as "all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags" to prove that even the good works of Christians are worthless and sinful before God, so they can play no part in salvation and merit is impossible.
why: In context, Isaiah is confessing the sins of unfaithful Israel during exile: "behold thou art angry, and we have sinned" (64:5). He describes the people's works while they were turned away from God.
Isaiah himself praises true righteousness: the fast God chooses, feeding the hungry and sheltering the poor, brings light and healing (58:6–8).

The New Testament says the opposite of the works of the saints: "the fine linen are the justifications of saints" (Revelation 19:8), and God "is not unjust, that he should forget your work" (Hebrews 6:10).
Works done in grace, by the Holy Spirit, are God's work in us (Philippians 2:13), and God does not call his own work filthy.
isaiah|64.cath: Works done apart from God cannot save. Works done in grace are pleasing to God and rewarded by him.

deep.ctx: Isaiah 63:7–64:12 is a communal lament, a prayer of Israel in exile. It recalls God’s mercies in the Exodus (63:7–14), then pleads: ‘Look down from heaven… where is thy zeal?’ (63:15). ‘Behold thou art angry, and we have sinned: in them we have been always, and we shall be saved. And we are all become as one unclean, and all our justices as the rag of a menstruous woman: and we have all fallen as a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away’ (64:5–6). ‘There is none that calleth upon thy name’ (64:7). The prayer ends begging God not to be angry for ever (64:9).
deep.who: Reformed theology uses this verse to show total depravity: even the best works of fallen humans, including Christians, are tainted by sin, so they cannot merit anything before God. Luther and Calvin taught that every good work of the justified is still sinful in God’s sight if judged by strict justice (Luther, Against Latomus, 1521; Calvin, Institutes III.14.9–11). Therefore justification must rest entirely on Christ’s imputed righteousness, never on works.
deep.lang:
Hebrew: ukhebeged ‘iddim kol-tsidqotenu: ‘and like a garment of menstruation all our righteous deeds’. ‘Iddim refers to menstrual cloths, ritually unclean under Leviticus 15:19–24. The image is of ritual uncleanness that excludes from worship, matching ‘we are all become as one unclean’ (tame’).

Verse numbering: 64:6 in the Douay, Vulgate and KJV; 64:5 in the Hebrew Bible.
steps: It is the confession of an unfaithful people

Read 64:5–7. The people have sinned ‘always’; ‘there is none that calleth upon thy name’. The ‘righteous deeds’ in question are the religious acts of Israel while it was in rebellion: sacrifices and fasts performed without conversion of heart. Isaiah condemned exactly those in chapter 1: ‘bring no more sacrifice in vain… your new moons… my soul hateth’ (1:13–14).
Isaiah praises the righteousness God gives

‘Is not this rather the fast that I have chosen? loose the bands of wickedness… Deal thy bread to the hungry… Then shall thy light break forth as the morning… and thy justice shall go before thy face’ (58:6–8). ‘Keep ye judgment, and do justice: for my salvation is near to come’ (56:1). Isaiah does not think all righteousness is filth; he distinguishes hypocritical religion from true justice.
Works done in grace are God’s own work

‘We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus in good works, which God hath prepared that we should walk in them’ (Ephesians 2:10). ‘It is God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish’ (Philippians 2:13). If the good works of the justified are filthy rags, then the Holy Spirit produces filth. Scripture instead says: ‘the fine linen are the justifications (dikaiōmata, righteous deeds) of saints’ (Revelation 19:8).
Scripture speaks constantly of God rewarding good works

‘God is not unjust, that he should forget your work, and the love which you have shewn in his name’ (Hebrews 6:10). ‘Whosoever shall give to drink… a cup of cold water… he shall not lose his reward’ (Matthew 10:42). ‘Come, ye blessed… for I was hungry, and you gave me to eat’ (Matthew 25:34–35). ‘There is laid up for me a crown of justice, which the Lord the just judge will render to me’ (2 Timothy 4:8).
Trent’s balanced teaching

Trent condemns the claims that the just sin in every good work (canon 25) and that the good works of the justified do not merit eternal life (canon 32). It also says Christians must not trust in themselves or glory in themselves but in the Lord, ‘whose bounty towards all men is so great, that he will have the things which are his own gifts be their merits’ (Session 6, ch. 16).
fathers: Jerome, Commentary on Isaiah, book 17 (c. 410)
Reads the verse as the confession of the Jewish people under God’s anger, recognizing that their works done in unfaithfulness were unclean (paraphrased).
Augustine, Letter 194, 5.19
God crowns his own gifts when he rewards our merits.
Council of Trent, Session 6, ch. 16 and canons 25, 32 (1547)
Good works of the justified truly merit increase of grace and eternal life, as gifts of God.
obj: “Even a Christian’s best work is mixed with selfishness.”

Often true, and Catholics confess it daily. But mixed motives make a work imperfect, not sinful through and through. And God, who knows our weakness, accepts the good he has worked in us for Christ’s sake (1 Peter 2:5: ‘spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ’).
“Isaiah says ‘all our righteousnesses’, including his own.”
He speaks in solidarity with his people, as Daniel does (Daniel 9:5–7) and Nehemiah does (Nehemiah 1:6). This is liturgical confession, not a philosophical claim about every act of every believer.
deep.talk: “Isaiah is praying for Israel during exile, confessing that the people had been worshipping while living in sin, and their religious acts were unclean. He’s right: works done without God are worthless. But Isaiah also says fasting by feeding the hungry makes God’s light break forth (58:8). And the New Testament says the saints are clothed in fine linen, which is their righteous deeds (Revelation 19:8). Works done in God’s grace aren’t filthy rags; they’re what the Holy Spirit does in us.”
deep.avoid: Do not say that our natural goodness, apart from grace, can earn salvation; that is Pelagianism and the Church condemned it (Council of Carthage, 418).
read: Council of Trent, Session 6, ch. 16, canons 25–26, 32

acts|17.claim: The Bereans tested even an apostle by Scripture, and Luke praises them as "more noble". So every Christian should test every teaching, including the Church's, by Scripture alone, using private judgment.
why: The Bereans were Jews checking whether the Old Testament supported Paul's claim that Jesus was the Messiah. They had no New Testament.
Having checked, they accepted Paul's oral preaching, which taught far more than the Old Testament said explicitly (the resurrection of Jesus, baptism, the Eucharist).
Luke says they were "more noble" because they "received the word with all eagerness", in contrast to the Thessalonians, who rioted (17:5).
Catholics also search the Scriptures and find there the faith the apostles preached. Searching Scripture is good; it is not the same as Scripture alone.
acts|17.cath: The Bereans are a model for reading Scripture eagerly and receiving the apostolic message, not for rejecting the apostles' living authority.

deep.ctx: Acts 17:1–15. In Thessalonica Paul ‘reasoned with them out of the scriptures, declaring and insinuating that the Christ was to suffer, and to rise again from the dead; and that this is Jesus Christ’ (17:2–3). Some believed, but jealous Jews raised a mob (17:5). Paul and Silas went to Berea. ‘Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, who received the word with all eagerness, daily searching the scriptures, whether these things were so. And many indeed of them believed’ (17:11–12). Then Jews from Thessalonica came to stir up trouble there too (17:13).
deep.who: A favourite verse for sola scriptura and the right of private judgment: the Bereans, ordinary believers, did not accept an apostle’s word on authority but checked it against the Bible, and Scripture commends them for it. So Christians today should check the Pope and the Church against Scripture.
deep.lang: “More noble” (eugenesteroi): of better disposition, more open-minded. The reason given is the participle clause: ‘who received (edexanto) the word with all eagerness (prothymias)’. ‘Searching’ (anakrinontes) means examining closely.
steps: They were searching the Old Testament

The only Scriptures available were the Jewish Scriptures. Paul was arguing that they foretold a suffering and risen Messiah (17:3). Checking that claim against the prophets was exactly what Paul wanted. Catholics do the same: the Church has always argued from the Old Testament to Christ (Luke 24:27).
They then accepted oral apostolic teaching

Having found the prophecies confirmed, ‘many of them believed’: they accepted Paul’s preaching, which went beyond what the Old Testament stated explicitly (the identity of the Messiah, his resurrection, the Church, baptism). The Bereans did not adopt ‘Old Testament alone’; they accepted a living apostle’s message as God’s word (cf. 1 Thessalonians 2:13: ‘you received it not as the word of men, but, as it is indeed, the word of God’).
The praise is for their eagerness, not their method

Luke contrasts them with the Thessalonian Jews who formed a mob. ‘More noble’ because they listened with eagerness and examined fairly instead of rejecting Paul outright. The Thessalonians who did believe also examined the Scriptures (17:2–4).
The verse does not describe settling doctrinal disputes among Christians

When Christians disagreed about doctrine (whether Gentiles must be circumcised), they did not each search Scripture and go their own way; they went ‘to the apostles and priests’ in Jerusalem, who decided in council (Acts 15:2, 6, 28). That is the model for disputes within the Church.
If the Bereans are the model of sola scriptura, the model fails
Applying their method strictly would mean accepting only what the Old Testament teaches, and rejecting any apostolic teaching not found there. No Protestant does that.
fathers: John Chrysostom, Homilies on Acts 37 (c. 400)
Praises the Bereans for receiving the word with readiness and examining it, not with hostility (paraphrased).
Dei Verbum 25 (1965)
‘Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ’ (quoting Jerome): all the faithful are urged to read Scripture often.
obj: “The principle is: test everything by Scripture, which Catholics refuse.”

Catholics test teaching by Scripture and Tradition, read in the Church. Nothing the Church teaches contradicts Scripture. But ‘test by Scripture’ does not settle whose interpretation is right when sincere Bible-readers disagree; that requires an authority Scripture itself points to (Matthew 18:17; Acts 15; 1 Timothy 3:15).
deep.talk: “The Bereans were Jews checking whether the Old Testament really foretold a suffering, rising Messiah, like Paul said. When they found it did, they believed Paul’s preaching, which taught a lot more than the Old Testament spelled out. Catholics search the Scriptures too, and they point us to Christ and to the Church he founded. When the early Christians had a disagreement about doctrine, in Acts 15, they didn’t each go to their Bibles separately; they went to the apostles in council.”
deep.avoid: Do not discourage personal Bible study; the Church urges it (Dei Verbum 25).

1-corinthians|4.claim: Paul's phrase "not to go beyond what is written" is taken as a general rule: no Christian doctrine may go beyond the Bible. Catholic teachings not stated in Scripture break the rule.
why: The phrase is notoriously obscure. Paul applies it to the Corinthians' pride in rival teachers: "that no one be puffed up for one against the other".
"What is written" most likely means the Old Testament texts he has just quoted against human boasting (1:19, 31; 3:19–20).
When Paul wrote, most of the New Testament did not exist. If the rule meant "Scripture alone", it would forbid accepting the Gospels and Paul's own later letters.
In the same letter Paul praises the Corinthians for keeping the traditions he delivered orally (11:2).
1-corinthians|4.cath: Do not be puffed up in human leaders beyond what God's word says. It is a warning against pride, not a theory of the canon.

deep.ctx: 1 Corinthians 1–4 addresses factions: ‘I indeed am of Paul; and I am of Apollo; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ’ (1:12). Paul insists that he and Apollos are only servants (3:5) and that the Corinthians should not boast in men (3:21). Then: ‘But these things, brethren, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollo, for your sakes: that in us you may learn, that one be not puffed up against the other for another, above that which is written’ (4:6). He goes on: ‘For who distinguisheth thee? Or what hast thou that thou hast not received?’ (4:7).
deep.who: Some Protestant writers use ‘not beyond what is written’ as an apostolic statement of sola scriptura: Paul teaches the church not to go beyond the written Scriptures in doctrine.
deep.lang: The Greek is compressed: to mē hyper ha gegraptai, literally ‘the not beyond what is written’. It may be a slogan Paul is quoting, or a reference to his scriptural citations. Scholars disagree; some even suspect a scribal note entered the text. The phrase is introduced by ‘that you may learn in us’, and the purpose clause that follows is about not being ‘puffed up’ (physiousthe).
steps: The application is to pride and factions

Paul states the purpose: ‘that one be not puffed up against the other for another’. The issue is boasting about Paul or Apollos. ‘Beyond what is written’ means: do not exalt teachers beyond what Scripture allows, for Scripture says ‘He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord’ (1:31, quoting Jeremiah 9:23–24).
‘What is written’ points to Paul’s Old Testament quotations

In chapters 1–3 Paul has repeatedly cited Scripture against human wisdom and boasting: Isaiah 29:14 (1:19), Jeremiah 9:24 (1:31), Isaiah 64:4 (2:9), Job 5:13 and Psalm 93:11 (3:19–20). ‘What is written’ is the formula he uses for those (gegraptai, ‘it is written’).
A general sola scriptura reading proves too much

If Paul meant ‘believe nothing beyond the Scriptures you have’, then the Corinthians should have rejected his own later letter (2 Corinthians), the Gospels and every other New Testament book written afterwards. That cannot be his meaning.
The same letter commends oral tradition

‘Now I praise you, brethren, that in all things you are mindful of me: and keep my ordinances (paradoseis) as I have delivered them to you’ (11:2). He hands on the Eucharist (11:23) and the creed of the resurrection (15:3) as traditions received and delivered, and promises to set other matters in order ‘when I come’ (11:34).
fathers: John Chrysostom, Homilies on 1 Corinthians 12 (c. 392)
Paul uses himself and Apollos as examples so the Corinthians would not be puffed up about their teachers (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on 1 Corinthians, ch. 4, lect. 1
‘Beyond what is written’: beyond what Scripture teaches about humility, that no one should glory in a man (paraphrased).
obj: “Even if obscure, the principle is that Scripture limits doctrine.”

Catholics agree that no doctrine may contradict Scripture, and that Scripture is the supreme written norm. But this verse doesn’t teach that only explicitly written doctrines may be held; Paul in this very letter relies on unwritten traditions.
deep.talk: “Paul is talking about the Corinthians being puffed up about their favourite preachers, ‘I’m with Paul, I’m with Apollos’, and he tells them not to go beyond what Scripture says about not boasting in men. If he meant ‘never believe anything beyond the written Bible’, they’d have had to reject the rest of the New Testament, which wasn’t written yet. And in chapter 11 he praises them for holding the traditions he passed on in person.”
deep.avoid: Do not overstate how certain any reading of this phrase is; scholars agree it is difficult.
read: Anthony Thiselton (2000) The First Epistle to the Corinthians. NIGTC. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, pp. 351–356
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on 1 Corinthians, ch. 4

galatians|1.t: "Though we, or an angel… preach another gospel… let him be anathema"
galatians|1.claim: Catholic additions (Mary, purgatory, saints, sacraments, merit) are "another gospel", and Paul curses anyone who preaches one.
why: Catholics accept the verse fully: no one, not even a pope or an angel, can change the gospel the apostles preached.
The gospel Paul defends is the one he "preached" and they "received" (1:9): oral, apostolic teaching handed on, not a set of books.
Paul himself went to Jerusalem to lay his gospel before Peter, James and John, "lest perhaps I should run, or had run in vain" (2:2).
The real question is which community has kept the gospel as first received. Catholics point to continuity in doctrine from the apostolic era.
galatians|1.cath: The gospel cannot be changed by anyone. The Church is its guardian, not its owner.

deep.ctx: Paul opens Galatians without his usual thanksgiving: ‘I wonder that you are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ, unto another gospel. Which is not another, only there are some that trouble you, and would pervert the gospel of Christ. But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach a gospel to you besides that which we have preached to you, let him be anathema. As we said before, so now I say again: If any one preach to you a gospel, besides that which you have received, let him be anathema’ (1:6–9). The ‘other gospel’ was the requirement of circumcision for Gentiles.
deep.who: Used against any Catholic teaching considered unbiblical: it is ‘another gospel’. Sometimes used against Marian apparitions, or against papal teaching: if even an angel cannot change the gospel, neither can a pope.
deep.lang: “Besides” (par’ ho): beyond, contrary to. “Anathema”: devoted to destruction, accursed; the term later used in councils to condemn heresy. “Received” (parelabete, 1:9) is the technical verb for receiving tradition (1 Corinthians 11:23; 15:1, 3).
steps: Catholics wholeheartedly agree

The Church teaches that public revelation closed with the apostles and that the Magisterium ‘is not above the word of God, but serves it, teaching only what has been handed on’ (Dei Verbum 10). Vatican I: the Holy Spirit was not promised to Peter’s successors ‘that they might make known new doctrine’, but that they might guard and expound the deposit of faith (Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4). A pope who taught a new gospel would fall under Paul’s anathema.
The gospel was oral and received

Paul refers to what ‘we have preached’ and what ‘you have received’. At this point there was no New Testament. Paul is defending apostolic tradition, which included the sacraments: in the same letter, baptism ‘into Christ’ (3:27).
The ‘other gospel’ was a specific error

Circumcision as a requirement for Gentiles, and with it the whole Law as the way of righteousness (5:2–4). Paul does not call every disputed practice ‘another gospel’. He tolerated disagreement on secondary matters (Romans 14).
Paul submitted his gospel to Peter and the apostles

‘I went up… and conferred with them the gospel, which I preach among the Gentiles… lest perhaps I should run, or had run in vain’ (2:2). Earlier he had gone to see (historēsai) Cephas for fifteen days (1:18). Even an apostle sought communion with Peter.
The test is continuity

Which teaching matches the gospel received from the beginning? Catholics point to the early Christian witness on baptismal regeneration, the real presence, the sacrifice of the Mass, the authority of bishops in succession and prayer for the dead, all attested in the first three centuries. A gospel without these is the newer one.
fathers: Vincent of Lérins, Commonitorium 9.14 (434)
Comments on this verse: to announce to Catholic Christians anything other than what they have received never was, never is and never will be lawful (paraphrased).
Tertullian, Prescription against Heretics 21 (c. 200)
What the apostles preached must be proved only through those churches which the apostles founded (paraphrased).
obj: “The Church has added doctrines over time.”

The Church has defined doctrines over time, usually in response to challenges (as Nicaea did in 325). Development is not addition: Newman’s criteria (preservation of type, continuity of principles, logical sequence) distinguish growth from corruption (Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine, 1845).
deep.talk: “Catholics agree with Galatians 1:8 completely: not even a pope or an angel can change the gospel. The Church teaches the Pope can’t invent new doctrine. But notice Paul is defending the gospel the Galatians received by preaching, before there was a New Testament. So the question is: who has kept that apostolic gospel? Catholics point to the early Church: baptism that regenerates, the Eucharist as Christ’s body, bishops in succession, prayer for the dead. That’s the original gospel.”
deep.avoid: Do not use ‘anathema’ language against fellow Christians lightly; Paul’s curse targeted a gospel-denying error.
read: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus ch. 4
John Henry Newman (1845) An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine

colossians|2.t: "The tradition of men… and not according to Christ"
colossians|2.claim: Paul warns against "philosophy" and "the tradition of men". Catholic tradition and scholastic philosophy (Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas) are exactly what Paul condemned.
why: Paul condemns tradition and philosophy that are "according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ". The qualifier matters.
The context shows the Colossian error: food rules, festivals, worship of angels and harsh treatment of the body (2:16–23).
Paul praises apostolic tradition elsewhere (2 Thessalonians 2:14; 1 Corinthians 11:2) and himself uses Greek thought when it serves the gospel (Acts 17:28).
Faith and reason are allies: philosophy that serves Christ is not "vain deceit" (Fides et Ratio, 1998).
colossians|2.cath: Tradition and philosophy that are against Christ are vain; tradition that hands on Christ, and reasoning that serves him, are gifts.

deep.ctx: Colossians 2 warns against a teaching that threatened the church at Colossae. ‘Beware lest any man cheat you by philosophy, and vain deceit; according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ: for in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead corporeally’ (2:8–9). The rest of the chapter describes the error: ‘Let no man therefore judge you in meat or in drink, or in respect of a festival day, or of the new moon, or of the sabbaths’ (2:16); ‘Let no man seduce you, willing in humility, and religion of angels’ (2:18); ‘Touch not: taste not: handle not’ (2:21); ‘not in any honour to the filling of the flesh’ (2:23).
deep.who: Used against Catholic Tradition generally, and against the use of Greek philosophy in Catholic theology (Thomism, transubstantiation’s use of ‘substance’). Sometimes against Catholic fasting rules as well.
deep.lang: “Philosophy” (philosophia) here is qualified as ‘vain deceit’ (kenēs apatēs, ‘empty deception’). “Elements of the world” (stoicheia tou kosmou): either elementary religious principles or elemental spirits/powers, connected with the ‘religion of angels’ (2:18). The error appears to be a mix of Jewish calendar and food rules with mystical angel-veneration and ascetic rules.
steps: Paul condemns a specific false system

The ‘philosophy’ is ‘according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ’. It made Christ less than the fullness of God and put angels and rules in his place. Catholics condemn it too.
Not every tradition is ‘of men’

Paul distinguishes: tradition ‘of men’ that is ‘not according to Christ’ is vain; the tradition he and the apostles delivered must be held (2 Thessalonians 2:14; 3:6; 1 Corinthians 11:2). In Colossians itself he urges: ‘As therefore you have received (parelabete) Jesus Christ the Lord, walk ye in him’ (2:6), the language of receiving tradition.
Paul uses reason and even pagan poets

At Athens Paul quotes Aratus: ‘For we are also his offspring’ (Acts 17:28), and argues from creation in Romans 1:20. Christian thinkers from Justin Martyr onward used philosophy to defend and explain the faith. The First Vatican Council and John Paul II teach that faith and reason cannot contradict each other (Dei Filius 4; Fides et Ratio 1998).
The ascetic rules Paul rejects were not Christian fasting

The Colossian rules (‘touch not, taste not’) sprang from contempt for the body and fear of spiritual powers. Christian fasting is done freely, for love of God, and affirms creation’s goodness (see note on 1 Timothy 4:3). Jesus said his disciples would fast (Matthew 9:15).
fathers: Justin Martyr, Second Apology 13 (c. 155)
Whatever things were rightly said by any philosophers belong to us Christians, because of the seeds of the Word in all people (paraphrased).
Clement of Alexandria, Stromata I.5 (c. 200)
Philosophy prepared the Greeks for Christ as the Law prepared the Jews (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Colossians, ch. 2, lect. 2
Philosophy is condemned when it is followed against faith; using philosophical reasons in service of faith is not condemned (paraphrased).
John Paul II, Fides et Ratio 1, 36–41 (1998)
Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the truth.
obj: “Transubstantiation imports Aristotle into the gospel.”

The doctrine that the bread becomes Christ’s body is in Scripture and the Fathers long before scholastic terminology (see notes on John 6 and 1 Corinthians 11). ‘Substance’ simply names ‘what a thing is’, which ordinary language already distinguishes from appearances. The Church uses the word without canonizing a full Aristotelian system (Paul VI, Mysterium Fidei 24).
deep.talk: “Paul is warning against a specific false teaching that put angels and food rules in place of Christ: ‘not according to Christ’ is the key phrase. In the same chapter he says ‘as you received Christ, walk in him’, using the word for receiving tradition. And Paul himself quoted pagan poets at Athens. Thinking carefully about the faith isn’t vain philosophy; it’s loving God with your mind.”
deep.avoid: Do not imply that faith depends on Aristotle; the Church’s doctrines are revealed, and philosophy only helps explain them.
read: John Paul II (1998) Fides et Ratio
First Vatican Council, Dei Filius ch. 4 (1870)
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Colossians, ch. 2

1-corinthians|3.t: "Other foundation no man can lay… which is Christ Jesus"
1-corinthians|3.claim: Christ is the only foundation of the Church, so Peter cannot be the rock on which it is built, and the papacy usurps Christ's place.
why: Scripture uses building images in more than one way. The same Paul writes that the Church is "built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone" (Ephesians 2:20).
Revelation 21:14: "the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them, the twelve names of the twelve apostles."
Christ is the foundation by his own power; the apostles, and Peter as their head, are foundations by sharing in his work. The two images do not compete.
In context, Paul is telling Corinthian teachers to build on Christ, not to boast in human leaders (3:4–10).
1-corinthians|3.cath: Christ is the one foundation; Peter is the rock by Christ's gift, so that the Church built on Christ stands firm.

deep.ctx: 1 Corinthians 3:5–15. Paul describes himself and Apollos as fellow workers: ‘I have planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the increase’ (3:6). ‘According to the grace of God that is given to me, as a wise architect, I have laid the foundation; and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon. For other foundation no man can lay, but that which is laid; which is Christ Jesus’ (3:10–11). Then: each builder’s work, whether gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay or stubble, will be tested by fire (3:12–15).
deep.who: This verse is used to answer Matthew 16:18: Christ alone is the rock and foundation; to call Peter the foundation of the Church contradicts Paul.
deep.lang: “Foundation” (themelios). Ephesians 2:20 uses the same word: ‘built upon the foundation (themeliō) of the apostles and prophets’. Revelation 21:14: ‘twelve foundations (themelious)’.
steps: Paul is speaking of preaching

In context, the ‘foundation’ Paul laid at Corinth is the preaching of Christ crucified (2:2), and other teachers must build on it with sound doctrine (3:10–15). He is not discussing church government.
Scripture calls the apostles foundations too

Ephesians 2:20 and Revelation 21:14 explicitly call the apostles the Church’s foundation. Since Scripture cannot contradict itself, ‘Christ is the only foundation’ and ‘the apostles are foundations’ must be true in different senses.
Christ is the primary foundation; the apostles are secondary, by participation

Thomas explains: Christ is the foundation by his own authority; the apostles by authority given them by Christ (Commentary on Ephesians, ch. 2, lect. 6). Peter is the rock in the same way: Christ is ‘the rock’ (1 Corinthians 10:4), and he names Simon ‘Rock’, giving him a share in his own stability (Luke 22:32).
The same pattern applies to every title of Christ

Christ is the light of the world (John 8:12), yet says ‘you are the light of the world’ (Matthew 5:14). He is the good shepherd (John 10:11), yet tells Peter ‘feed my sheep’ (John 21:17). He is the one high priest, yet makes believers ‘a kingly priesthood’ (1 Peter 2:9). Sharing Christ’s titles by participation never rivals him.
fathers: Jerome, Against Jovinian I.26 (393)

The Church is founded on Peter, though elsewhere the same is said of all the apostles; yet one is chosen among the twelve so that, a head being appointed, the occasion of schism may be removed (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on 1 Corinthians, ch. 3, lect. 2
Christ is the foundation principally; the apostles and their teaching secondarily (paraphrased).
obj: “Ephesians 2:20 means the apostles’ teaching, not their persons.”

Revelation 21:14 puts the twelve names on the foundations. And teaching and teachers cannot be separated: the apostles taught with authority received from Christ (Luke 10:16: ‘He that heareth you, heareth me’).
deep.talk: “Christ is absolutely the foundation of the Church. But Paul also says the Church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), and Revelation puts the twelve apostles’ names on the foundations of the heavenly city. Jesus is the light of the world, and he tells us ‘you are the light of the world’. He shares his titles. Peter being the rock doesn’t compete with Christ; it’s Christ’s gift.”
deep.avoid: Do not argue that Peter is the foundation ‘instead of’ Christ in any sense; the Catholic claim is participation.
read: Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Ephesians, ch. 2, lect. 6

acts|10.t: Peter: "Arise: I myself also am a man"
acts|10.claim: When Cornelius knelt before Peter, Peter refused. So bowing to the Pope or kneeling before saints' images is wrong, and Peter would have rejected the honours given to popes.
why: Cornelius, a Gentile, "falling at his feet adored" (prosekynēsen); Peter corrects what looked like worship of a man as a heavenly messenger.
Catholics do not worship the Pope or the saints. Worship (latria) is for God alone (CCC 2096).

Scripture also records honour rightly shown to God's servants: the sons of the prophets "worshipping him [Elisha] falling to the ground" (2 Kings 2:15) and Abigail bowing before David (1 Samuel 25:23).
Peter's humility is the model for every pope; one of the papal titles is "servant of the servants of God".
acts|10.cath: Honour for God's servants is good; worship belongs to God alone. Peter's humility is the pattern for his successors.

deep.ctx: Acts 10 tells of Cornelius, a Roman centurion, devout and God-fearing, who sees an angel telling him to send for Peter (10:3–6). Peter, meanwhile, has the vision of the sheet with unclean animals (10:9–16). When Peter arrives: ‘And it came to pass, that when Peter was come in, Cornelius came to meet him, and falling at his feet adored. But Peter lifted him up, saying: Arise, I myself also am a man’ (10:25–26). Peter then preaches, the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles, and Peter commands them to be baptized (10:44–48).
deep.who: Used against kneeling before the Pope, kissing his ring and honours given to clergy, and against venerating saints and their images: if Peter, the first pope, refused such honour, Catholics are wrong to give it to his successors or to saints.
deep.lang: “Adored” (prosekynēsen, from proskyneō): to prostrate oneself. The word can mean worship of God or the reverence given to a king or superior (Matthew 18:26; Revelation 3:9, where Christ says he will make enemies ‘come and adore (proskynēsousin) before thy feet’ of the faithful church).
steps: Cornelius probably took Peter for more than a man

Cornelius had just seen an angel who sent him to Peter. A pagan-born Roman meeting the messenger announced by an angel could easily think him a divine or heavenly being. Peter’s answer, ‘I myself also am a man’, corrects exactly that. The same reaction is at Lystra, where the crowd want to sacrifice to Paul and Barnabas as gods (Acts 14:11–15).
Prostration as honour is not always wrong

Revelation 3:9: Christ promises the faithful church in Philadelphia that its enemies will come and prostrate themselves (proskynēsousin) before their feet. In the Old Testament, the sons of the prophets bow to the ground before Elisha (2 Kings 2:15; 4 Kings in the Douay), Abigail before David (1 Samuel 25:23), Joseph’s brothers before Joseph (Genesis 42:6). What matters is the meaning of the act: worship of God or honour of a person.
The Church distinguishes worship from honour

Latria (adoration) is given to God alone; dulia (honour) to the saints; hyperdulia to Mary (ST II-II q.103 a.3–4; CCC 971, 2132). Respect shown to the Pope is civil and religious honour for the office of Christ’s vicar, not worship.
Peter’s humility binds his successors

The papal title servus servorum Dei, ‘servant of the servants of God’, used since Gregory the Great (590–604), expresses Christ’s command: ‘he that is the greater among you, let him become as the younger’ (Luke 22:26). In recent decades popes have simplified court ceremonial for this very reason.
fathers: John Chrysostom, Homilies on Acts 23 (c. 400)
Peter teaches humility: he does not accept honour beyond what is fitting, even when offered (paraphrased).
Gregory the Great, Letters (c. 595)
Adopts the title ‘servant of the servants of God’ in protest against the title ‘universal bishop’ claimed by the patriarch of Constantinople (paraphrased).
obj: “Kissing the Pope’s ring is still too much.”
It is a customary gesture of respect for an office, like bowing to a monarch or kissing a bishop’s ring, and is optional; recent popes have often declined it. It is not part of doctrine.
deep.talk: “Cornelius had just seen an angel who told him to send for Peter, so when Peter came in he fell down as if before a heavenly being. Peter corrected him: ‘I’m only a man.’ Catholics agree: the Pope is a man and we don’t worship him. But Scripture shows people bowing to honour God’s servants, like the prophets bowing to Elisha. Honour and worship are different, and Peter’s humility is the model every pope is supposed to follow.”
deep.avoid: Do not defend excessive court ceremonial; the Church herself has reformed it. Stick to the distinction between honour and worship.
read: ST II-II q.84 a.1; q.103 a.3–4

revelation|17.claim: The great harlot Babylon sits on seven hills; Rome is the city of seven hills; therefore the harlot is the Roman Catholic Church and the Pope is the Antichrist.
why: In John's day, "the great city which hath kingdom over the kings of the earth" (17:18) was pagan imperial Rome, which was killing Christians.
The woman is "drunk with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus" (17:6): the persecuting empire of Nero and Domitian, not the Church whose saints those martyrs were.
Peter, writing from Rome, sends greetings from "the church that is in Babylon" (1 Peter 5:13). For the early Christians, "Babylon" was a code-name for imperial Rome.
The Church of Rome is the Church of the martyrs Peter and Paul, built on their tombs. The harlot is the power that killed them.
revelation|17.cath: Babylon is the persecuting world-empire of John's day, and every power that makes war on the saints; it is not the Church of the martyrs.

deep.ctx: Revelation 17 describes ‘the great harlot that sitteth upon many waters’ (17:1), seated on a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns, dressed in purple and scarlet, holding a golden cup, ‘and on her forehead a name was written: A mystery; Babylon the great, the mother of the fornications, and the abominations of the earth. And I saw the woman drunk with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus’ (17:5–6). The angel explains: ‘The seven heads are seven mountains, upon which the woman sitteth, and they are seven kings: five are fallen, one is, and the other is not yet come’ (17:9–10). ‘And the woman which thou sawest, is the great city, which hath kingdom over the kings of the earth’ (17:18). Chapter 18 describes the fall of Babylon, a commercial empire whose merchants grew rich from her (18:11–19).
deep.who: From the Reformation onwards (Luther, Calvin, the Westminster Confession of 1646, which called the Pope ‘that Antichrist, that man of sin’, XXV.6, a clause later removed by many Presbyterian bodies), and in modern fundamentalist literature, the harlot is identified with the Catholic Church: Rome is built on seven hills; the colours purple and scarlet are those of bishops and cardinals; the golden cup is the chalice; she has shed the blood of Protestant martyrs.
deep.lang: “Mountains” (orē) and “kings” (basileis): the seven heads have a double meaning. Roman writers routinely called Rome ‘the city of seven hills’ (Virgil, Horace, Cicero). “Five are fallen, one is”: a reference to the line of Roman emperors at the time of writing. The ‘number of the beast’ 666 (13:18) is most commonly explained by scholars as the numerical value of ‘Nero Caesar’ in Hebrew letters (nrwn qsr); some manuscripts read 616, which matches the Latin spelling ‘Nero’.
steps: John is addressing seven churches under persecution in the 1st century

Revelation is written to Christians in Asia Minor (1:4, 11), suffering under Rome. Antipas has been killed (2:13); John is exiled on Patmos ‘for the word of God’ (1:9). The ‘beast’ demands worship (13:4, 15), as the imperial cult did. Revelation’s immediate meaning concerns that empire.
Babylon was early Christian code for pagan Rome

1 Peter 5:13: ‘The church that is in Babylon… saluteth you’, written from Rome. Jewish writings after AD 70 (4 Ezra, 2 Baruch, the Sibylline Oracles) call Rome ‘Babylon’, since like Babylon it destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple. The seven hills, ‘five kings fallen’ and ‘the great city which hath kingdom over the kings of the earth’ (17:18) all fit imperial Rome in John’s day.
The harlot kills the martyrs; the Church is the Church of the martyrs

The woman is ‘drunk with the blood of the saints and martyrs of Jesus’ (17:6). Peter and Paul were killed in Rome under Nero (1 Clement 5; Tertullian, Prescription 36; Eusebius II.25). The Roman Church is built on their tombs. To identify the persecutor with the persecuted Church turns the image upside down.
The Church in Revelation is a different woman

Revelation 12 shows a woman ‘clothed with the sun’, who gives birth to the Messiah and is persecuted by the dragon; and 19:7–8; 21:2, 9 show the Bride of the Lamb, the holy city Jerusalem. Babylon is the anti-Church: the world in its power, wealth and idolatry, which every age must resist, including Christians tempted by wealth and power.
Some Catholic commentators also read a warning to Christians

Catholic interpretation has also seen in Babylon every worldly power that seduces and persecutes the faithful, and even unfaithful Jerusalem (11:8, ‘where their Lord also was crucified’). The warning ‘Go out from her, my people’ (18:4) applies to Christians in every age, Catholics included. But nothing in the text identifies the Church of the martyrs with the harlot.
fathers: Tertullian, Against Marcion III.13 and Answer to the Jews 9 (c. 200–210)
Says Babylon in John is a figure of the city of Rome, mighty and proud and the persecutor of the saints (paraphrased).
Augustine, City of God XVIII.2, 22 (c. 420)
Calls Rome ‘a second Babylon’, the earthly city that persecutes the city of God (paraphrased).
Haydock’s Catholic Bible Commentary (1811–14), on Revelation 17
Follows the Fathers in reading Babylon as pagan Rome, persecutor of Christians (paraphrased).
obj: “The colours purple and scarlet are cardinals’ colours.”

Purple and scarlet were the colours of wealth and royalty in the ancient world (Mark 15:17; Luke 16:19). Cardinals’ red is meant to signify readiness to shed blood for Christ, and dates from the 13th century. You cannot interpret a 1st-century text by medieval vestments.
“The Catholic Church persecuted Protestants.”

Catholics and Protestants both persecuted one another in the 16th and 17th centuries, and Catholics have acknowledged their share (John Paul II, Jubilee day of pardon, 12 March 2000). But Revelation 17 is not about the Reformation; it describes the empire killing ‘the martyrs of Jesus’ in John’s own day.
“Vatican City is on Vatican Hill, which is one of the seven hills.”
The Vatican Hill is not among Rome’s classical seven hills (Palatine, Capitoline, Aventine, Caelian, Esquiline, Quirinal, Viminal); it lies across the Tiber, outside the ancient city.
deep.talk: “John is writing to Christians being persecuted by the Roman Empire. The early Christians called Rome ‘Babylon’; Peter even signs off his letter from Rome as ‘the church in Babylon’. The woman is drunk with the blood of the martyrs, and Rome killed Peter and Paul. The Catholic Church in Rome is built over their graves. So the harlot is the empire that killed the martyrs, not the Church that honours them.”
deep.avoid: Do not get drawn into date-setting or speculative end-times charts. Do not deny that Christians, including Catholics, have sometimes behaved like ‘Babylon’; the Church calls her members to conversion.
read: Richard Bauckham (1993) The Theology of the Book of Revelation. Cambridge: CUP, ch. 2 (an Anglican scholar on Babylon as Rome)
Scott Hahn (1999) The Lamb’s Supper. New York: Doubleday

john|19.claim: Jesus declared the work of salvation finished on the Cross. So nothing can be added: no Mass, no purgatory, no penance, no merit.
why: Catholics agree that Christ's sacrifice was completed on the Cross and needs no addition.

John's word (tetelestai) means the work given him by the Father, the sacrifice and the fulfilment of Scripture, is accomplished. It does not mean that nothing more happens: the Resurrection, Ascension and Pentecost follow, and Paul says Christ "rose again for our justification" (Romans 4:25).
The finished work must still be applied to each person through faith, baptism, the Eucharist and penance. Protestants too believe it must be applied, through faith.
Paul even says: "I fill up those things that are wanting of the sufferings of Christ, in my flesh, for his body, which is the church" (Colossians 1:24).
john|19.cath: The sacrifice is finished; its fruits are applied to every generation until the end of time.

deep.ctx: John 19:28–30: ‘Afterwards, Jesus knowing that all things were now accomplished, that the scripture might be fulfilled, said: I thirst. Now there was a vessel set there full of vinegar. And they, putting a sponge full of vinegar about hyssop, put it to his mouth. Jesus therefore, when he had taken the vinegar, said: It is consummated. And bowing his head, he gave up the ghost.’ John then reports the piercing of his side, ‘and immediately there came out blood and water’ (19:34).
deep.who: ‘It is finished’ (tetelestai) is said to be a commercial term for ‘paid in full’, written on receipts: Christ paid the whole debt of sin, so purgatory (which implies a remaining debt of temporal punishment), indulgences, penance and the Mass (an ongoing sacrifice) all deny that the debt was paid in full.
deep.lang: Tetelestai: perfect passive of teleō, ‘to finish, complete, accomplish, fulfil’. John uses the same verb two verses earlier: ‘knowing that all things were now accomplished (tetelestai)’ (19:28), linked to fulfilling Scripture. The ‘paid in full’ meaning rests on its use in some papyri receipts (where it can mark a bill paid); it is a possible overtone, but John’s own usage points to the completion of the work the Father gave him (4:34; 17:4: ‘I have finished (teleiōsas) the work which thou gavest me to do’).
steps: Catholics agree Christ’s work of redemption was accomplished
Christ’s Passion merited all grace and made superabundant satisfaction for all sins (ST III q.48 a.2; CCC 616–617). There is no deficiency in Christ’s sacrifice that we could make up.
‘Finished’ refers to the work the Father gave him and the fulfilment of Scripture

John links tetelestai to Scripture being fulfilled (19:28) and to Jesus’ mission (17:4). The Passover Lamb has been sacrificed. Not everything in salvation history ended at that moment: the Resurrection (‘he rose again for our justification’, Romans 4:25), the Ascension, the sending of the Spirit and Christ’s heavenly intercession (Hebrews 7:25) were still to come.
Everyone agrees the finished work must be applied

A Protestant who says ‘it is finished’ still believes a person is not saved until he believes. Faith is the means of applying Christ’s finished work. Catholics say Christ also appointed sacraments as means of applying it: baptism (Acts 2:38), the Eucharist (John 6:54), absolution (John 20:23). Applying the work does not add to it.
Purgatory and penance are applications, not additions

Temporal punishment and purification remain after forgiveness because our sins leave disorder in us, as David was forgiven yet suffered consequences (2 Samuel 12:13–14). Purgatory is Christ’s finished work completing our healing; its power comes entirely from his Cross (CCC 1030–1032, 1472–1473). Paul himself speaks of ‘filling up what is wanting of the sufferings of Christ for his body’ (Colossians 1:24), not because Christ’s sufferings lacked anything, but because Christ wills his members to share in them.
The Mass makes the finished sacrifice present
The Mass offers no new work; it presents the finished one (see Hebrews 10:10). It is like a fountain that flows from a finished spring.
fathers: Augustine, Tractates on John 119.6 (c. 420)
‘It is finished’: all that prophecy foretold of him has been accomplished; he who had power to lay down his life laid it down (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on John, ch. 19, lect. 5
‘It is consummated’: the Passion fulfilled the prophecies, the figures of the Law, and the work of our redemption (paraphrased).
obj: “‘Paid in full’ means no temporal punishment remains.”

The eternal debt of sin was paid, and nothing we do adds to Christ’s satisfaction. But Scripture shows forgiven people undergoing discipline and purification (Hebrews 12:6–11; 1 Corinthians 3:15). Even Protestants accept that forgiven Christians still suffer the consequences of sin in this life.
deep.talk: “Jesus finished the work the Father gave him: the sacrifice for sin is complete and perfect, and nothing can be added to it. Catholics believe that. But it still has to reach each person. Even Protestants say you’re not saved until you believe. Catholics just add that Christ also gave sacraments to apply it. The Mass, confession and even purgatory don’t add to the Cross; they’re the Cross reaching us.”
deep.avoid: Do not dispute the ‘paid in full’ overtone aggressively; it is a possible nuance. Make the main point: completion of the sacrifice, application to us.
read: Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on John, ch. 19

hebrews|7.claim: Christ's priesthood is "unchangeable" (or "untransferable", aparabatos): it cannot pass to anyone else. So there can be no Catholic priests succeeding him.
why: Catholic priests do not succeed Christ or replace him. Christ remains the one high priest; ordained priests share in his priesthood as his ministers (CCC 1545).
The contrast in Hebrews is with Levitical priests who died and were replaced (7:23). Christ never dies, so he has no successor.
Thomas Aquinas: "Christ alone is the true priest; the others are only his ministers."
The same Christ who holds the eternal priesthood said to the apostles "Do this" and "whose sins you forgive".
hebrews|7.cath: One eternal priest, Christ; many ministers acting in his person, not in his place.

deep.ctx: Hebrews 7 argues from Psalm 109:4 (‘Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech’) that Christ’s priesthood surpasses the Levitical one. ‘And the others indeed were made many priests, because by reason of death they were not suffered to continue: but this, for that he continueth for ever, hath an everlasting priesthood: whereby he is able also to save for ever them that come to God by him; always living to make intercession for us’ (7:23–25).
deep.who: Since Christ’s priesthood is ‘untransferable’, there can be no human priests who carry on a priestly ministry. Catholic priests, especially as those who ‘offer sacrifice’, usurp Christ’s office.
deep.lang: “Everlasting” (aparabatos) occurs only here in the New Testament. Its meaning is debated: ‘permanent, unchangeable’ (the usual sense in Greek legal texts) or ‘not passing to another, without successor’. Either way, the contrast is with priests who die and are replaced (7:23).
steps: Christ has no successor, and Catholics say none

Catholic priests are not Christ’s successors. Christ is alive and is ‘the one priest’. The Church says the ministerial priest acts in persona Christi: Christ himself acts through him (CCC 1548). A minister is not a replacement.
Participation, not substitution

‘The redemptive sacrifice of Christ is unique… it is made present in the Eucharistic sacrifice of the Church. The same is true of the one priesthood of Christ; it is made present through the ministerial priesthood without diminishing the uniqueness of Christ’s priesthood’ (CCC 1545). As Christ is the one Shepherd and yet appoints shepherds (John 21:16; 1 Peter 5:1–4, where Peter calls Christ ‘the prince of pastors’).
Thomas’ formula

‘Christ alone is the true priest; the others are his ministers’ (Thomas, Commentary on Hebrews, ch. 7, lect. 4, paraphrased). Christ is the principal agent of every sacrament; the priest is his living instrument (ST III q.64 a.1, 5; q.82 a.1).
The apostles received a share in Christ’s mission

‘As the Father hath sent me, I also send you’ (John 20:21). ‘Do this for a commemoration of me’ (Luke 22:19). ‘He that heareth you heareth me’ (Luke 10:16). Paul describes his ministry as priestly service (Romans 15:16).
fathers: Augustine, Tractates on John 6.7 (c. 407)
When Peter baptizes, it is Christ who baptizes; when Judas baptizes, it is Christ who baptizes (paraphrased): the minister is Christ’s instrument.
Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.22 a.4; q.82 a.1 ad 4
Christ is the principal priest; the priest consecrates in the person of Christ.
obj: “If Christ does everything, why need a priest?”
Because Christ chose to act visibly through human ministers, as he chose to save through his visible human nature. ‘How shall they preach unless they be sent?’ (Romans 10:15).
deep.talk: “Exactly: Christ has no successor because he never dies. Catholic priests don’t replace him; they’re his ministers, and Christ acts through them. When a priest says ‘This is my body’, he’s speaking in Christ’s person, not his own. It’s one priesthood, Christ’s, shared out, just as there’s one Good Shepherd who still told Peter ‘feed my sheep’.”
deep.avoid: Do not speak of priests as ‘other Christs’ in a way that suggests rivalry; the phrase (alter Christus) is traditional but must be explained as configuration to Christ, not substitution.
read: Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on Hebrews, ch. 7

matthew|26.t: "I will not drink… of this fruit of the vine"
matthew|26.claim: After the words of consecration Jesus still calls the cup "this fruit of the vine". So it was still wine, and transubstantiation is false.
why: In Luke's fuller account, Jesus says "I will not drink of the fruit of the vine" (Luke 22:18) over a cup before the consecration of the chalice (22:20). The evangelists do not all keep the same order.
Even after consecration, the appearances of wine remain, and Scripture names things by how they appear: the steward tastes "the water made wine" (John 2:9).
Jesus has just said "This is my blood of the new testament, which shall be shed for many unto remission of sins" (26:28). That statement is the one to interpret plainly.
The phrase also looks forward to the kingdom ("until that day when I shall drink it with you new"), not backward to the chemistry of the cup.
matthew|26.cath: Christ called the cup his blood; the words "fruit of the vine" fit its appearance and look ahead to the heavenly banquet.
matthew|26.src: CCC 1374–1377; ST III q.75 a.2 ad 1

deep.ctx: Matthew 26:26–29: ‘And whilst they were at supper, Jesus took bread, and blessed, and broke: and gave to his disciples, and said: Take ye, and eat. This is my body. And taking the chalice, he gave thanks, and gave to them, saying: Drink ye all of this. For this is my blood of the new testament, which shall be shed for many unto remission of sins. And I say to you, I will not drink from henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I shall drink it with you new in the kingdom of my Father.’ Luke’s account has two cups: one before the bread, with the saying ‘I will not drink of the fruit of the vine, till the kingdom of God come’ (22:17–18), and the eucharistic chalice after supper (22:20).
deep.who: An argument popular since the Reformation: Jesus himself, after consecrating, calls the contents ‘fruit of the vine’. If it had become his blood, he would not call it wine.
deep.lang: “Fruit of the vine” (gennēmatos tēs ampelou) is the Jewish blessing over wine (‘Blessed are you, Lord… who creates the fruit of the vine’). Passover meals included several cups of wine, which explains Luke’s two cups.
steps: The order differs between Gospels

Luke places the ‘fruit of the vine’ saying over an earlier Passover cup (22:17–18), before the institution of the Eucharist (22:19–20). Matthew and Mark place it after. The evangelists group sayings; we cannot build a doctrine on the sequence in one Gospel when another places the words before consecration.
Things are named by their appearance

After consecration the species (appearances) of wine remain: colour, taste, smell. Scripture often names things by how they appear: angels are called ‘men’ (Genesis 18:2; Mark 16:5); the steward tastes ‘the water made wine’ (John 2:9); Aaron’s rod that became a serpent is still called a ‘rod’ when it swallows the others (Exodus 7:12). Thomas answers exactly this objection (ST III q.75 a.2 ad 1, on ‘bread’ in 1 Corinthians 11).
The decisive words are ‘This is my blood’
Jesus identifies the cup as his blood of the covenant, ‘shed… unto remission of sins’. Symbolic blood does not remit sins. The eschatological saying that follows does not cancel this identification.
The saying points to the kingdom

The emphasis is ‘until that day… new in the kingdom of my Father’: a vow that his next festive cup will be in the kingdom, which the Passion and Resurrection inaugurate. The Fathers connected it with his eating and drinking with the disciples after the Resurrection (Acts 10:41) and with the heavenly banquet.
fathers: Cyril of Jerusalem, Mystagogical Catecheses 4.2 (c. 350)
He once turned water into wine at Cana; is he not worthy of belief when he changes wine into blood (paraphrased)?
Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.75 a.2 ad 1; q.81 a.1
Christ drank his own blood at the Supper, according to some Fathers; things keep the names of their appearances.
obj: “This proves the substance of wine remained.”

It proves only that Jesus used the name the cup’s appearance suggested, if the saying in Matthew does follow the consecration. Lutherans, who believe the real presence, faced this argument too and did not find it decisive.
deep.talk: “Luke actually puts that saying before the cup is consecrated, so you can’t rely on the order. And even after consecration it still looks and tastes like wine, and the Bible names things by how they appear: after Cana, the steward tastes ‘the water made wine’. The key words are ‘This is my blood of the covenant, poured out for the forgiveness of sins’. Symbolic blood can’t forgive sins.”
deep.avoid: Do not claim certainty about which Passover cup is meant in each Gospel; scholars disagree.
read: Brant Pitre (2011) Jesus and the Jewish Roots of the Eucharist, chs. 6–7

hebrews|4.t: "Let us go… with confidence to the throne of grace"
hebrews|4.claim: Every Christian can approach God directly through Christ, so there is no need for priests, confession, saints or Mary as go-betweens.
why: Catholics approach God directly every day, in personal prayer and in the liturgy. The Our Father is addressed straight to the Father.
Direct access to God and asking others to pray for us are not alternatives. Paul, who had direct access, constantly asked others to pray for him (Romans 15:30; Ephesians 6:19).
Christ, who gives us direct access, also gave the apostles authority to forgive sins (John 20:23) and told the sick to call the presbyters (James 5:14).
In the liturgy, the whole Church approaches the throne together with angels and saints (Hebrews 12:22–24).
hebrews|4.cath: We approach the throne of grace with confidence, as a family that prays together, using the means Christ gave.

deep.ctx: Hebrews 4:14–16: ‘Having therefore a great high priest that hath passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God: let us hold fast our confession. For we have not a high priest, who can not have compassion on our infirmities: but one tempted in all things like as we are, without sin. Let us go therefore with confidence to the throne of grace: that we may obtain mercy, and find grace in seasonable aid.’
deep.who: Used against the ‘mediation’ of priests, saints and Mary: because of Christ every believer has direct access to God, so Catholic practices that route prayer and forgiveness through others obscure that access.
deep.lang: “Confidence” (parrēsia): boldness, freedom of speech. “Let us go” (proserchōmetha): let us keep approaching, a word used for approaching God in worship and sacrifice (10:22; 12:18, 22).
steps: Catholic prayer is constantly direct

The Mass, the Divine Office, the Our Father and most Catholic prayers are addressed directly to God the Father, through Christ, in the Holy Spirit. The Catechism describes prayer as a personal relationship with God (CCC 2558–2565).
Intercession of others is biblical alongside direct access

Paul has direct access and still says: ‘I beseech you therefore, brethren… that you help me in your prayers for me to God’ (Romans 15:30). James: ‘pray one for another, that you may be saved. For the continual prayer of a just man availeth much’ (5:16). Asking a friend, or a saint in heaven, to pray with us is not a detour around Christ; it is the Body of Christ praying together.
The plural ‘let us’ is liturgical

Hebrews envisions the community approaching together (10:19–25, ‘not forsaking our assembly’), and in 12:22–24 describes it: ‘you are come to mount Sion… and to the company of many thousands of angels, and to the church of the firstborn… and to the spirits of the just made perfect’. The saints are part of the worshipping assembly.
Christ himself gave sacramental means
The same high priest instituted confession (John 20:23) and the anointing of the sick through presbyters (James 5:14–15). Using the means Christ gave is approaching him, not avoiding him.
fathers: Origen, On Prayer 11 (c. 233)
Not only the High Priest prays with those who pray, but also the angels and the souls of the saints who have fallen asleep (paraphrased).
CCC 2683
The witnesses who have gone before us into the kingdom share in the living tradition of prayer; they contemplate God, praise him and constantly care for those on earth.
obj: “Why ask a saint when you can ask God?”

Why ask your pastor or your mother to pray for you, when you can ask God? Because God wills us to love and help one another, and ‘the prayer of a just man availeth much’. The saints are the most just people there are.
deep.talk: “Catholics go straight to God all the time; the Mass and the Our Father are addressed directly to the Father. But going directly to God doesn’t stop us asking others to pray too. Paul had direct access and still begged churches to pray for him. Hebrews 12 says when we worship we’re joined by angels and ‘the spirits of the just made perfect’. We approach the throne as a family.”
deep.avoid: Do not imply that Catholics must go through saints or Mary to reach God; they need not.

1-john|1.t: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful… to forgive"
1-john|1.claim: We confess our sins to God and he forgives us. There is no mention of a priest, so confession to a priest is unnecessary.
why: The verse says we must confess, but not to whom, or how. Scripture elsewhere specifies: "Confess your sins one to another" (James 5:16), in the context of calling the presbyters (5:14).
Jesus gave the apostles authority to forgive and retain sins (John 20:23), which requires hearing them confessed.
In the early Church, confession was public and made in church (Didache 4.14; Acts 19:18).
Catholics do confess to God; in the sacrament they confess to God through the minister Christ appointed.
1-john|1.cath: God is faithful to forgive the sins we confess, and Christ appointed a ministry through which that forgiveness is spoken.

deep.ctx: 1 John 1:5–2:2: ‘If we walk in the light, as he also is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves… If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all iniquity… My little children, these things I write to you, that you may not sin. But if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the just: and he is the propitiation for our sins’ (1:7–2:2).
deep.who: Private confession of sins directly to God is all Scripture requires. Auricular confession to a priest is a later human invention (often dated to the Fourth Lateran Council, 1215, which required annual confession).
deep.lang: “Confess” (homologōmen): to acknowledge, agree, say the same thing; often used of public acknowledgement (Matthew 10:32; Romans 10:9). It is plural: ‘if we confess’, written to a community.
steps: The verse commands confession without specifying the form
It establishes that confession leads to forgiveness. It does not exclude confession to a minister; in fact the word typically means an open acknowledgement.
Scripture elsewhere specifies a human hearer

James 5:16: ‘Confess therefore your sins one to another’, right after telling the sick to call ‘the priests (presbyterous) of the church’ (5:14). Acts 19:18: ‘many of them that believed came confessing (exomologoumenoi) and declaring their deeds’. Matthew 3:6: the people were baptized by John ‘confessing their sins’.
Christ’s commission requires confession

John 20:23: the apostles forgive or retain sins. They cannot judge which sins to retain without hearing them. Trent concluded that confession of grave sins to a priest is of divine law (Session 14, ch. 5, canon 7).
The 1215 council did not invent confession

Lateran IV required confession at least once a year: a minimum frequency for an existing practice.
