Confession and absolution are attested long before: Didache 4.14 (‘in the church thou shalt confess thy transgressions’), Origen (Homilies on Leviticus 2.4, c. 245: the sinner ‘does not shrink from declaring his sin to a priest of the Lord’), Cyprian (On the Lapsed 28), Basil (Short Rules 288).
fathers: Didache 4.14 (late 1st century)
‘In the church thou shalt acknowledge thy transgressions, and thou shalt not come to thy prayer with an evil conscience.’
Origen, Homilies on Leviticus 2.4 (c. 245)
Among the ways of remission of sins: the hard and laborious way of penance, when the sinner does not shrink from declaring his sin to the priest of the Lord and seeking remedy (paraphrased).
Basil the Great, Short Rules 288 (c. 370)
Sins must be confessed to those entrusted with the dispensation of the mysteries of God (paraphrased).
obj: “The Bible never says ‘confess to a priest’.”
James 5:14–16 links confession with calling the presbyters; John 20:23 implies hearing sins; the early Church practised it. Scripture never says ‘confess only privately to God’ either.
deep.talk: “1 John 1:9 says we have to confess, but not to whom. James tells the sick to call the presbyters and then says ‘confess your sins to one another’. Jesus told the apostles ‘whose sins you forgive are forgiven, whose sins you retain are retained’, and they can’t retain sins they’ve never heard. The Didache, from the first century, already says ‘confess your sins in church’. So confession to a priest is confessing to God, the way Christ arranged.”
deep.avoid: Do not imply private prayer of repentance is useless; it is good and necessary. Perfect contrition even restores grace before confession (CCC 1452).

john|4.t: "Adore him in spirit and in truth"
john|4.claim: True worship is inward and spiritual. Catholic liturgy, with its altars, vestments, candles, incense, images and set rituals, is the kind of external worship Jesus replaced.
why: Jesus contrasts worship confined to Mount Gerizim or Jerusalem with worship "in spirit and in truth" that is open everywhere (4:21). He is not abolishing visible worship.
The heavenly worship shown in Revelation has an altar, incense, vestments, harps, hymns and prostration (Revelation 4–5; 8:3–4).
The Incarnation means God acts through visible things: water, bread, wine, oil, the laying on of hands.
Every Christian tradition uses some outward forms: buildings, music, set times, bread and wine. The question is whether the outward expresses the inward.
john|4.cath: Worship in spirit and truth is worship in the Holy Spirit and in Christ, who is the Truth, and it takes body in the liturgy.

deep.ctx: John 4: Jesus speaks with the Samaritan woman at Jacob’s well. She raises the dispute between Samaritans and Jews: ‘Our fathers adored on this mountain [Gerizim], and you say, that at Jerusalem is the place where men must adore.’ Jesus answers: ‘Woman, believe me, that the hour cometh, when you shall neither on this mountain, nor in Jerusalem, adore the Father… But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true adorers shall adore the Father in spirit and in truth. For the Father also seeketh such to adore him. God is a spirit; and they that adore him, must adore him in spirit and in truth’ (4:20–24). She speaks of the Messiah; Jesus replies: ‘I am he’ (4:26).
deep.who: Used by Puritan and Reformed traditions (the ‘regulative principle’ of worship: only what Scripture commands is allowed) and by many evangelicals against liturgical, sacramental and sensory worship. Spiritual worship means sincere inner devotion, not ritual.
deep.lang: “In spirit and in truth” (en pneumati kai alētheia): in John, ‘Spirit’ is the Holy Spirit given by Christ (7:39; 14:17, ‘the Spirit of truth’), and ‘truth’ is Christ himself (14:6, ‘I am the way, and the truth’; 1:14, ‘full of grace and truth’). Jesus is announcing a new kind of worship made possible by himself and the Spirit, not a contrast between inner and outer.
steps: The contrast is between places, not between inner and outer

The question was where to worship: Gerizim or Jerusalem. Jesus answers that the time is coming when worship will not be tied to one holy mountain, but offered by the true worshippers everywhere: the fulfilment of Malachi 1:11 (‘in every place… a clean oblation’).
Spirit and truth are the Holy Spirit and Christ

True worship is in the Holy Spirit and in Christ, who is the Truth and the new Temple (2:19–21: ‘he spoke of the temple of his body’). Christian liturgy is exactly this: worship of the Father, through Christ, in the Spirit (CCC 1110).
Heavenly worship is full of signs

Revelation shows the elders prostrating, casting crowns, holding harps and ‘golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints’ (5:8), an angel at a golden altar with a censer (8:3–4), white robes (7:9), hymns (4:8; 5:9–14). If spiritual worship excluded signs, heaven would not be spiritual.
Christ worships with visible signs

He commanded baptism with water, the Eucharist with bread and wine, the laying on of hands and anointing (Mark 6:13; James 5:14). He used spittle and mud to heal (John 9:6) and attended the Temple feasts. God became flesh; the material world is the means he chose.
The inner must animate the outer

Catholics agree that external ritual without faith and love is worthless (Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:8). The liturgy is meant to express and nourish the heart’s worship (Sacrosanctum Concilium 11: the faithful must take part ‘with right dispositions… their minds attuned to their voices’).
fathers: Thomas Aquinas, ST II-II q.81 a.7; q.84 a.2
External worship is ordered to internal worship: we use bodily signs because we are bodily creatures, and they stir up devotion (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on John, ch. 4, lect. 2
‘In spirit’: with the fervour of the Holy Spirit; ‘in truth’: not in figures, as the Old Law did, but in the reality of Christ (paraphrased).
Sacrosanctum Concilium 7–8 (1963)
In the earthly liturgy we share by foretaste in the heavenly liturgy of the holy city.
obj: “Only what Scripture commands is allowed in worship.”
Scripture does not command church buildings, hymnals, pulpits, Sunday schools or worship bands either. And Scripture shows heavenly worship with incense and altar, which the earthly Church imitates.
deep.talk: “The Samaritan woman was asking where to worship: her mountain or Jerusalem. Jesus says soon it won’t be one holy mountain; it’ll be in the Spirit and in the Truth, which is himself. That’s what the Mass is: worship of the Father, through Christ, in the Spirit, all over the world. And the worship of heaven in Revelation has an altar, incense, robes and singing. Bodies and signs aren’t the opposite of spirit; they’re how embodied people worship.”
deep.avoid: Do not defend liturgy as merely aesthetic; ground it in the Incarnation and in Revelation.
read: Joseph Ratzinger (2000) The Spirit of the Liturgy

luke|1.t: "My spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour"
luke|1.claim: Mary calls God her Saviour, so she was a sinner who needed saving, and the Immaculate Conception is false.
why: Catholic teaching says the same: Mary needed a Saviour and was saved by Christ. The definition says she was preserved from sin "in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Saviour of the human race" (1854).
She was redeemed in a more perfect way: preserved from falling rather than lifted up after falling.
God saves from many things: sin, danger, death. "God my Saviour" is common Old Testament language (Psalm 24:5; Isaiah 12:2; Habakkuk 3:18, which Mary echoes).
Mary rejoices because "he that is mighty hath done great things to me" (1:49), which fits a singular grace.
luke|1.cath: Mary had a Saviour: Christ saved her first and most perfectly, by preserving her from all sin.

deep.ctx: After the Visitation, Elizabeth greets Mary: ‘Blessed art thou among women… blessed art thou that hast believed’ (1:42, 45). Mary responds with the Magnificat: ‘My soul doth magnify the Lord. And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour. Because he hath regarded the humility of his handmaid; for behold from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed. Because he that is mighty hath done great things to me; and holy is his name’ (1:46–49). The canticle is woven from Old Testament texts, especially Hannah’s song (1 Samuel 2:1–10).
deep.who: Only sinners need a Saviour. Mary’s words prove she knew herself to be a sinner, contradicting the Catholic doctrine that she was conceived without original sin and never sinned.
deep.lang: “God my Saviour” (tō theō tō sōtēri mou) echoes Habakkuk 3:18 (‘I will joy in God my Jesus’, in the Hebrew ‘the God of my salvation’) and Hannah’s ‘I have joyed in thy salvation’ (1 Samuel 2:1). ‘Saviour’ in the Old Testament is used of God delivering from enemies, danger and death as well as sin.
steps: The Church teaches Mary was saved by Christ

Ineffabilis Deus (1854): Mary, ‘in the first instance of her conception, by a singular grace and privilege granted by almighty God, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Saviour of the human race, was preserved free from all stain of original sin’. The doctrine affirms that Mary was redeemed. Her ‘God my Saviour’ is the Immaculate Conception in her own words.
Preservation is a more perfect redemption

Scotus’ argument: it is more perfect to preserve someone from a debt than to pay it after it is incurred. Christ, the perfect Redeemer, would redeem his mother in the most perfect way. CCC 492: Mary is ‘redeemed in a more exalted fashion, by reason of the merits of her Son’.
‘He hath done great things to me’

Mary herself attributes her privileges to God’s power. Everything she is comes from grace (Luke 1:28: ‘full of grace’, kecharitōmenē). Her humility (‘the humility of his handmaid’) is not a confession of sin but of creaturely lowliness.
Old Testament language of salvation
Hannah, David and Habakkuk call God their Saviour for deliverance from enemies and trouble. Mary sings as daughter of Zion for Israel’s salvation (1:54–55: ‘He hath received Israel his servant’).
fathers: Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus (1854)
Preserved ‘in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Saviour of the human race’.
Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.27 a.2 ad 2

Thomas held that Mary needed redemption and therefore contracted original sin; the later definition retains his principle (she needed Christ) while teaching preservation. An honest example of doctrine developing.
Bede, Homily on the Visitation (8th century)
Mary rejoices in the Saviour she bears, who is the source of her own salvation (paraphrased).
obj: “Saved from what, if she had no sin?”

From the original sin she would have contracted as a daughter of Adam, had she not been preserved; and from all the evils that come from sin. A child pulled back from a cliff edge has been saved even though he never fell.
deep.talk: “Catholics agree Mary needed a Saviour. The definition of the Immaculate Conception literally says she was preserved from sin ‘in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Saviour’. Think of it this way: you can save someone by pulling them out of a pit or by stopping them before they fall in. Both are saved; the second is saved better. Mary was saved first and best, and she sings ‘God my Saviour’ because she knew it.”
deep.avoid: Do not claim Thomas taught the Immaculate Conception; he did not. Use him for the principle that Mary needed redemption.

luke|11.t: "Yea rather, blessed are they who hear the word of God"
luke|11.claim: When a woman blessed Jesus' mother, Jesus corrected her: the truly blessed are those who hear and keep God's word. So Catholics are wrong to honour Mary so highly.
why: The Greek menoun can mean "yes indeed" as well as "rather". Jesus does not deny that his mother is blessed; he points to the deeper reason.

Mary is the supreme example of one who hears and keeps God's word: "Be it done to me according to thy word" (1:38); "blessed art thou that hast believed" (1:45); she "kept all these words, pondering them in her heart" (2:19, 51).
Luke himself records Mary's prophecy: "all generations shall call me blessed" (1:48).
Catholics honour Mary first of all for her faith and obedience, exactly as this verse teaches.
luke|11.cath: Mary is blessed twice: as mother of the Lord, and above all as the first and most faithful hearer of the word.

deep.ctx: Luke 11:27–28: ‘And it came to pass, as he spoke these things, a certain woman from the crowd, lifting up her voice, said to him: Blessed is the womb that bore thee, and the paps that gave thee suck. But he said: Yea rather, blessed are they who hear the word of God, and keep it.’ It follows a dispute in which Jesus is accused of casting out devils by Beelzebub (11:14–26).
deep.who: Jesus deflects honour from Mary to obedient believers in general. Catholic devotion to Mary, which focuses on her motherhood, goes against Jesus’ own correction.
deep.lang: “Yea rather” (menoun): a particle that can correct (‘rather’), affirm and intensify (‘yes indeed’), or both (‘yes, and more than that’). In Romans 10:18 menounge means ‘yes, verily’. The Douay ‘yea rather’ captures both.
steps: Jesus does not deny his mother is blessed

He does not say ‘No, she is not blessed’. He points to the deeper blessedness: hearing and keeping God’s word. Since Luke has already shown Mary doing exactly that, the saying praises her more, not less.
Luke presents Mary as the model hearer of the word

‘Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word’ (1:38). Elizabeth: ‘blessed art thou that hast believed, because those things shall be accomplished that were spoken to thee by the Lord’ (1:45). ‘Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart’ (2:19, 51). And in Acts she is among the praying disciples awaiting the Spirit (1:14).
Mary predicted her own honour
‘For behold from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed’ (1:48). Catholics fulfil this verse.
The Fathers saw both blessings in Mary
Augustine: Mary is more blessed in receiving the faith of Christ than in conceiving the flesh of Christ (On Holy Virginity 3). This is the Catholic emphasis: her faith comes first.
fathers: Augustine, On Holy Virginity 3 (401)
‘More blessed was Mary in receiving the faith of Christ than in conceiving the flesh of Christ’ (paraphrased).
Bede, Commentary on Luke, on 11:28 (8th century)
The Lord shows that his mother is blessed not only because she bore the Word in the flesh, but because she kept it in her heart (paraphrased).
Lumen Gentium 58 (1964)
Jesus declared blessed those who hear and keep the word, ‘as she was faithfully doing’.
obj: “If Mary were so special, Jesus would have agreed with the woman.”
He did agree, and deepened it. Notice he does not rebuke the woman. He teaches the crowd that what made his mother blessed is open to all who hear and keep the word, and she did so first.
deep.talk: “Jesus doesn’t say his mother isn’t blessed. The word can mean ‘yes, and even more’. He says the deeper blessing is hearing God’s word and keeping it. And who did that better than Mary? ‘Let it be done to me according to your word.’ Elizabeth called her blessed because she believed. Luke tells us twice she kept God’s words in her heart. That’s why Catholics honour her: first for her faith.”
deep.avoid: Do not ignore the real point of the verse, the priority of faith and obedience; Catholics agree with it.

mark|3.t: "Who is my mother and my brethren?"
mark|3.claim: When his mother and brothers came looking for him, Jesus pointed to his disciples instead. This shows he did not give his mother special honour, and that Catholics over-exalt her.
why: Jesus' answer: "whosoever shall do the will of God, he is my brother, and my sister, and mother" (3:35). He widens his family to all who do God's will, without disowning Mary.
Mary is the first to do God's will: "Be it done to me according to thy word" (Luke 1:38). She belongs to Jesus' family twice over.
Mark 3:21 ("his friends went out to lay hold on him, for they said: He is become mad") does not say Mary thought him mad; "his own" (hoi par' autou) is a general term for his relatives or associates.
Jesus honoured his mother to the last: from the Cross he entrusted her to the beloved disciple (John 19:26–27).
mark|3.cath: Jesus founds a new family of faith, and his mother is its first member.

deep.ctx: Mark 3:20–35. Crowds press around Jesus so that he cannot eat. ‘And when his friends had heard of it, they went out to lay hold on him. For they said: He is become mad’ (3:21). Scribes from Jerusalem say he casts out devils by Beelzebub (3:22–30). ‘And his mother and his brethren came; and standing without, sent unto him, calling him… And answering them, he said: Who is my mother and my brethren? And looking round about on them who sat about him, he saith: Behold my mother and my brethren. For whosoever shall do the will of God, he is my brother, and my sister, and mother’ (3:31–35).
deep.who: This scene is used to show Jesus distancing himself from Mary, and sometimes to claim that Mary thought Jesus was mad (3:21), so she cannot be the sinless, faithful woman Catholics venerate.
deep.lang: “His friends” (hoi par’ autou): literally ‘those from him’, his people, relatives or associates. It does not name Mary. The subject of ‘they said’ may even be indefinite (‘people were saying’).
steps: Jesus opens his family; he does not reject his mother

His point is that discipleship creates bonds as close as family. ‘Whosoever shall do the will of God’ belongs to his family. Mary, who did God’s will perfectly, is therefore doubly his mother: by nature and by faith.
Mary is not said to think him mad

3:21 refers to ‘his own’ (relatives or associates) and does not mention Mary. In 3:31 Mary comes with the brethren, plausibly out of concern for his safety given the hostility of the scribes. Nothing in Mark attributes unbelief to her.
Luke’s parallel highlights Mary’s faith

Luke places this saying (8:19–21) after the parable of the sower and phrases it: ‘My mother and my brethren are they who hear the word of God, and do it.’ Luke has already shown Mary as the one who hears and keeps the word (1:38, 45; 2:19, 51).
Jesus’ care for his mother continues to the Cross
John 19:25–27: Mary stands at the Cross; Jesus entrusts her to the disciple and the disciple to her.
fathers: Augustine, On Holy Virginity 3 (401)
Mary did the will of the Father, and so it is more for her to have been Christ’s disciple than his mother (paraphrased).
Lumen Gentium 58 (1964)
In the course of her Son’s preaching she received his words, ‘advanced in her pilgrimage of faith’.
obj: “Jesus deliberately didn’t go out to see her.”
He used the moment to teach; we are not told he refused to see her afterwards. Teaching through a family occasion is not a snub.
deep.talk: “Jesus isn’t rejecting his mother; he’s widening his family: whoever does God’s will is his brother, sister and mother. And nobody did God’s will like Mary: ‘Let it be done to me according to your word.’ She’s his mother twice over. And the verse about people thinking he was mad doesn’t mention Mary at all.”
deep.avoid: Do not overstate what Mary knew or understood at each moment; Luke says she pondered and did not always understand (2:50).

john|2.t: "Woman, what is that to me and to thee?"
john|2.claim: Jesus addressed his mother coldly as "Woman" and rebuffed her request at Cana. This shows he did not want her interceding, against Catholic belief in Mary's intercession.
why: "Woman" (gynai) was a respectful address; Jesus uses it from the Cross when lovingly entrusting her to John (19:26).
"What is that to me and to thee" is a Semitic idiom whose tone depends on context; it can mean "how does this concern us?" without rudeness.
Mary's response shows she did not hear a refusal: she tells the servants "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye" (2:5).
Jesus then does what she asked: his first sign, at her intercession, and "his disciples believed in him" (2:11).
john|2.cath: At Cana Mary intercedes, points to Christ, and Jesus works his first sign at her request.

deep.ctx: John 2:1–11: a wedding at Cana. ‘And the wine failing, the mother of Jesus saith to him: They have no wine. And Jesus saith to her: Woman, what is that to me and to thee? my hour is not yet come. His mother saith to the waiters: Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye.’ Jesus has six stone jars filled with water and turns it into the best wine. ‘This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee; and manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him’ (2:3–5, 11).
deep.who: Jesus rebukes Mary (‘Woman, what have I to do with you?’) for intruding, showing that she has no special role in his work and that we should not seek her intercession.
deep.lang:
“Woman” (gynai): Jesus addresses the Samaritan woman (4:21), Mary Magdalene (20:15) and his mother on the Cross (19:26) this way. Ancient writers used it as a polite and even honorific address.

“What is that to me and to thee?” (ti emoi kai soi): a Hebrew idiom (mah-li walakh) used in the Old Testament with varying tones: Judges 11:12; 2 Samuel 16:10; 1 Kings 17:18; 2 Kings 3:13. It can express hostility or simply mean ‘that is not our concern’ or ‘leave it to me’.

“My hour” in John is the hour of his Passion and glorification (7:30; 12:23; 13:1; 17:1).
steps: ‘Woman’ is not a rebuke

Jesus uses the same word on the Cross in his most tender act toward her (19:26). John uses it, in both places, to evoke ‘the woman’ of Genesis 3:15, whose offspring crushes the serpent. Mary appears in John’s Gospel only at Cana and at the Cross, the beginning and end of Jesus’ signs, both times called ‘Woman’.
Mary did not take it as a refusal
Her next words are: ‘Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye.’ She confidently instructs the servants, which she would not do if she had been rebuffed.
Jesus grants her request

He provides the wine, about 120 to 180 gallons of the best wine. His first sign is worked at his mother’s request, and it leads his disciples to faith. This is the Catholic model of Marian intercession: Mary notices a need, brings it to Jesus, and points people to him.
‘My hour’ links Cana to the Cross

By acting at Cana, Jesus begins the path to his ‘hour’. At the Cross, when the hour has come, Mary is there again, and he gives her as mother to the disciple. Her role as intercessor begins at Cana and is confirmed at Calvary.
Mary’s last recorded words
‘Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye’ are the last words of Mary recorded in the Gospels. Her whole intercession points away from herself to obedience to Christ.
fathers: Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on John, ch. 2, lect. 1
Mary’s request shows her compassion and confidence; Christ’s answer does not refuse but teaches that the miracle comes from his divinity, not from what he received from her (paraphrased).
John Paul II, Redemptoris Mater 21 (1987)
At Cana Mary puts herself between her Son and mankind in their needs; she acts as a mediator, not as an outsider, but in her position as mother (paraphrased).
obj: “The idiom always means ‘leave me alone’.”
Not always. In 2 Kings 3:13 and 2 Samuel 16:10 it marks disagreement but not contempt. And here the outcome decides: Jesus does what she asked.
deep.talk: “‘Woman’ wasn’t rude; Jesus calls her the same thing from the Cross when he gives her to John as his mother. And watch what happens: Mary tells the servants ‘do whatever he tells you’, and Jesus does exactly what she asked, his very first miracle. That’s what Catholics mean by Mary’s intercession: she notices our needs, brings them to Jesus, and tells us to do what he says.”
deep.avoid: Do not claim Mary forced Jesus’ hand; he acts freely. Emphasize her role as pointing to Christ.

acts|4.t: "There is no other name… whereby we must be saved"
acts|4.claim: Salvation is in Jesus' name alone. So praying to Mary and the saints, using sacramentals, or seeking their help gives credit to "other names".
why: Catholics believe exactly this: salvation is only in Jesus. The saints are not saviours; they are saved by him.
The saints' prayers are made "through Christ our Lord", in his name. Asking them to pray for us is asking them to pray in Jesus' name.
Peter speaks these words right after healing a lame man "in the name of Jesus Christ" (4:10) through his own apostolic ministry: Christ saves through his servants without sharing his name with them.
In context Peter is answering the Sanhedrin, which rejected Jesus: no other Messiah, no other covenant, saves.
acts|4.cath: One name saves: Jesus. Every Christian, in heaven or on earth, prays and works in that name.

deep.ctx: Acts 3–4: Peter and John heal a man lame from birth at the Temple gate ‘in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth’ (3:6). Arrested and brought before the Sanhedrin, Peter, ‘filled with the Holy Ghost’, declares: ‘be it known to you all… that by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God hath raised from the dead, even by him, this man standeth here before you whole… Neither is there salvation in any other. For there is no other name under heaven given to men, whereby we must be saved’ (4:10, 12).
deep.who: Since only Jesus’ name saves, asking the saints for help is calling on other names. Catholics pray the Litany of the Saints; that is calling on many names.
deep.lang: “Name” (onoma) in Scripture means the person and his power and authority. ‘In the name of Jesus’ means by his authority and power.
steps: Catholics affirm it fully
‘There is no salvation outside Christ’ (CCC 846 and the whole Catechism). Every grace the saints received and every grace they obtain for us comes through Christ alone.
The apostles acted in Jesus’ name

Peter’s point is that the healing came by Jesus’ name, through Peter’s ministry. Christ works through his servants. The same is true of the saints’ intercession: they pray through Christ, and God answers through Christ.
Asking a saint’s prayer is asking for prayer in Jesus’ name
The Church’s liturgical prayer to the saints asks: ‘pray for us’. They do not save; they pray. Every collect for a saint’s feast ends ‘through our Lord Jesus Christ’.
The context is the Sanhedrin’s rejection of Jesus

Peter tells the religious authorities that they cannot be saved by rejecting Jesus: no other Messiah, no other way of salvation exists. The verse is about Christ’s uniqueness, which Catholics proclaim.
fathers: Cyril of Jerusalem, Mystagogical Catecheses 5.9 (c. 350)
We commemorate the saints so that God, at their prayers and intercessions, would receive our petition (paraphrased): their prayer is always directed to God.
The name of Jesus is at the heart of Christian prayer; all liturgical prayer concludes ‘through our Lord Jesus Christ’.
obj: “A litany calling on dozens of saints obscures Christ.”
Each invocation is ‘pray for us’; the litany begins with ‘Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy’ and addresses the Trinity directly. It is the communion of saints praying together through Christ.
deep.talk: “Catholics believe Jesus is the only Saviour, period. The saints aren’t saviours; they were saved by him. When we ask them to pray for us, they pray in Jesus’ name, just like when you ask your friends to pray. Peter healed that lame man through his own ministry, but in Jesus’ name. That’s how God works: through his people, always through Jesus.”
deep.avoid: Do not use language that suggests saints save; say they pray for us.

revelation|19.t: "See thou do it not… adore God"
revelation|19.claim: John fell down to worship an angel and was rebuked. So it is wrong to bow before or honour angels and saints.
why: John, an apostle, did this twice (19:10; 22:8–9). He would have known not to worship a creature; he was overwhelmed by a being he may have taken for divine, or showed a reverence the angel humbly declined.
The angel's reason is that he is a "fellow servant" of John and of those who have "the testimony of Jesus". Worship belongs to God alone.
Elsewhere Scripture shows reverence to angels without rebuke: Joshua falls on his face before the commander of the Lord's army (Joshua 5:14–15); Lot bows before angels (Genesis 19:1).
Catholics worship God alone (latria) and honour angels and saints (dulia). This verse condemns worship, not honour.
revelation|19.cath: Adoration is for God alone; the angels and saints are our fellow servants, whom we honour and with whom we worship.

deep.ctx: Revelation 19:9–10: the angel tells John to write ‘Blessed are they that are called to the marriage supper of the Lamb’. ‘And I fell down before his feet, to adore him. And he saith to me: See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren, who have the testimony of Jesus. Adore God. For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.’ The same happens in 22:8–9.
deep.who: Used against any reverence (kneeling, bowing, praying) toward angels, saints or Mary: if the apostle John was forbidden to fall before an angel, Catholics are forbidden to kneel before statues of saints or pray to them.
deep.lang: “Adore” (proskynēsai): prostrate oneself; here in the sense of worship, since the angel answers ‘Adore God’.
steps: What the angel forbids is worship
The angel’s reply contrasts himself (‘fellow servant’) with God (‘Adore God’). He forbids treating him as divine. Catholics agree: only God receives latria (CCC 2096).
John’s action shows how overwhelming the vision was

John, an apostle who had written ‘Little children, keep yourselves from idols’ (1 John 5:21), would not knowingly commit idolatry. He fell before the angel twice, perhaps mistaking him for the Lord or giving excessive reverence. The angel corrects with humility, as a fellow servant.
Reverence to angels is shown elsewhere without rebuke

Joshua falls on his face before the commander of the Lord’s army, who tells him to take off his shoes (Joshua 5:14–15). Lot bows to the ground before the two angels (Genesis 19:1). Balaam bows before the angel (Numbers 22:31). The difference is between honour and worship.
Angels and saints are fellow servants with whom we worship

The angel’s words express the communion of saints: angels, prophets and believers are one family serving God. At every Mass the Church sings the Sanctus ‘with the angels and archangels and with all the company of heaven’.
fathers: Augustine, City of God X.7 (c. 420)
The holy angels do not wish us to sacrifice to them but to God, whose sacrifice they know themselves to be along with us (paraphrased).
Thomas Aquinas, ST II-II q.84 a.1 ad 1; q.103 a.3–4
Adoration due to God is latria; the reverence due to creatures of excellence is dulia, distinct in kind.
obj: “Bowing to statues is exactly what John did.”

John’s act was meant as adoration, which the angel refused. A Catholic bowing before a statue of a saint is giving honour, not adoration, and the saint is not even physically present. Intention decides.
deep.talk: “The angel refused worship, and Catholics agree: we worship God alone. But reverence isn’t always worship. Joshua fell on his face before an angel and was told to take his shoes off, not rebuked. Catholics honour angels and saints as fellow servants of God, and we worship God together with them at every Mass.”
deep.avoid: Do not deny that excessive or superstitious devotion can happen; correct it with the distinction between latria and dulia.

hebrews|9.t: "Once to die, and after this the judgment"
hebrews|9.claim: Death is followed immediately by judgment, which settles each person's destiny for good. There is no room for an intermediate purgatory or for prayers to help the dead.
why: Catholic teaching agrees: at death each person receives the particular judgment, and his eternal destiny is fixed (CCC 1021–1022).
Purgatory comes after the judgment for those judged to be saved but not yet perfect. It does not change anyone's destiny; it prepares the saved for heaven.
Hebrews 9:27 does not describe what follows judgment for the saved; Hebrews 12:23 speaks of "the spirits of the just made perfect", implying perfecting.
The verse also rules out reincarnation, which Catholics also reject.
hebrews|9.cath: Judgment at death decides each soul's eternal destiny; purification afterwards prepares the saved for glory.

deep.ctx: Hebrews 9:24–28: Christ entered heaven ‘to appear now in the presence of God for us’, not to offer himself often, ‘but now once at the end of ages, he hath appeared for the destruction of sin, by the sacrifice of himself. And as it is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment: so also Christ was offered once to exhaust the sins of many; the second time he shall appear without sin to them that expect him unto salvation’ (9:26–28).
deep.who: The sequence ‘death, then judgment’ leaves no room for a time of purification or for prayers after death to make any difference: one’s fate is sealed at death.
deep.lang: “Appointed” (apokeitai): laid up, reserved. “Once” (hapax): death happens once. “Judgment” (krisis).
steps: The verse’s point is the analogy with Christ
As human beings die once, Christ was offered once. The verse is about the uniqueness of Christ’s sacrifice, not a detailed eschatology.
Catholics affirm judgment immediately after death
The ‘particular judgment’: ‘each man receives his eternal retribution in his immortal soul at the very moment of his death’ (CCC 1022). Heaven (immediately or through purification) or hell.
Purgatory follows judgment, it does not replace it
The souls in purgatory have been judged and are saved. Purgatory is not a second chance; it is the completion of the work in those already judged to be God’s.
Hebrews implies perfection after death
Hebrews 12:23: ‘the spirits of the just made perfect (teteleiōmenōn)’. The just are ‘made perfect’, which fits a final purification.
Prayers for the dead help those already judged as saved

They do not change anyone’s eternal destiny; they help the saved through their purification (2 Maccabees 12:46: ‘It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins’).
fathers: Council of Lyons II (1274) and Benedict XII, Benedictus Deus (1336)
Souls are judged immediately after death; those needing purification are purified, others enter heaven at once, the damned go to hell (paraphrased).
Death puts an end to human life as the time open to accepting or rejecting grace; each person receives particular judgment.
obj: “If destiny is fixed, prayer for the dead is pointless.”
Prayer does not change their destiny; it helps their purification, as Christians help one another in this life. The communion of saints continues after death.
deep.talk: “Catholics completely agree: you die once, then you’re judged, and your eternal destiny is settled. Purgatory isn’t a second chance; it’s for people already judged as saved who aren’t perfect yet. Hebrews 12 even talks about ‘the spirits of the just made perfect’. Our prayers help them along the way to heaven.”
deep.avoid: Do not imply purgatory is a place where people can still be lost or saved.

1-timothy|3.t: "A bishop… the husband of one wife"
1-timothy|3.claim: Paul requires a bishop to be married. So the Catholic requirement of celibacy for bishops and (Latin) priests contradicts Scripture.
why: The point is "of one wife": a bishop must not have remarried or be unfaithful. Paul is setting a maximum, not requiring marriage.
Paul himself was unmarried (1 Corinthians 7:7–8) and recommends celibacy for those who can accept it, because the unmarried man "is solicitous for the things that belong to the Lord" (7:32).
Timothy, to whom the letter is written and who ordained presbyters, was apparently unmarried; if the rule required marriage, Paul and Timothy would be disqualified.
Eastern Catholic Churches ordain married men as priests; celibacy in the Latin Church is a discipline, not a doctrine that marriage is wrong.
1-timothy|3.cath: Paul forbids remarried or unfaithful men as bishops; he does not command bishops to marry, and he praises celibacy for the kingdom.

deep.ctx: 1 Timothy 3:1–7 lists qualifications for a bishop (episkopos): ‘It behoveth therefore a bishop to be blameless, the husband of one wife, sober, prudent, of good behaviour, chaste, given to hospitality, a teacher, not given to wine, no striker, but modest, not quarrelsome, not covetous, but one that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all chastity’ (3:2–4). Similar lists apply to deacons (3:8–13) and presbyters (Titus 1:5–9).
deep.who: Paul’s list requires bishops (and presbyters, Titus 1:6) to be married men with children. Rome’s requirement of celibacy imposes a rule Scripture contradicts, and some add 1 Timothy 4:3 (‘forbidding to marry’).
deep.lang: “Husband of one wife” (mias gynaikos andra): literally ‘a one-woman man’. The emphasis falls on ‘one’ (mias). Paul uses the parallel phrase for widows enrolled by the Church: ‘the wife of one husband’ (5:9), meaning married only once.
steps: The emphasis is ‘one’

‘A one-woman man’ excludes polygamy, divorce and remarriage, and unfaithfulness. The early Church read it as excluding men married twice (digamy), the same sense as ‘wife of one husband’ for widows (5:9). It sets a limit, not a requirement.
Taken literally, it would disqualify Paul and Timothy

Paul was unmarried and wished others were like him (1 Corinthians 7:7–8). Timothy appears to have been unmarried. If marriage were required, the apostle writing the rule and the bishop receiving it would be disqualified, as would widowers and childless men.
Paul and Jesus praise celibacy for the kingdom

Jesus: ‘there are eunuchs, who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. He that can take, let him take it’ (Matthew 19:12). Paul: ‘he that is without a wife, is solicitous for the things that belong to the Lord… but he that is with a wife, is solicitous for the things of the world… and he is divided’ (1 Corinthians 7:32–33). Peter: ‘we have left all things’ (Matthew 19:27–29).
Celibacy is a discipline, not doctrine

The Catholic Church has married priests in the Eastern Catholic Churches and some convert clergy in the Latin Church. Celibacy for Latin priests grew from early discipline (the Council of Elvira, c. 305, required clerical continence) and became universal law in the West in the Middle Ages. It is changeable in principle; the Church keeps it because it configures the priest to Christ and frees him for service (CCC 1579–1580).
fathers: Tertullian, To His Wife I.7 (c. 205)
Notes that men married twice are not admitted to the priesthood (paraphrased), the early understanding of ‘husband of one wife’.
Council of Elvira, canon 33 (c. 305)
Requires bishops, presbyters and deacons to abstain from relations with their wives.
Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on 1 Timothy, ch. 3, lect. 1
Paul does not command a bishop to have a wife, but forbids one who has had more than one (paraphrased).
obj: “Peter was married (Mark 1:30).”

Yes, and Catholics have never said marriage is incompatible with ordination as such; the Eastern Churches show it. But Peter also says he ‘left all things’ to follow Christ (Matthew 19:27), and the discipline of celibacy is a legitimate development the Church may choose.
deep.talk: “The emphasis is on ‘one’: a one-woman man, not remarried or unfaithful. Paul used the same phrase for widows: ‘wife of one husband’. If he meant bishops had to be married, he’d have disqualified himself, since he wasn’t married and wished others were like him. And the Catholic Church does have married priests in the Eastern Catholic Churches; celibacy in the West is a discipline, not a teaching that marriage is bad.”
deep.avoid: Do not argue that celibacy is required by divine law; it is not.
read: Christian Cochini (1990) Apostolic Origins of Priestly Celibacy. San Francisco: Ignatius Press
